title: DexGraspFlow: Topology-Aware SE(3) Flow Matching for Cross-Embodiment Dexterous Grasp Generation
summary: Differences in hand geometry, joint parameterization, and kinematic topology pose challenges for cross-embodiment dexterous grasp generation. However, spatial relations among links alone are insufficient to fully capture the hand's kinematic topology. We propose DexGraspFlow, a conditional link-level $\mathrm{SE}(3)$ flow-matching framework integrating geometric relations and kinematic topology. The framework encodes local object geometry, link geometry, and current poses. A dual-stream DiT models link--link coordination and link--object interaction, while attention biases derived from kinematic-tree distances provide explicit structural information for modeling evolving geometric interactions. The model jointly learns translational and rotational velocity fields, integrates them to generate link poses, and recovers joint configurations through inverse kinematics. Additionally, inference-time palm-orientation guidance enables controllable grasp generation without retraining. Across three robotic hands and 30 object--hand pairs, DexGraspFlow achieves a 95.33\% average simulation success rate, with an average generation latency, including inverse kinematics, approximately 49\% lower than that of a state-of-the-art baseline. Further experiments demonstrate zero-shot adaptability to seven finger-removal variants and palm-orientation control. A model trained on demonstrations for the deployed hand achieves a 91\% success rate over 100 real-robot grasping trials, supporting the framework's applicability to physical grasp execution.
full_text: Introduction Dexterous hands are robotic end-effectors that interact directly with the physical world, performing the last centimeter of robotic manipulation. Through coordinated finger motions, they enable versatile grasping and precise manipulation, supporting the practical deployment of embodied intelligence dong2026learning,wang2026lifelong . Reliable dexterous grasping requires jointly accounting for object geometry, hand--object interactions, and kinematic constraints dexgraspnet . Differences in link geometry and kinematic topology across hands further complicate cross-embodiment grasp generation. Embodiment-specific joint representations differ in dimensionality and physical meaning, making it difficult to learn a unified model directly from grasp demonstrations collected across different hands gendexgrasp . Training a separate model for each hand also increases training and deployment costs. These challenges motivate cross-embodiment dexterous grasp generation methods that share grasping knowledge while accommodating differences in hand morphology and kinematics, facilitating the reuse of grasping capabilities across robotic platforms. Existing approaches address cross-embodiment grasp synthesis through optimization or shared interaction representations. Optimization-based methods require computationally intensive iterative search for each grasp instance~ dfc , while contact- and distance-based formulations necessitate auxiliary matching or complex reconstruction to recover executable configurations~ gendexgrasp,dro . Recently, Grasp (TRO-Grasp) introduced a transformation-graph diffusion model via object-centric link poses and relative spatial relations without requiring a shared joint parameterization~ tro . However, relying solely on continuous spatial relations ignores kinematic topology: spatially adjacent links across diverse hands may belong to distant topological branches with fundamentally different kinematic meanings. GraspGraphNet~ graspgraphnet incorporates kinematic structure through local message passing, but propagating information between distant links along the kinematic tree requires multiple graph hops. Beyond unconditioned synthesis, practical deployment also requires efficient control over grasp approach orientations while maintaining grasp stability across different hand embodiments. To this end, we propose DexGraspFlow, a cross-embodiment dexterous grasp synthesis framework that unifies continuous flow matching with URDF-derived kinematic topology (Fig.~ fig:method_overview ). To resolve structural ambiguities across heterogeneous hands, DexGraspFlow augments dynamic link states and spatial relations with kinematic-tree shortest-path distances, providing complementary geometric and structural information that explicitly separates spatial arrangement from kinematic connectivity. Grasp synthesis is formulated as link-level flow matching with separate translational reference paths in and geodesic rotational reference paths on ~ flow,RFM . This formulation preserves valid link orientations and supports inference-time palm-orientation guidance through tangent-space velocity corrections without retraining. A geometry- and topology-aware dual-stream DiT~ dit predicts these coupled velocity fields, followed by batched inverse kinematics~ pyroki to recover executable joint configurations. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec:related_work reviews related work on cross-embodiment grasp representations and geometric generative models. Section~ sec:framework presents the grasp representation and geometry- and topology-aware dual-stream DiT architecture of DexGraspFlow. Section~ sec:experiments evaluates DexGraspFlow through grasp generation on unseen objects, zero-shot generation on finger-removal variants, and palm-orientation-conditioned generation, along with ablation studies and real-robot experiments. Section~ sec:conclusion_limitations concludes the study and discusses the limitations of the proposed framework and directions for future research. The main contributions of this work are as follows: We address the core discrepancy that geometric spatial relations do not reflect kinematic topological connectivity across diverse embodiments, proposing a topology-aware link representation that couples dynamic spatial interactions with kinematic-tree distances to preserve structural coordination under hand topology changes. We formulate grasp synthesis via link-level flow matching that couples Euclidean translation with Riemannian rotation on , and design a geometry- and topology-aware dual-stream DiT, demonstrating superior grasp success with substantially reduced generation latency compared to diffusion baselines in our empirical evaluations. We propose a training-free directional grasp guidance formulation. By injecting geodesic velocity corrections directly into the tangent space of the continuous flow during inference, DexGraspFlow achieves high-precision, user-specified palm-orientation steering without requiring conditional retraining or auxiliary classifiers. We conduct extensive empirical evaluations across multi-embodiment simulations, zero-shot generalization to seven finger-removal variants, and 100 real-robot physical trials (91 success rate), demonstrating the superior adaptability and physical viability of DexGraspFlow. Related work sec:related_work Cross-embodiment grasp representations GraspIt!~ graspit supports optimization-based grasp planning, while DFC~ dfc and DexGraspNet~ dexgraspnet employ iterative optimization for grasp synthesis and dataset construction, incurring per-instance computational costs. FFHNet~ ffhnet and UniDexGrasp~ unidexgrasp represent grasp configurations through global hand poses and joint coordinates, while UniDexGrasp++~ unidexgraspplus learns grasping policies for a hand-specific state and action space. However, differences in joint dimensionality and semantics complicate sharing these configurations across embodiments, motivating hand--object interaction representations that do not require a common joint parameterization. GenDexGrasp~ gendexgrasp uses hand-agnostic contact maps and recovers hand configurations through contact matching and optimization. Grasp (DRO-Grasp)~ dro predicts robot--object point-to-point distances using a configuration-invariant pretrained hand encoder, followed by link-pose reconstruction and joint-configuration recovery. Its dense pairwise representation incurs memory overhead, while encoder pretraining adds a separate training stage. TRO-Grasp~ tro models hands via relative spatial transformations on fully connected link--object and link--link edges. However, spatial link proximity alone is insufficient across diverse embodiments, as spatially adjacent links can belong to disparate topological branches that convey fundamentally different kinematic semantics. Alternatively, GraspGraphNet~ graspgraphnet encodes articulated hand states using a kinematic-tree MPNN and incorporates object information through cross-attention and dynamic interaction edges. Within its kinematic-tree encoder, information exchange between distant links relies on successive local message-passing steps. DexGraspFlow instead uses link--link self-attention to directly model interactions between all valid link pairs, with kinematic-tree distance biases providing structural information alongside state-dependent geometric relations. This design combines direct long-range link interaction with explicit kinematic proximity encoding. Geometric generative models Generative grasp synthesis has been explored through adversarial and diffusion models~ dexgangrasp,dexdiffuser,dexgraspnet2 , drawing on broader denoising and score-based formulations~ ddpm,scoresde . Flow-based approaches learn continuous transport dynamics in Euclidean and non-Euclidean spaces~ flow,rectified_flow,RFM . Complementary advances in equivariant geometric modeling~ se3transformer,egnn , diffusion-based grasp and motion optimization~ se3diffusionfields , and Transformer generative architectures~ dit provide foundations for geometry-aware generation. For cross-embodiment grasping, these formulations differ in their conditioning requirements and the computational path to executable grasps. DRO-Grasp~ dro combines CVAE latent variables with features of an initial hand configuration and the object to predict grasp distances. Although latent sampling enables diversity, generation remains conditioned on the initial hand state and requires subsequent pose reconstruction. TRO-Grasp~ tro instead samples link poses from noise through graph diffusion in Lie-algebra coordinates. Its denoiser processes node and edge features through multiple graph layers, with repeated evaluations accumulating sampling costs. DexGraspFlow adopts link-level \( (3)\) flow matching, jointly learning translational and rotational velocities from Euclidean and geodesic reference paths, respectively. Geometric interactions and kinematic topology condition the velocity field within a unified formulation supporting both unconditioned and condition-guided grasp generation. Our experiments demonstrate lower generation latency than DRO-Grasp and TRO-Grasp while maintaining competitive grasp success. DexGraspFlow framework sec:framework DexGraspFlow generates cross-embodiment dexterous grasps by conditioning continuous flow matching on object geometry, hand morphology, and kinematic topology (Fig.~ fig:method_overview ). First, the object and hand encoders extract object-patch tokens and static link tokens from object and local link point clouds, respectively (Sec.~ sec:geometry_encoding ). Next, grasp generation is formulated as link-level flow matching (Sec.~ sec:link_flow_matching ), where a geometry- and topology-aware dual-stream DiT jointly predicts translational and rotational velocities via parallel link--link and link--object attention (Sec.~ sec:dual_stream_network ). Finally, flow integration can be steered via training-free velocity corrections for palm-orientation guidance, after which batched inverse kinematics resolves the generated link poses into executable joint configurations (Sec.~ sec:guided_sampling_recovery ). The point clouds describe object and link geometry, while the URDF specifies the hand's kinematic tree and link connectivity~ fktree . This link-level representation accommodates different hand embodiments without requiring a shared joint parameterization. title: EGGHead: Efficient Generalizable Gaussian Heads from a Single Image
summary: Creating photorealistic human heads typically involves trade-offs between representation power, efficiency, and generalizability. Traditional mesh-based solutions relying on 3DMMs generally sacrifice representation power but are efficient to render. On the other hand, NeRF-based methods improve representation power and fidelity while sacrificing efficiency. Gaussian splatting methods attempt to resolve these trade-offs by offering both high representation power and efficiency with real-time rendering. However, their efficiency nonetheless depends on the number of rasterized Gaussians, and the time needed to optimize and prepare the head (the enrollment time) is often high. In light of this, we propose EGGHead, which introduces a novel Gaussian allocation algorithm that efficiently assigns Gaussians to the head's semantic regions given a fixed Gaussian budget. Our algorithm reduces the number of Gaussians needed while minimizing the impact on representation power. EGGHead operates in a single forward pass and outperforms previous single-image face modeling methods in reconstruction quality, novel view synthesis, and rendering speeds.

Traditional mesh-based solutions relying on DMMs generally sacrifice representation power but are efficient to render. On the other hand, NeRF-based methods improve representation power and fidelity while sacrificing efficiency. Gaussian splatting methods attempt to resolve these trade-offs by offering both high representation power and efficiency with real-time rendering. Our algorithm reduces the number of Gaussians needed while minimizing the impact on representation power. EGGHead operates in a single forward pass and outperforms previous single-image face modeling methods in reconstruction quality, novel view synthesis, and rendering speeds. Introduction sec:intro Modeling photorealistic human heads has received widespread attention from the computer vision and graphics communities. It has a wide array of applications, including movie production~ therelightables , digital humans in AR/VR~ park2021nerfies, gaussianheadavatar, relightablegaussianavatars, NeRFace , and downstream tasks in the face domain~ joint-face-alignment, disentangling-features . There are several important axes to consider when designing a head reconstruction method, including representation power, the efficiency of the D representation, and data requirements. An ideal method produces a high-quality head that captures fine identity details, enables real-time generation and novel view synthesis, and requires minimal data. Traditional head representation methods adopt mesh-based approaches that rely on DMMs~ 3DMM to model the face. Although generally efficient to rasterize and render, and despite a plethora of single-image based methods~ wang2022faceverse, towards-high-fidelity-nonlinear-3d-face-morphable-model, UncertaintyFaceReconstruction, LuanCVPR18, MonocularNeuralReflectance , these D representations generally lack high representation power due to reliance on PCA bases, carrying over artifacts from intrinsic decomposition into rendering. The follow-up methods~ park2021nerfies, park2021hypernerf, infamousnerf, NeRFace, zhuang2022mofanerf, hong2021headnerf relied instead on the implicit NeRF~ NeRF representation, which allowed for higher representation power thanks to per-pixel raytracing, the ability to model view-specific texture variations, and the volumetric rendering design. However, NeRF-based methods sacrifice efficiency since the raytracing inference stage is often costly. More recently, the face modeling community has favored mesh-driven 3D Gaussian Splatting~ gaussiansplatting (3D-GS): a hybrid explicit-implicit representation that allows for both high fidelity and real-time rendering. Gaussian Splatting, however, is not without limitations. While considered a representation that enables real-time rendering, the efficiency is still affected by the number of Gaussians used to represent the head. In practice, high-quality Gaussian heads require a large number of Gaussians to capture fine geometric and appearance details. Reducing the number of Gaussians is thus an important priority, but if done naively will simply reduce the head's fidelity. To address this trade-off between fidelity and efficiency, we propose a novel Gaussian Allocation Module (GAM), which efficiently allocates a fixed budget of Gaussians while minimizing the impact on the head's fidelity. Moreover, 3D-GS traditionally relies on monocular or multi-view image/video inputs, is trained per subject instead of being generalizable, and requires an expensive optimization for each subject ranging from a few minutes to one hour~ qiangaussianavatars, chen2024monogaussianavatar, gaussianheadavatar . GPS-Gaussian~ Zheng2023GPSGaussianGP resolves some of these limitations by producing a generalizable method that takes a stereo pair of images as input and predicts Gaussian attributes. However, it requires a monocular video as input, since the method depends on the nearest-neighbor stereo pair for each queried viewpoint. Moreover, it makes the naive assumption of assigning one Gaussian to each pixel, which will naturally reduce the rendering speed. We instead reduce this requirement from a monocular video to a single image while also proposing a generalizable method given one image as input. Our novel GAM improves rendering speed by allocating Gaussians over semantic regions rather than on a per-pixel basis, achieving high fidelity with fewer Gaussians. In addition, we employ Voronoi tessellation~ Budninskiy2016OptimalVT to guide Gaussian attribute computation in a single-view setting with sparse Gaussians. Finally, we introduce a lightweight, network-free Face Symmetry Module to render occluded face regions, avoiding expensive post-processing networks and diffusion-based multi-view generation during inference. Our contributions are thus as follows: We propose EGGHead, a single-image and generalizable Gaussian head model that outperforms existing approaches in rendering quality and speed while achieving competitive enrollment time. We introduce a Gaussian Allocation Module (GAM) that allocates Gaussians under a fixed budget with minimal impact, employ Voronoi tessellation to guide Gaussian shape computation in a single-view setting with sparse Gaussians, and incorporate a lightweight Face Symmetry Module to improve head completeness without relying on additional networks. We demonstrate superior head representation capabilities and fidelity among single-image head reconstruction methods, both quantitatively and qualitatively. Related Work sec:rw Face Modeling. Existing D face representations include explicit mesh-based methods~ LuanCVPR18, 3d-face-modeling-from-diverse-raw-scan-data, towards-high-fidelity-nonlinear-3d-face-morphable-model, TowardsHighFidelityFaceReconstruction, face-relighting-with-geometrically-consistent-shadows, disentangling-features, wang2022faceverse, UncertaintyFaceReconstruction, MonocularNeuralReflectance, shang2020self, joint-face-alignment, riggable-3d-face-reconstruction-via-in-network-optimization, DFNRMVS, on-learning-3d-face-morphable-model-from-in-the-wild-images , implicit NeRF-based~ NeRF methods~ NeRFace, LOLNeRF, park2021nerfies, 3DMM-RF, RigNeRF, NHA, park2021hypernerf, Gao-portraitnerf, CompositionalRF, zhuang2022mofanerf, hong2021headnerf, chanmonteiro2020pi-GAN, zhang2022fdnerf, infamousnerf , diffusion models conditioned with D priors~ diffusionrig, Kant2025Pippo , D-aware GANs that incorporate triplane representations~ PanoHead, lan2022e3dge, EG3D, stylenerf, QuantManip, NeRFInvertor, shi2023pof3d, GRAF, GeoD, deng2022gram, yu25gaia, he2025head , and D Gaussian Splatting ( D-GS)~ gaussiansplatting, relightablegaussianavatars, gagavatar, qiangaussianavatars, ma2024gaussianblendshapes, chen2024monogaussianavatar, shao2024splattingavatar, gaussianheadavatar, TaoAvatar, tang2024gaf, WangARXIV2025, kirschstein2024gghead . Mesh-based 3DMMs~ 3DMM enable fast rendering but are limited in fidelity by their PCA basis. NeRF-based methods improve fidelity through view-dependent neural rendering, but require costly ray sampling. 3D-GS offers high-quality real-time rendering, yet its efficiency depends on the number of Gaussians and still requires seconds to minutes of per-subject enrollment. To address this, we introduce EGGHead, a generalizable model that effectively reduces the Gaussian budget. Generalizable Gaussian Splatting. Although 3D-GS is traditionally optimized per scene or subject, generalizable 3D-GS methods have recently gained attention. GPS-Gaussian~ Zheng2023GPSGaussianGP synthesizes unseen identities but assigns one Gaussian per pixel, limiting efficiency. GAGAvatar~ gagavatar predicts Gaussians from a single image using FLAME~ FLAME and dual lifting, but its additional neural renderer may compromise identity consistency. Diffusion-based methods~ cap4d, facelift achieve high quality but rely on costly multi-view generation. In contrast, EGGHead uses GAM to merge Gaussians in fidelity-insensitive regions, avoiding dense per-pixel allocation, and multi-view generation. Efficient Gaussian Splatting. Several methods improve the efficiency of D-GS by compressing Gaussian parameters or pruning low-impact Gaussians. Compression methods~ Lee_2024_CVPR, Niedermayr_2024_CVPR, navaneet2023compact3d reduce storage and rendering costs by removing parameter redundancy, while pruning-based methods~ fan2023lightgaussian, eagles, reducingmemfootprintGS reduce the Gaussian count. However, they still rely on costly multi-view optimization. In contrast, our GAM operates from a single image and directly allocates a compact set of Gaussians. Symmetry in Face Modeling. Face symmetry is a strong prior that preserves the naturally symmetrical structure of human faces, especially in the ill-posed single-image setting where occluded regions rely on face priors to be properly reconstructed. While previous methods~ 3DFaceFill,towards-high-fidelity-nonlinear-3d-face-morphable-model,FFHQUV impose symmetry as a loss function to guide networks toward symmetric D face reconstruction, EGGHead introduces a lightweight Face Symmetry Module that directly mirrors visible Gaussians across the facial symmetry plane to complement occluded regions without additional networks. Method sec:method Problem Formulation. Given a single source image , our goal is to reconstruct a photorealistic head of an unseen subject. To tackle this non-trivial task, we employ the D Gaussian Splatting ( D-GS) pipeline~ gaussiansplatting . D-GS models a scene with a set of D Gaussians, each defined by a D covariance matrix and a center (mean) position : Each Gaussian is parameterized by where is the center position, is the rotation quaternion, is the scaling factor, is the opacity, and is the color. Applying D-GS to our task is non-trivial, as we aim to render novel views under (1) a single-view setting, (2) a generalizable model without per-subject fine-tuning, and (3) a reduced number of Gaussians rather than a per-pixel allocation. We explain our solution in the following sections. Architecture. Fig.~ fig2 illustrates our pipeline. Given a single source image, our approach generates a photorealistic head representation using a fixed Gaussian budget without per-subject optimization. During training, we introduce the Gaussian Allocation Module (GAM) to achieve an effective trade-off between the number of Gaussians and rendering quality (Sec.~ sec:gaussianallocation ). We employ a Gaussian Attribute Regressor to predict Gaussian attribute maps (Sec.~ sec:gspred ), guided by Voronoi tessellation~ Budninskiy2016OptimalVT for more accurate shape computation (Sec.~ sec:voronoi ). The framework is trained to minimize the difference between the rendered and input images (Sec.~ sec:training ). In inference, GAM is replaced with density-based sampling for efficiency (Sec.~ sec:sampling ), and a Face Symmetry Module completes the occluded regions (Sec.~ sec:symm ). Gaussian Allocation Module sec:gaussianallocation Our objective is to efficiently allocate a fixed Gaussian budget while preserving rendering quality. title: Beckmann World Models: Direct Terminal-Map Learning for One-Step Action-Conditioned Prediction
summary: Action-conditioned world models support planning and policy evaluation by predicting future states. However, learning an accurate one-step predictor can require substantial training computation. We introduce Beckmann World Models (BWM), which learn a direct map from noise, visual history, and actions to future frames without a pretrained generative teacher. We adapt the terminal-map conservation law of Beckmann Transport Models to action-conditioned video prediction, training directly from noise-data pairs without conditional populations of generated samples required by DriftWorld. However, transport consistency on interpolated inputs does not ensure accurate prediction from the pure noise used at inference. We address this gap with endpoint-aligned training that directly supervises the source prediction, emphasizes motion and spatial structure, and teaches recovery from generated histories. All components train the same map and retain one network call per future chunk. On PushT and Robomimic Can, the final model reduces 64-frame prediction MSE by 68% and 57%, respectively, relative to same-backbone regression baseline. For policy evaluation, BWM achieves the lowest mean IoU error among the evaluated models, 0.0100, at 24.8 ms per four-frame PushT prediction. On Robomimic Can, the BWM stage trained with motion supervision and generated histories achieves 3.3 times higher throughput and 78% lower peak memory than local one-step DriftWorld. In a latent-space extension to RT-1 and Bridge-V2, equal-update controls show that feature supervision under generated histories improves perceptual prediction. These findings show how terminal-map learning can combine efficient training with accurate one-step visual prediction.

Introduction An action-conditioned visual world model predicts future states given past observations and a sequence of actions. Such predictions support visual planning, policy evaluation, and learning from imagined interaction finn2016video,ebert2018visual,ha2018worldmodels,hafner2020dreamer,hafner2023dreamerv3 . Recent video simulators extend these capabilities to richer environments and manipulation tasks yang2024unisim,bruce2024genie,zhu2025irasim,zhu2025uwm,guo2026ctrlworld . Their practical value depends on both accuracy and inference cost. Diffusion and flow models offer expressive conditional generators, but standard samplers repeatedly evaluate a neural network to predict each future state ho2020ddpm,song2021sde,lipman2023flow,ho2022video,voleti2022mcvd . Their sampling cost motivates learning a direct map from noise to future frames with one-step prediction. Distillation obtains such predictors from pretrained generators salimans2022progressive,yin2024dmd,yin2024dmd2 , while direct training learns them from data song2023consistency,song2024improvedcm,geng2025meanflow,geng2026imf . Drifting models provide another route to one-step generation deng2026drifting . DriftWorld applies drifting to action-conditioned video prediction lu2026driftworld . These methods enable one-step prediction, but their training objectives can have substantially different computational costs. We study terminal-map learning as a way to train accurate action-conditioned predictors efficiently. We introduce Beckmann World Models (BWM), which adapt the terminal-map formulation of Beckmann Transport Models lee2026btm to action-conditioned visual prediction (Figure~ fig:method-overview ). For fixed history and actions, a terminal map assigns each noise input the endpoint of an autonomous transport. The terminal map is constant along each autonomous transport trajectory. This conservation property yields a training objective with a stop-gradient target constructed from pairs of noise samples and ground-truth future frames. The terminal map is conditioned on observation history and actions, without an explicit transport-time input. This construction requires neither a pretrained generative teacher nor a population of generated futures for each condition. Unlike feature-space drifting, the terminal-map objective does not require a pretrained similarity encoder. Turning this construction into an accurate world model requires supervising the inputs used at inference. The transport objective constrains the map on interpolated inputs, while boundary reconstruction teaches it to reproduce the ground-truth future frames. Neither directly supervises the prediction obtained from pure noise. In Robomimic Can, a stabilized map has higher prediction MSE at the source than at the target boundary. Thus, accurate boundary reconstruction can coexist with an inaccurate prediction from initial noise. We address this gap with endpoint-aligned Beckmann training, which directly supervises predictions from initial noise. Because much of a given scene is static, uniform pixel error can underweight the changes that distinguish action outcomes. We therefore emphasize moving pixels and temporal differences, then supervise spatial structure with frozen visual features. To prepare the map for autoregressive use, we also train subsequent predictions under detached generated histories. Together, these objectives address the discrepancy between transport training and inference under source noise and self-generated histories, without increasing inference cost. All components train the same map and preserve one forward pass per future chunk. On PushT and Robomimic Can, the final staged model reduces 64-frame MSE by and relative to same-backbone regression. Improvements are also seen in moving regions and perceptual metrics, showing that the gains extend beyond static background reconstruction. The displayed qualitative results illustrate these gains in object pose and robot configuration (Figure~ fig:rgb ). The downstream benefit is clearest in policy evaluation. BWM estimates simulator policy scores with mean IoU error , compared with for local DriftWorld and for its released checkpoint, while predicting four frames in \,ms. Compared with DriftWorld, which also uses single-pass inference, BWM substantially reduces training-step cost. On Robomimic Can, BWM achieves lower perceptual error in less cumulative training time than DriftWorld (Figure~ fig:efficiency ). Complete-update profiling gives higher throughput and lower peak allocated memory with equal batches of windows. These measurements cover the stage trained with motion supervision and generated-history recovery, including generated prefixes, and precede the final stage with VGG feature supervision. We further evaluate generated-history feature supervision on RT-1 and Bridge-V2 in the latent space. The hybrid objective combines terminal-map training with feature drifting. Adding feature supervision to predictions conditioned on generated histories reduces LPIPS by and against equal-update continuations from the same initial checkpoints. This extension retains one forward pass per frame and uses generated samples during training. Our contributions are summarized below. Conditional terminal-map learning. We adapt Beckmann training to action-conditioned prediction and reduce the gap between target-boundary reconstruction and prediction from initial noise. Endpoint-aligned supervision. We integrate source supervision with motion, spatial, and generated-history signals to improve one-step prediction without additional network evaluations. Training efficiency and downstream evaluation. We evaluate complete training recipes, demonstrate improved rollouts and policy-score estimation, and test generated-history feature supervision through controlled experiments on real videos. Related Work sec:related Visual prediction for decision making. Visual world models predict future observations for candidate action sequences, enabling model-based planning finn2016video,ebert2018visual . Latent world models learn compact dynamics where a policy can be trained through imagined interactions ha2018worldmodels,hafner2020dreamer,hafner2023dreamerv3 . Explicit visual prediction instead allows existing visual policies and outcome readers to interact with predicted observations. In this setting, small errors in object configuration can change the apparent consequence of an action. DIAMOND demonstrates the importance of such details for decision making and studies how diffusion sampling affects autoregressive stability alonso2024diamond . BWM follows this explicit prediction setting and studies how to train accurate predictions while retaining a single model evaluation per chunk. Controllable video simulation. Expressive video generation provides a foundation for visual simulation ho2022video,voleti2022mcvd,blattmann2023lvdm , but useful robot prediction also requires a close correspondence between controls and visual outcomes. UniSim brings heterogeneous interaction data into a common action-conditioned generation framework yang2024unisim . IRASim develops fine-grained robot action conditioning zhu2025irasim , while Ctrl-World addresses partial observability and sustained interaction through joint camera prediction, frame-level pose conditioning, and retrieval from visual history guo2026ctrlworld . These methods improve action conditioning, history conditioning, and consistency across camera views. BWM instead investigates how one-step generative training objectives affect prediction accuracy and training cost for single-view robotic dynamics. Our evaluations concern prediction, training cost, and policy-score estimation within the reported benchmarks. Learning predictors with few sampling steps. Diffusion and Flow Matching learn local generative dynamics that are integrated during sampling ho2020ddpm,lipman2023flow . Improved samplers and rectified flow reduce the cost of this integration song2021ddim,karras2022edm,liu2023rectified . Distillation moves more computation into training by transferring a pretrained generative process to a faster student. Step-distillation, distribution matching, and adversarial supervision provide different ways to conduct that transfer salimans2022progressive,yin2024dmd,yin2024dmd2,sauer2024add . For robot video, concurrent DIDO combines distribution matching distillation with supervision of gripper and object trajectories and DINO feature alignment before coupling the predictor to an action expert lyu2026dido . This highlights the need to preserve interaction details as sampling is accelerated. title: ACE-Brain-0.6: Scaling Spatial Grounding for Physical Foundation Models
summary: General-purpose multimodal models, including GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, demonstrate broad capabilities in embodied manipulation. Our analysis indicates that this generality is accompanied by strong spatial perception, as Astra can determine where to interact with task-relevant entities amid visual distractors. Because spatial perception connects high-level reasoning to the physical scene, we investigate scaling visual grounding to strengthen the perceptual foundation of general embodied operation. We develop a unified data pipeline that combines robot manipulation recordings with complementary visual data from diverse sources. After automatically annotating the robot recordings, the pipeline converts the collected data into verifiable grounding supervision. Fine-tuning Qwen3.5-9B on approximately 1.5 million samples produced by this pipeline yields ACE-Brain-0.6. The model outperforms GPT-6 Astra on four of seven public grounding benchmarks, with an overall average score of 75.41 compared with Astra's 73.68. Under a fixed Qwen3.5-9B fine-tuning setup, aggregate grounding performance improves steadily as successive data releases expand the training collection to cover a broader range of grounding scenarios. These results show that scaling verifiable grounding supervision from diverse sources can strengthen the spatial perception of an open 9B model for general embodied operation.
full_text: section Abstract Introduction sec:introduction General-purpose reasoning models are beginning to generalize across diverse embodied settings. GPT-6 Astra~ openai2026gpt6astra , in particular, demonstrates strong performance in embodied manipulation. A closer examination of its behavior shows that this embodied competence is accompanied by strong spatial perception. It can localize task-relevant interaction targets in cluttered scenes despite the presence of visually similar distractors. This observation highlights the role of spatial perception in translating high-level reasoning into physical action. Grounding provides this connection by linking natural-language descriptions to their visual referents in an image~ kamath2021mdetr,shridhar2021cliport . Reliable grounding requires precise localization of all image regions that satisfy a description, with explicit recognition when no match exists~ liu2023gres . In embodied environments, clutter and occlusion make this correspondence particularly difficult to establish~ wang2021ocid . A grounding error can therefore misdirect an agent's actions even when its high-level reasoning is sound. We therefore examine Astra's spatial grounding capabilities in greater detail. Our analysis in Section~ sec:astra-grounding-analysis illustrates its ability to handle diverse grounding queries, while also revealing localization errors in tasks with precise spatial requirements. Using Astra as a reference, we ask whether an open 9B-parameter vision-language model can match or surpass Astra's grounding performance by expanding the scale and coverage of grounding supervision, with the model architecture and training recipe held fixed. To investigate this question, we develop a unified pipeline for constructing grounding supervision from existing open datasets. The pipeline combines robot manipulation recordings from more than thirty dataset families with complementary visual data to broaden task coverage. We automatically annotate the robot recordings to supply the object-level labels they generally lack. All sources are then converted into question--answer supervision that is verifiable against the supporting annotations, with controls to reduce shortcuts between question wording and answer format. This pipeline yields approximately 1.5 million training samples, which we use to fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B~ qwen3.5 for a single epoch, producing ACE-Brain-0.6. Figure~ fig:overview provides an overview of our approach. We evaluate ACE-Brain-0.6 on seven public grounding benchmarks. The model outperforms the Qwen3.5-9B baseline on six benchmarks and remains behind on PixMo-Count. It exceeds GPT-6 Astra on four benchmarks and achieves a slightly higher seven-benchmark average (75.41 versus 73.68), while remaining behind on PixMo-Count, RefSpatial, and PointArena. These results suggest that a 9B open model trained with diverse, verifiable grounding supervision can match Astra's aggregate performance on the evaluated benchmarks. We further examine data scaling by fine-tuning from the same base checkpoint with a fixed training recipe for each data release. Across releases that expand both sample count and supervision coverage, the seven-benchmark average increases approximately linearly with the logarithm of sample count over the evaluated range, slightly exceeding Astra's average at about 1.5 million samples. In a control experiment, adding samples only from existing sources improves this average by less than one point, suggesting that broader supervision coverage contributes to the observed gains. Our contributions are threefold: A data pipeline for grounding. We collect large-scale open-source robot, egocentric, object-centric, and spatial data, automatically annotate robot recordings, and convert these sources into verifiable question--answer supervision for target identification, complete instance coverage, and precise localization. An empirical study of grounding-data scaling. Through a controlled series of training runs, we show that grounding performance improves steadily with data scale and that expanding the coverage of supervision contributes substantially more than increasing the volume of existing sources. ACE-Brain-0.6. By scaling verifiable grounding data to approximately 1.5 million samples, we train a 9B model that exceeds GPT-6 Astra on four of seven grounding benchmarks and achieves a higher overall average. Related Work sec:related_work Visual Grounding and Embodied Spatial Understanding Visual grounding links language descriptions to image locations. Detector-based methods such as GLIP and Grounding DINO align visual and language features for phrase grounding and open-set localization~ li2022,liu2024 . Generative approaches represent spatial outputs as token sequences, from coordinate and class prediction in Pix2Seq~ chen2022pix2seq to multi-task visual prediction in Florence-2~ xiao2023 and detection, referring, and pointing in Rex-Omni~ jiang2025 . Grounding also supports broader embodied understanding: PaLM-E integrates sensor inputs into language modeling~ driess2023palme , Gemini Robotics-ER develops spatial understanding and embodied reasoning~ geminirobotics2025 , and RynnBrain and Embodied-R1.5 combine localization with embodied understanding and reasoning~ dang2026,yuan2026 . These works connect spatial prediction with increasingly broad model capabilities. We focus on grounding itself, keeping the base vision-language model and training recipe fixed to examine the effect of training data. Grounding Data and Supervision Grounding supervision comes from human annotation, automatic labeling, and geometric derivation. Molmo-and-PixMo collects language-conditioned point annotations, including complete instance sets and absent-target examples~ deitke2024molmopixmoopenweights . GrIT pairs caption phrases with predicted image regions~ peng2023 . SpatialVLM constructs spatial question--answer data using segmentation, depth, and object descriptions~ chen2024 , while RoboPoint derives instruction-point supervision from simulated scene geometry~ yuan2024robopoint . We build on these approaches by combining robot recordings, egocentric interactions, dense object and part annotations, and 3D scenes. Our pipeline automatically annotates robot recordings and converts these heterogeneous sources into a common question--answer format. Answers remain linked to supporting annotations, with checks for instance completeness, spatial constraints, and target absence. This training collection allows us to study how supervision scale and composition affect grounding performance. Analysis of GPT-6 Astra sec:astra-grounding-analysis Our experiments with GPT-6 Astra (hereafter Astra) as a robotic manipulation policy highlight how visual grounding supports analytic geometry in translating task objectives into physical actions. Grounding identifies relevant objects, interaction regions, and spatial references in the observed scene, and analytic geometry uses spatial quantities derived from these references to determine positions, relative displacements, and motion parameters. In this section, we first illustrate this dependency through two manipulation cases, and then examine Astra's grounding capabilities in greater detail. Case Studies: From Grounding to Geometric Robot Manipulation sec:astra-manipulation-cases The two cases illustrate complementary forms of grounding used in geometric manipulation (Figure~ fig:astra_manipulation_cases ). Fruit basket placement requires selecting points on the manipulated object and its destination, whereas T-shirt folding requires extracting the garment's spatial extent. In both cases, these visual references determine the geometric quantities used to construct the action. basket placement. To place a loaded fruit basket onto a black sponge, Astra selected points along the basket rim and the corners of the destination surface. Using calibrated RGB-D observations, it fitted the basket rim and support plane to estimate their relative configuration. The resulting planar centers of the basket and destination, and , defined an initial displacement . Astra used these estimates to construct coordinated arm motions and reassessed the basket's pose during placement. Here, grounding specifies the object geometry and support surface to which the placement calculation applies. -shirt folding. To fold an already side-tucked T-shirt into a square, Astra constructed a color-based mask within a selected image region and extracted the garment contour. Projecting this contour onto an assumed cloth plane gave an estimated length and width . These dimensions informed a bottom fold of depth , with a corresponding hem displacement . Both arms executed the staged fold, and Astra extracted the contour again after release to assess the resulting shape. Grounding the garment's extent thus supplies the dimensions needed to select a fold that satisfies the task's shape requirement. Together, these cases illustrate how task-relevant grounding supplies the spatial inputs needed for geometric action construction and subsequent visual verification. These observations motivate studying grounding as a measurable component of spatial perception and using Astra's capabilities as a reference for improving our model. A Closer Look at Astra's Grounding Capabilities sec:astra-grounding-capabilities Figure~ fig:astra_grounding illustrates Astra's grounding through eight examples of its strengths and two examples of its limitations. The queries require selecting objects, locating all members of a set, identifying spatial regions, or associating functions and actions with visual locations. These examples make concrete the range of visual references that Astra can supply for subsequent geometric reasoning and the localization errors that can arise. . Astra can resolve descriptions that distinguish a particular instance from other objects of the same category. In the object grounding example (a), it identifies the chair farthest from the viewer. In the ordinal referring example (b), it selects the picture that is third from the top in the second column from the left. Grounding also extends to sets of instances. In the counting example (c), Astra returns ten points corresponding to ten books, with the number of predictions matching the reference count. In the multi-instance example (f), it returns a point on each of the 15 bottles. Both queries ask for all matching objects, and both responses represent the target set through individual locations. The examples of region grounding and spatial relations require locating unoccupied space under relational descriptions. In (d), Astra places points in the free space between the green and white blocks at the back of the scene. In (g), it locates vacant space to the right of the toilet. The predictions lie within the corresponding reference regions. Functional descriptions and interaction goals provide further ways to specify a visual target. In the affordance example (e), Astra locates the window from a description of a structure that can be opened or closed to admit light and air. For the interaction task in (h), it predicts a point within the annotated end-effector interaction region for cutting with a knife. The former identifies an object through its function; the latter localizes a region relevant to a specified action. . The fine-grained localization example (i) asks which part of a mug should be gripped to lift it. Astra's point lies close to the handle but just outside the valid reference mask. title: GTSM: Gaussian Splatting with Thermal State-Space Dynamics for Spatio-Temporal Thermal Field Reconstruction and Prediction
summary: Temperature-field reconstruction and prediction are important for condition monitoring, process analysis, and state assessment in industrial and dynamic environments. This work aims to recover a four-dimensional spatio-temporal thermal state field directly from two-dimensional observations, without requiring a predefined 3D model, prescribed thermodynamic equation, or predefined heating/cooling trajectory. To this end, we propose the Gaussian Thermal State-Space Model (GTSM), which represents thermal evolution through a shared scene-level latent process and Gaussian-specific local thermal states. The resulting continuous dynamics are propagated using differentiable RK2 integration, allowing thermal evolution to be inferred from multi-view and multi-temporal observations and continuously extrapolated beyond the observed interval. GTSM is designed as a backbone-agnostic thermal dynamics module for Gaussian representations and can be integrated with both static 3D Gaussian Splatting and dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting, supporting thermal reconstruction and prediction under both static and time-varying target geometry. The reconstructed representation further enables novel-view thermal rendering and future-time thermal-state prediction. Experiments on real infrared sequences and synthetic dynamic thermal data demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and substantially stronger temporal extrapolation than representative baselines, while also validating the applicability of GTSM to deforming targets.
full_text: GTSM: Gaussian Splatting with Thermal State-Space Dynamics for Spatio-Temporal Thermal Field Reconstruction and Prediction Yunpeng Zhao,~ , Haoxiang Zhang, and Chao Liu Yunpeng Zhao and Haoxiang Zhang are with the Key Laboratory for Information Science of Electromagnetic Waves (MoE), Fudan University, Shanghai 200433, China (e-mail:ypzhao23@m.fudan.edu.cn) (corresponding author: Yunpeng Zhao) Shell : A Sample Article Using IEEEtran.cls for IEEE Journals Temperature-field reconstruction and prediction are important for condition monitoring, process analysis, and state assessment in industrial and dynamic environments. To this end, we propose the Gaussian Thermal State-Space Model (GTSM), which represents thermal evolution through a shared scene-level latent process and Gaussian-specific local thermal states. The resulting continuous dynamics are propagated using differentiable RK2 integration, allowing thermal evolution to be inferred from multi-view and multi-temporal observations and continuously extrapolated beyond the observed interval. GTSM is designed as a backbone-agnostic thermal dynamics module for Gaussian representations and can be integrated with both static 3D Gaussian Splatting and dynamic 4D Gaussian Splatting, supporting thermal reconstruction and prediction under both static and time-varying target geometry. The reconstructed representation further enables novel-view thermal rendering and future-time thermal-state prediction. Experiments on real infrared sequences and synthetic dynamic thermal data demonstrate improved reconstruction accuracy and substantially stronger temporal extrapolation than representative baselines, while also validating the applicability of GTSM to deforming targets. Gaussian Splatting, thermal field reconstruction, spatio-temporal thermal modeling, temperature prediction Introduction emperature is an important physical indicator for characterizing the operating state, energy dissipation, and potential anomalies of industrial equipment and dynamic targets~ OZ10682482 . Accurate temperature field reconstruction has therefore been widely applied to equipment condition monitoring~ WANG2022105359 , combustion analysis~ YANG2026128592 , and infrared target perception~ YAMASHITA2026128398 . In many practical scenarios, however, a temperature field at a single instant provides only limited state information. Its temporal evolution often reflects changes in heat input, operating conditions, and heat-transfer processes. Therefore, reconstructing not only the current temperature distribution but also its temporal evolution is important for understanding target states and predicting their future thermal behavior. Traditional thermal reconstruction and prediction methods typically formulate temperature evolution using heat-transfer equations and solve the resulting physical models through numerical techniques such as finite-element or CFD-based simulation~ YANG2020111448 . These methods can provide physically consistent solutions when the target geometry, material properties, heat sources, and boundary conditions are known. Data-driven methods, including long short-term memory networks (LSTMs)~ FANG2025111170 and Transformer-based models~ wu2024transolver , provide an alternative way to learn temperature evolution directly from observations. physics-informed/physics-guided learnings~ LU2026128309,gong_tfrd, Hadzhamolla_2026 further introduce physical constraints or continuous dynamics into thermal prediction. Nevertheless, most of these approaches operate on predefined spatial domains, meshes, or image coordinates, and generally assume that the spatial correspondence of the temperature field is already known. When an accurate geometric model and thermal-process prior are unavailable, thermal reconstruction becomes a substantially more difficult computational inverse-imaging problem. In many practical scenarios, the available measurements consist only of two-dimensional infrared or temperature observations acquired at different times and viewpoints, while the underlying three-dimensional geometry and spatio-temporal thermal states are unknown. The challenge is therefore to recover both the spatial representation and its time-varying thermal state directly from these image measurements, without relying on a predefined mesh, known thermophysical coefficients, or a prescribed temperature-evolution law. Differentiable neural rendering provides a natural computational imaging framework for addressing the geometric part of this inverse problem. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has attracted considerable attention because of its explicit primitive representation, efficient optimization, and high-quality differentiable rendering~ Kerbl . By introducing time-dependent deformation or dynamic Gaussian attributes, 4DGS methods further extend this capability to scenes and targets whose geometry changes over time Wu_2024_CVPR,yang2023deformable3dgs . These developments provide an explicit and differentiable image-formation model for recovering either static or dynamic three-dimensional geometry from multi-view image observations. However, dynamic thermal-field reconstruction remains much less explored. Compared with conventional geometric reconstruction, this problem involves two coupled inverse processes. The first is the spatial inversion from two-dimensional observations to a three-dimensional target representation. The second is the recovery of a thermal state on this representation, requiring spatial consistency between temperature and surface primitives as well as temporal consistency across observations. The ultimate goal is therefore to recover a four-dimensional spatio-temporal thermal state field from two-dimensional measurements. This problem is particularly challenging because the underlying thermal process is generally unknown, while different surface elements can exhibit distinct temporal responses due to variations in material properties, spatial location, thermal exposure, and local boundary conditions. A straightforward strategy is to directly regress the temperature of each Gaussian as a function of time using a time-conditioned MLP or a generic temporal network. However, such formulations mainly describe the observed temperature trajectory and do not explicitly distinguish between the thermal process shared by the scene and the heterogeneous local responses of individual surface primitives. This lack of structured thermal dynamics can make it difficult to capture spatially heterogeneous temporal responses and to robustly propagate the learned state beyond the observed temporal interval. To address these challenges, we propose the Gaussian Thermal State-Space Model (GTSM), a structured Gaussian-level thermal dynamics representation for spatio-temporal thermal-field reconstruction and prediction. Instead of independently regressing the temporal temperature trajectory of each Gaussian, GTSM decomposes thermal evolution into a scene-level latent thermal process and Gaussian-specific local thermal states. The scene-level latent process captures the shared temporal thermal driving pattern of the target, while the Gaussian-specific states model spatially heterogeneous responses to this common process. The coupled thermal states evolve through continuous differential dynamics and are jointly inferred from multi-view and multi-temporal observations through differentiable Gaussian rendering. Importantly, GTSM does not require a prescribed thermodynamic equation, known thermophysical coefficients, or a predefined heating or cooling trajectory. Instead, it learns a structured continuous thermal dynamics model directly from observations. This formulation enables the reconstructed Gaussian representation not only to explain the observed spatio-temporal thermal field, but also to propagate the learned thermal state beyond the observation interval for future-time thermal prediction. The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We propose GTSM for reconstructing four-dimensional spatio-temporal thermal fields from multi-view and multi-temporal two-dimensional observations. GTSM augments Gaussian primitives with continuous thermal states represented through a shared scene-level latent process and Gaussian-specific local dynamics. We introduce continuous Gaussian-level state-space dynamics that infer temporal thermal evolution directly from observations without prescribing a specific heating or cooling trajectory. The learned dynamics support both reconstruction within the observed interval and continuous rollout for future-time prediction. GTSM is designed as a backbone-agnostic thermal dynamics module for Gaussian representations and can be integrated with both static 3DGS and dynamic 4DGS frameworks. Experiments on real infrared sequences and synthetic dynamic thermal data validate its effectiveness for within-interval reconstruction, novel-view rendering, and future-time thermal prediction. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section~ sec2 reviews related work. Section~ sec3 presents the proposed method in detail. Section~ sec5 describes the experimental setup, reports results, and includes ablation studies. Finally, Section~ sec5 concludes the paper. Related work sec2 Static and Dynamic Scene Reconstruction with Gaussian Splatting 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ Kerbl represents a scene using explicit anisotropic Gaussian primitives and reconstructs the scene through differentiable rasterization. Its explicit representation, high rendering efficiency, and strong novel-view synthesis quality have motivated extensive follow-up research in scene reconstruction and related rendering tasks~ GS2Physics,Recon . Subsequent studies extend 3DGS from static scenes to time-varying environments. Dynamic Gaussian methods, commonly referred to as 4DGS, introduce temporal deformation or time-dependent Gaussian representations to describe scene motion and geometric changes. Representative approaches model temporal variation using deformation fields~ yang2023deformable3dgs , spatio-temporal grids~ Wu_2024_CVPR , control-point-based transformations ~ huang2024scgs,yang2023gs4d , or explicit space-time Gaussian representations~ duan:2024:4drotorgs . These methods enable Gaussian primitives to evolve with time and therefore support high-quality reconstruction and novel-view rendering of dynamic scenes. More recently, research has begun to move beyond reconstruction at observed timestamps toward learning the underlying temporal dynamics of scene motion. Methods such as TRACE~ li2025trace introduce continuous dynamics into Gaussian motion modeling, allowing the evolution pattern of geometric states to be inferred from temporal observations and further propagated to unseen future timestamps. This development extends dynamic Gaussian reconstruction from time-conditioned scene representation toward temporal state prediction. Despite these advances, most existing dynamic Gaussian methods primarily model the evolution of geometry and visual appearance. Compared with geometric dynamics, explicitly attaching a thermal state to Gaussian primitives, learning its temporal evolution from image observations, and propagating the learned thermal state to future timestamps remain relatively underexplored. title: Controllable Multi-Object Insertion for Detection Data Augmentation
summary: Controllable object insertion provides a targeted approach to augmenting object detection datasets that require category--count fidelity, annotation alignment, and source-content preservation beyond visual realism. Several approaches have been proposed to address this grand challenge, but most suffer from different constraints in precise category--count requests and visual consistency, limited coordination across categories and instances, and poor localization of multiple objects of specific category and count. We design SceneP2F, a two-stage trainable framework that connects scene-aware joint planning with layout-aligned generation leveraging explicit instance-level layouts. SceneP2F consists of two novel designs. The first is ScenePlan which allocates one class-labeled query per requested instance, jointly predicts scene-compatible object centers, and separately estimates box sizes conditioned on the planned centers and scene context. The second is SceneAlign-Fill which combines geometry- and appearance-aware conditioning, box--class-guided regional attention, and an annotation-region-weighted flow-matching objective to render the planned objects while limiting unintended changes to source content. Extensive experiments on three challenging benchmarks UAVDT, VisDrone, and BDD100K show that SceneP2F outperforms representative general-purpose editors and object-insertion methods consistently, demonstrating the value of coordinating instance-level planning and generation for category-targeted detection augmentation.
full_text: Controllable object insertion provides a targeted approach to augmenting object detection datasets that require category--count fidelity, annotation alignment, and source-content preservation beyond visual realism. Several approaches have been proposed to address this grand challenge, but most suffer from different constraints in precise category–count requests and visual consistency, limited coordination across categories and instances, and poor localization of multiple objects of specific category and count. We design SceneP2F, a two-stage trainable framework that connects scene-aware joint planning with layout-aligned generation leveraging explicit instance-level layouts. SceneP2F consists of two novel designs. The first is which allocates one class-labeled query per requested instance, jointly predicts scene-compatible object centers, and separately estimates box sizes conditioned on the planned centers and scene context. The second is which combines geometry- and appearance-aware conditioning, box--class-guided regional attention, and an annotation-region-weighted flow-matching objective to render the planned objects while limiting unintended changes to source content. Extensive experiments on three challenging benchmarks UAVDT, VisDrone, and BDD100K show that SceneP2F outperforms representative general-purpose editors and object-insertion methods consistently, demonstrating the value of coordinating instance-level planning and generation for category-targeted detection augmentation. Introduction Object-detection data often suffer from a long-tail class distribution, motivating controllable object insertion as a targeted approach to adding selected instances to real images. Rather than collecting and annotating entirely new scenes, object insertion preserve existing backgrounds and annotations while enriching the training distribution with selected instances. To make such augmentation effective, the inserted objects must be visually consistent with the source scene and occupy plausible locations, while content outside the intended editing regions is preserved. Reliable control over object categories and counts is equally important for achieving reliable augmentation benefits. Existing methods have demonstrated the feasibility of object insertion and its utility for downstream tasks. General-purpose image editors, such as GPT-Image-2.5, FLUX.2~ blackforestlabs2025flux2 , and Qwen-Image-Edit~ wu2025qwenimage , provide strong generative priors for instruction-guided editing. More directly relevant to our task, task-specific object-insertion methods~ yang2024addsd,zhao2024diffree,tewel2025addit improve controllability through specialized training or inference-time guidance. However, general-purpose editors may transfer poorly to specialized domains, limiting their utility for detection augmentation, while existing object-insertion methods often rely on free-form requests without instance-level constraints for coordinating new objects with the scene, resulting in unpredictable placement and unreliable category count control. Some methods~ yeh2026xplanner,pmlr-v306-hou26a,petersen2025sceneaware explicitly predict or sample the spatial layout before image synthesis, improving the plausibility of candidate insertion locations. But they still are not able to jointly achieve precise multi-object control, visual consistency with the source scene, plausible placement, and background preservation, potentially limiting the benefits of downstream data augmentation. We propose SceneP2F, a two-stage planning--generation framework for scene-conditioned, category- and count-controlled multi-object insertion in challenging downstream domains. Given a source scene, the objective of SceneP2F is to add the specified number of new instances at plausible locations and scales while maintaining visual consistency and preserving existing content, with the ultimate goal of enabling effective object-level augmentation for downstream detection. SceneP2F comprises two key designs, namely, ScenePlan and SceneAlign-Fill. ScenePlan decomposes box prediction into size and position components while retaining their conditional dependence, conditioned on the source image, existing annotations, and admissible insertion regions. It jointly models dependencies among the requested instances and incorporates scene context and geometric feasibility constraints to produce a scene-compatible layout with the requested cardinality. Given this layout, SceneAlign-Fill jointly renders the planned objects using geometry and appearance conditioning. Regional attention guided by box--class tokens associates each planned region with its target category, while an annotation-region-weighted flow-matching objective emphasizes generation within the designated regions. These mechanisms encourage the synthesized instances to follow the planned boxes and remain visually compatible with the source scene, while limiting unintended changes outside the editing regions. Together, the two stages connect explicit category--count constraints at the layout level with instance-level control during image synthesis. We evaluate our framework on two challenging UAV object detection benchmarks, UAVDT~ du2018unmannedaerialvehiclebenchmark and VisDrone~ zhu2021detection , with BDD100K~ yu2020bdd100kdiversedrivingdataset providing a complementary driving-scene benchmark. Our task-aligned evaluation suite covers two dimensions: request fidelity, which measures adherence to the requested categories and counts of newly inserted instances, and scene fidelity, which assesses insertion naturalness and preservation of the original scene and existing objects. Comparisons against FLUX.2-dev, Qwen-Image-Edit-2511, Add-SD, and Add-it suggest that SceneP2F improves category–count adherence and provides competitive scene consistency under our evaluation protocol. SceneP2F achieves the lowest mTCE (Mean Total Count Error) across all three datasets, with particularly large reductions over the best competing baseline on UAVDT (2.744 to 0.817) and BDD100K (5.523 to 1.924). It also improves Outsides PSNR by 5.49, 3.94, and 3.33 dB on UAVDT, VisDrone, and BDD100K, respectively, while achieving the highest DINO similarity and CLIP-I across all three benchmarks. Adding the resulting synthetic images to detector training improves bus from 22.9 to 31.0 and truck from 7.2 to 12.2, demonstrating the potential value of category-targeted insertion for detection augmentation. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We introduce SceneP2F, a trainable framework for annotated detection data generation that integrates category--count control, object-size modeling, appearance alignment, and source-content preservation through explicit instance-level layouts; (2) We propose to jointly plan scene-compatible layouts through coupled size and position modeling. uses box-class-guided regional attention and an annotation-region-weighted flow-matching objective to align generated objects with the planned instances while preserving source content; (3) We show that SceneP2F-generated images and corresponding annotations improve detection of long-tail categories on UAVDT, demonstrating the potential utility of our framework for targeted data augmentation. Related Work General-Purpose Image Editing and Object Addition. General-purpose Image Editing models, including Qwen-Image-Edit~ wu2025qwenimage , FLUX.2 [dev]~ blackforestlabs2025flux2 , GLM-Image~ zai2026glmimage , BAGEL~ deng2025bagel , and OmniGen~ xiao2025omnigen , support flexible text- and image-conditioned generation and editing. Object-addition methods can be organized by their dominant control interface. Mask-free editing leaves placement to the model: InstructPix2Pix~ Brooks_2023_CVPR establishes instruction-guided editing; Diffree~ zhao2024diffree and Paint by Inpaint~ Wasserman_2025_CVPR learn insertion from removal-based supervision; and Add-it~ tewel2025addit uses training-free attention control. Spatially grounded editing uses user-specified regions in SmartBrush~ xie2023smartbrush and ObjectAdd~ zhang2025objectaddaddingobjectsimage , or instruction-derived plans in X-Planner~ yeh2026xplanner and MIRAGE~ liu2026mirage , with the latter supporting multi-instance editing. Reference-conditioned composition transfers exemplar content: Paint by Example~ yang2023paintbyexample and ObjectStitch~ song2023objectstitch perform diffusion compositing; AnyDoor~ chen2024anydoor emphasizes identity and detail preservation; and Insert Anything~ song2026insertanything , FreeInsert~ zhang2025freeinsert , and Multitwine~ tarres2025multitwine extend prompting flexibility, geometric and style control, and joint multi-object composition, respectively. Detection-Oriented Synthetic Data Generation. Compositional augmentation constructs training samples by transferring foreground instances, as in Copy-Paste~ Dwibedi_2017_ICCV, Dvornik_2018_ECCV and Simple Copy-Paste~ Ghiasi_2021_CVPR . X-Paste~ pmlr-v202-zhao23f and Stable Diffusion for Aerial Object Detection~ jian2023stablediffusionaerialobject extend this strategy with diffusion-generated foregrounds. Layout-conditioned synthesis generates images from categories and spatial constraints, as in LayoutDiffusion~ Zheng_2023_CVPR and GLIGEN~ Li_2023_CVPR . GeoDiffusion~ chen2023geodiffusion , ODGEN~ zhu2024odgen , AeroGen~ tang2024aerogen , and UAVGen~ li2026uavgen extend this paradigm to detection-oriented data generation, while PlanGen~ He_2025_ICCV incorporates global layout planning. DatasetDM~ wu2023datasetdm instead generates images and predicts their perception annotations. Task-aware synthesis improves training utility through data-distribution modeling or detector feedback. These strategies address synthetic-data composition and utility, complementing our focus on per-image category--count control. Scene-Conditioned Object Insertion and Layout Planning. Scene-conditioned insertion ranges from implicit placement to explicit geometric planning. Add-SD~ yang2024addsd learns insertion from object-removal pairs; Imagining the Unseen~ yun2024imagining predicts class-conditioned 2D boxes for inpainting; Scene-Aware Location Modeling~ petersen2025sceneaware samples placements using scene geometry and dataset statistics; MonoPlace3D~ Parihar_2025_CVPR learns distributions over plausible 3D boxes; and PDA~ pmlr-v306-hou26a combines physics-grounded planning with appearance adaptation. Joint layout modeling also appears in traffic simulation: SceneGen places actors autoregressively, while Scenario Diffusion and SceneControl use diffusion to generate actor configurations under scene constraints~ Tan_2021_CVPR,pronovost2023scenario,scenecontrol2024 . Scenario Dreamer jointly generates lane graphs and actor boxes, and ScenarioControl supports text- or image-conditioned vectorized scenes~ Rowe_2025_CVPR,scenariocontrol2026 . For detection-oriented insertion, the challenge extends beyond plausible placement to maintaining instance-level consistency between a complete category--count request and the generated image. Our framework uses an explicit, class-labeled 2D layout to connect scene-aware joint planning with layout-aligned generation, promoting request fidelity, image-annotation alignment, and source-content preservation. title: EmbodyHOI: Embodiment-Aware Generation of Hand-Object Interactions for Humanoid Dexterous Manipulation
summary: Humanoid dexterous manipulation needs reference motions that are both semantically rich and kinematically feasible for the target robot. Text-conditioned hand-object interaction (HOI) generators supply diverse, language-specified demonstrations, but they synthesize motion in human (MANO) space. The embodiment gap is therefore deferred to post-hoc retargeting, where trajectories deployed on the robot can fail to maintain contact with objects and also degrade policy learning. Our key idea is that robot reachability should constrain the interaction trajectories while they are being generated. We present EmbodyHOI, which runs a differentiable inverse-kinematics (IK) solver for a specific humanoid embodiment inside the sampling loop of a frozen flow-matching HOI trajectory generator. We feed back gradients from the embodiment-aware IK solver into the HOI sampler and jointly optimize the position of the humanoid with respect to the object. Because guidance acts only at inference, one HOI trajectory generator trained on human hand poses transfers across humanoid embodiments without retraining. On ARCTIC trajectories with two contrasting humanoids (Unitree G1 and H1-2), our proposed guidance-based method cuts the retargeted wrist error from 8.9 cm to 0.6 cm while leaving text-to-HOI generation quality intact, and raises task success from 68% to 79% on 50 random G1 tasks and from 62% to 76% on a four-task H1-2 suite. Critically, cheaper alternatives for bridging the embodiment gap fail to beat EmbodyHOI. Post-hoc wrist refinement and compute-matched best-of-N selection both reach lower IK energy than our guidance yet train worse policies. For simulation results, see our website: https://embodyhoi.github.io/
full_text: steers a human-space HOI trajectory generation method toward motions that are more reachable for specific humanoid embodiments. During diffusion sampling in the HOI generation, a differentiable IK solve on the target robot scores wrist trajectories, and its gradient is fed back into the sampler while the robot's base placement is optimized jointly. The generator is never retrained, so the same model and the same IK objective serve the Unitree G1 and H1-2. fig:teaser Humanoid dexterous manipulation needs reference motions that are both semantically rich and kinematically feasible for the target robot.
