For simulation results, see our website: Introduction sec:intro Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands remains difficult for humanoids that can reliably walk and loco-manipulate~ he2025hover,liao2025beyondmimic,qiu2025humanoid,weng2025hdmi . A robot must coordinate reaching, finger contact, and whole-arm motion under embodiment-specific kinematic constraints to execute trajectories that actually manipulate objects. A human trajectory when kinematically retargeted to a humanoid is often not executable, due to differences in finger morphology, joint limits, and wrist reachability. We study how to generate human interactions which can easily close the above gap. Given a language prompt and an articulated object, we produce bimanual hand--object trajectories specific to a humanoid, which are easily executable by the robot. A natural route to this goal of end-to-end policies is generate-then-track, but today's Hand-Object Interaction (HOI) generators have no notion of the robot that will execute their output. In this route, a generator proposes diverse task-conditioned reference motions and a physics-based RL policy learns to track them under contact and actuation limits~ kalaria2025dreamcontrol . Hand-centric HOI generators are the natural source of dexterous references as they model finger-object contact, but they generate in MANO~ romero2017mano space with no term that couples the wrist to a robot's kinematic chain. This mismatch only surfaces during retargeting, after the finger and object motions are committed, and the tracking policy inherits wrist targets that the arm cannot reach. Previous works resolve this on either side of generation. Training the motion prior in robot space~ harithas2026dreamcontrol yields one generator per robot, which rules out cross-embodiment reuse. Whereas repairing a generated human motion~ park2025demodiffusion,chen2024object only makes delta modifications, and cannot always rectify retargeted wrist trajectories unreachable for the robot. Tracking systems such as DexMachina~ mandi2025dexmachina and ManipTrans~ li2025maniptrans sidestep the question by commanding a floating wrist with no arm. We take a different approach: keep a frozen MANO HOI generator as a reusable motion prior and make its samples embodiment-aware during generation (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). We build on MAD-HOI~ madhoi , a text-conditioned HOI generator that fills object and hand tokens over a sequence of unmasking steps, integrating a flow-matching ODE for the unmasked tokens at each step. Inside every ODE step, we decode the current wrist trajectories, solve a differentiable IK problem on the target humanoid, and add a gradient of the IK residual (IK energy) to the learned velocity field, in a manner of classifier guidance. A wrist correction made in one unmasking step conditions the finger and object tokens generated in later ones, so the interaction re-forms around the corrected wrist instead of being patched afterward. A full humanoid raises another problem that floating hands and fixed-base arms do not, where the robot stands. The base placement decides whether both arms stay reachable over the whole interaction, and a fixed-base IK cannot differentiate between a feasible interaction performed from the wrong standing position from an infeasible one. We therefore solve for the base translation together with the arm joints, and re-solve it at every unmasking step so that the base follows the partially generated motion. Finally, we retarget the guided motions and train a PPO tracking policy with separate imitation rewards for arm and hand, as they differ in error scale and contact requirements. IK energy is a diagnostic, not a quantity to minimize on its own. Guidance costs a native sample (5\,s to 160\,s on an A100), paid once per reference, so we compare it with alternatives that lower the energy after generation at the same or lower cost. Post-hoc IK refinement of a finished sample reaches the lowest energy of any method, and compute-matched best-of- selection also beats guidance on energy, yet both train worse policies (Table~ tab:necessity ). Refinement moves the wrists after the fingers and object are fixed, and selection returns a different interaction instead of correcting the requested one. Reachability has to be imposed while the interaction is still being generated. Our contributions are as follows. Training-free IK guidance for a frozen HOI generator. A differentiable IK solve on the target humanoid runs inside every ODE step of the sampler, and its gradient steers the hand tokens. One objective with one set of weights serves the Unitree G1 and H1-2, and it also lowers the IK energy of a second generator, Text2HOI~ cha2024text2hoi , without modification. Base placement inside guidance. Solving for the base removes near-singular G1 arm configurations (2.6 to 0.2 of test samples) even when applied once to a finished sample, and re-solving it at every unmasking step accounts for 2.8 of the 5.7 success-rate points that guidance adds over post-hoc base optimization on the four-task G1 suite (Table~ tab:ablation ). Lower IK energy after generation does not give better references. Post-hoc refinement and compute-matched best-of-32 selection reach lower energy than guidance (0.35 and 1.21 vs.\ 1.81), yet their policies succeed less often (32.8 and 74.0 vs.\ 79.7 , Table~ tab:necessity ). Downstream gains on two humanoids. Policies trained on guided references with decoupled hand and arm reward streams, raise success from 68 to 79 on 50 randomly drawn ARCTIC tasks on the G1 and from 62 to 76 on a four-task H1-2 suite. We will release the guidance code, the generated references and the trained policies. Related Work sec:related draws on three lines of work, and none of them adapts the reference motion to a humanoid's arm chain while the interaction is being generated. Human-space HOI generation and test-time guidance. Text-to-motion models generate full-body SMPL~ loper2015smpl motion with pose-space diffusion~ tevet2023mdm,zhang2022motiondiffuse or masked-token generation~ guo2024momask . Full-body HOI methods~ xu2023interdiff,peng2023hoidiff model contact only coarsely at the body surface. Hand-centric methods parameterized by MANO~ romero2017mano model fine-grained finger--object contact on datasets such as ARCTIC~ fan2023arctic , GRAB~ taheri2020grab , and OakInk~ yang2022oakink , from grasp synthesis and interaction denoising~ taheri2020grab,liu2024geneoh to language-conditioned sequence generation~ cha2024text2hoi,li2025latenthoi,zhang2026openhoi,christen2024diffh2o,madhoi . Test-time guidance steers such generators toward keyframes, trajectories, and contacts, but always toward targets specified in human space~ karunratanakul2023gmd,xie2024omnicontrol . Our guidance has the same form but no human-space target: it scores the decoded wrist against a robot's kinematic chain, so its optimum moves when the robot or its base changes. Retargeting and RL from human demonstrations. Human-to-robot retargeting typically optimizes joint angles against keypoint and end-effector errors~ kim2025pyroki,he2024omnih2o , and it underpins teleoperation~ he2024omnih2o,luo2025sonic and robot-space datasets~ harithas2026dreamcontrol . Dexterous-hand retargeting~ qin2023anyteleop,pan2025spider,shaw2024leap is a standard preprocessing step for RL from human demonstrations. ManipTrans~ li2025maniptrans pretrains a hand-trajectory imitator and then fine-tunes a residual policy. DexMachina~ mandi2025dexmachina uses retargeted joints and contacts as auxiliary rewards under a decaying virtual-object curriculum. DexMan~ hsieh2025dexman extends this recipe to RGB video, and HERMES~ yuan2025hermes unifies heterogeneous motion sources for mobile bimanual manipulation. In all of them the reference is fixed before the robot is considered. ManipTrans and DexMachina command a floating 6-DoF wrist with no arm chain, and DexMan drives a G1 arm through IK but keeps the robot at the origin, so neither arm reachability nor base placement is ever optimized. We reuse their object-side recipe (Sec.~ sec:rl ) and make the reference itself the variable. Generative priors for policy learning. Example-guided RL~ peng2018deepmimic,peng2021amp extends to HOI imitation~ wang2023physhoi,xu2025intermimic and to tracking-as-reward execution~ luo2024omnigrasp,kalaria2025dreamcontrol . The two works closest to ours resolve the embodiment mismatch after the motion exists. Chen et al.~ chen2024object guide an RL finger controller with a generative prior that emits only wrists, fixed before the robot is considered, and DemoDiffusion~ park2025demodiffusion denoises a retargeted human trajectory with a robot diffusion policy that stays close to that trajectory and so inherits its reachability. DreamControl-v2~ harithas2026dreamcontrol avoids retargeting by training in robot space, and fine-tuning a human-space generator on reachable data would likewise remove our inference cost; both need robot-feasible data for every embodiment, which a method like ours would have to produce, and yield one generator per robot. However, none of them keeps one frozen human-space generator: we resolve reachability inside its sampling loop and handle base placement for a full humanoid arm chain. Method sec:method makes a frozen HOI generator embodiment-aware at inference time (Fig.~ fig:pipeline ). The generator only needs to expose a decodable wrist pose and separate hand and object tokens (Sec.~ sec:gen ). A differentiable IK energy on the target humanoid steers its sampler and solves for the robot's base (Sec.~ sec:ik ), and we retarget the guided motion and train a PPO tracking policy on it (Sec.~ sec:rl ). title: What Would Removing This Corruption Change? Failure Attribution for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are sensitive to visual corruptions, but knowing that a corruption is typically harmful does not establish whether removing it would benefit the current episode. Furthermore, when several corruptions co-occur, deciding what to correct requires understanding which ones contribute to failure risk and how much their removal would help. We define this problem as failure attribution. Detecting corruption presence alone cannot answer this question, as corruptions can be present but relatively harmless, while directly measuring removal benefits requires costly paired policy rollouts with and without the corruption present. To address this, we introduce a factorized risk model that learns separate representations of the scene and corruptions, allowing us to estimate removal benefits through latent intervention from the current image and task instruction, without paired clean images or additional counterfactual rollouts. We evaluate our approach on OpenVLA and $π_{0.5}$ in simulation and $π_{0.5}$-DROID on a Franka robot. Our method outperforms monolithic and vision-language-model (VLM) baselines, including achieving approximately 3x lower attribution error than frontier VLMs. We also demonstrate our method adapts to execution context and corruption intensity, and can be used for online failure monitoring on hardware.

The plot shows the predicted failure risk and per-corruption attribution estimates at every execution step. Because of their high values, fog and light receive high-priority correction recommendations, while the distractor receives low attribution. To address this, we introduce a factorized risk model that learns separate representations of the scene and corruptions, allowing us to estimate removal benefits through latent intervention from the current image and task instruction, without paired clean images or additional counterfactual rollouts. We evaluate our approach on OpenVLA and in simulation and -DROID on a Franka robot. Our method outperforms monolithic and vision-language-model (VLM) baselines, including achieving approximately 3x lower attribution error than frontier VLMs. We also demonstrate our method adapts to execution context and corruption intensity, and can be used for online failure monitoring on hardware. Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models~ kim2024openvla,black2024pi0,black2025pi05 have emerged as generalist robotic policies capable of performing manipulation tasks directly from images and natural language instructions. However, their reliance on visual input makes them sensitive to visual corruptions~ fei2026liberoplus . For example, viewpoint changes and sensor noise have considerable impact on OpenVLA's performance, reducing success rate from 76.5 to 1.1 and 19.3 , respectively~ fei2026liberoplus . These effects motivate knowing how each corruption influences a policy during execution. A straightforward approach is to estimate average failure rates for each corruption combination based on historical data. However, these averages assign the same prediction to episodes with the same corruption combination, regardless of corruption intensity or the current scene context. Knowing that a corruption is harmful on average therefore does not establish whether removing it would reduce failure risk in the current episode. When several corruptions co-occur, this problem is compounded: we need to determine which corruptions contribute to the current failure risk and which would offer the greatest benefit if removed. We call this failure attribution: quantifying each corruption's contribution by asking, ``How much would failure risk decrease if this corruption were removed?'' Answering this question can guide whether and how to correct an execution failure. However, failure attribution presents two challenges. First, corruption presence alone does not establish its effect on performance. A corruption may be clearly visible yet have little impact on a particular policy, so detecting it does not indicate whether correcting it would help. Prior works address neighboring problems, including improving robustness through corruption-inclusive training~ fei2026liberoplus,xie2026strongvla or input restoration~ orjuela2026improving , and predicting failure through online monitoring~ gu2025safe,li2026sentinelvla,agia2024sentinel,xu2025faildetect . However, these approaches do not directly answer the attribution question of how much removing each corruption would reduce failure risk. Second, directly measuring this removal benefit requires intervention: executing the policy repeatedly with and without each corruption from the same underlying state. Because a corruption's effect depends on which others remain present, exhaustively characterizing these interactions requires covering a large majority of combinations, rather than just single corruptions. Such comparisons are expensive in simulation and difficult to reproduce during deployment, where repeated failed executions can also put hardware at risk. We therefore seek to estimate removal effects from the available observation, without executing these counterfactual rollouts. To address these challenges, we introduce a factorized risk model that estimates each corruption's contribution to failure risk from the current image and task instruction alone. The model learns separate latent representations of the scene and corruptions. By intervening on the corruption latent while holding the scene latent fixed, it estimates how failure risk would change if a corruption were removed ( ), without modifying the physical scene or rerunning the policy. We evaluate the model on OpenVLA and in simulation and -DROID on hardware. Our experiments validate that our approach accurately estimates per-corruption attributions, captures interactions between co-occurring corruptions, and learns sensitivity to scene context and corruption intensity. Under co-occurring corruptions, it achieves approximately 3x lower attribution error than frontier VLMs. Hardware experiments demonstrate our approach can be used for online monitoring ( ) as corruptions change during an episode. In summary, we: Formulate failure attribution for VLA models as estimating the reduction in failure risk from removing individual visual corruptions. Introduce a factorized risk model that estimates these removal effects through latent interventions, using only the current image and task instruction. Evaluate the method on OpenVLA and in simulation and -DROID on hardware, demonstrating attribution under co-occurring corruptions, sensitivity to execution context and corruption intensity, and online failure monitoring. Related Work Robustness Analysis Prior works evaluate VLA robustness to visual and environmental disturbances through benchmarks such as LIBERO-Plus~ fei2026liberoplus and The Colosseum~ pumacay2024colosseum , as well as adversarial attacks~ wang2025exploringadversarial . Other approaches improve robustness through corruption-aware training~ fei2026liberoplus,xie2026strongvla or input restoration~ orjuela2026improving . These works characterize or mitigate aggregate sensitivity, but do not attribute an observed failure to the responsible corruption, which is the gap this work addresses. Failure Detection and Uncertainty Quantification Online failure monitors use internal policy representations~ gu2025safe,li2026sentinelvla , action consistency~ agia2024sentinel , failure-free training~ xu2025faildetect , out-of-distribution detection~ sinha2022ood , or conformal prediction~ ren2023knowno . VLM-based methods provide post-hoc failure explanations~ liu2023reflect,duan2025aha , while image-region attribution links reliance on nuisance features to poor performance~ zhang2026embodied . These approaches predict whether failure is likely or identify generic visual cues, but do not quantify the counterfactual effect of removing a specific corruption. Our factorized latent model estimates this effect without paired counterfactual trajectories. title: Design and Control of a Multimodal Legged-Aerial Robot Through Separate Control Contraction Metrics
comment: Presented at 2026 IEEE International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems, Pittsburgh PA
summary: The integration of dynamic legged locomotion and aerial mobility offers versatility that is deterred by challenges in payload distribution, actuation, and the contrasting requirements of both domains. In this paper, we present the design and operation of a multimodal quadrupedal aerial-legged robot. The presence of legged aerial systems also allows for thruster-assisted legged locomotion, which we make possible with a unified control framework using Control Contraction Metrics (CCM). We search for separate domain-specific contraction metrics for walking and flight independently offline and unify them using an online energy-based Control Lyapunov Function Quadratic Program (CLF QP). This enables optimal, cross-domain control allocation, which we show using simulations. We also show experimental results that validate the mechanical viability of our hardware and the paradigm of thruster-assisted trotting. The stability of said experiments motivates the deployment of the control framework for multimodal operations.
full_text: The integration of dynamic legged locomotion and aerial mobility offers versatility that is deterred by challenges in payload distribution, actuation, and the contrasting requirements of both domains. In this paper, we present the design and operation of a multimodal quadrupedal aerial-legged robot. The presence of legged aerial systems also allows for thruster-assisted legged locomotion, which we make possible with a unified control framework using Control Contraction Metrics (CCM). We search for separate domain-specific contraction metrics for walking and flight independently offline and unify them using an online energy-based Control Lyapunov Function Quadratic Program (CLF QP). This enables optimal, cross-domain control allocation, which we show using simulations. We also show experimental results that validate the mechanical viability of our hardware and the paradigm of thruster-assisted trotting. The stability of said experiments motivates the deployment of the control framework for multimodal operations. Introduction Robotic biomimicry of birds' dynamic bipedal and flight locomotion can be a significant ordeal. The prohibitive design restrictions, such as a tight power budget, limited payload, complex multi-modal actuation and perception, an excessive number of active and passive joints involved in each mode, sophisticated control, and environment-specific models, just to name a few, have alienated these concepts. It is worth noting that, as multi-modality has secured birds' (and other species) survival in complex environments, similar manifestations in mobile robots lock_multi-modal_2013 can be rewarding and important. In this work, we will report our legged-aerial quadrupedal robot's first multi-modal operations, including thruster assisted dynamic trotting and hovering. Our long-term objective has remained to integrate dynamic legged locomotion and aerial mobility in a single platform. Our robot design primarily focused on mass allocation to minimize the total cost of transport, which consequently yields smaller actuation bulk in the system, and component selection for the flight unit was systematically made to achieve successful lift-off while not too much negatively affecting dynamic legged mobility. Standard control theory have struggle with dynamic, changing trajectory tracking. A contraction metric is a Riemannian metric, with respect to which the distance between any two solutions of a differential equation is decreasing. Unlike a Lyapunov function, which measure the decreasing generalized distance between a point and an attractor such as an equilibrium, contraction does not require any knowledge about the position of the attractor. Simply, contraction ensures incremental stability between two trajectories, instead of the stability of an equilibrium point. Control Contraction Metrics (CCM) ensures that small displacements in directions orthogonal to the span of the control inputs must be contracting. The existence of a CCM can be formulated as a convex problem as specified in previous works manchester_control_2017, singh_robust_2023 . To overcome the computational bottleneck of global stability analysis for this coupled hybrid system, we propose a unified control framework inspired by CCMs. We outline this work's contributions as follows: The design and operation of a multimodal legged-aerial robot. A proposed control framework using contraction theory to create separate metrics for walking and flight, which are then unified online using an energy-based control Lyapunov function quadratic programming (CLF-QP). Experimental results on hardware, with a decoupled heuristic control policy to demonstrate the capabilities of thruster-assisted trotting and flying. These experiments seek to prove that the physical paradigm of combining thrusters with legs is robust. The paper is then structured as follows: we begin with showing the related work with multi-modal robot and CCM, followed by a brief discussion and design choice of the robot's hardware, actuators, and aerial subsystems. Then, we will proceed to the derivations of the CCM synthesis and the online controller, followed by the experimental results and discussions, and ended with the concluding remarks. Related Work Multi-modality in a robot expands the robot's capability in performing tasks that a single mode can't do, such as a ground-aerial robot that can use ground locomotion to traverse a relatively flat terrain efficiently and fly over an obstacle when the ground locomotion is unable to drive through it. Therefore, the robot's range and reach can be expanded greatly by utilizing both locomotion modes, and they can augment each other if the design allows it. There are various robot designs related to ground-aerial robots, such as, a bipedal robot with quadrotor propulsion attached to its torso kim_bipedal_2021 , a transforming quadruped that can switch between legged and aerial modes wang_dynamic_2025 , thruster-assisted hopping robot haldane_repetitive_2017 , a quadrotor with active wheels underneath araki2017multi, meiri_flying_2019 , a quadrotor encased in a rolling cage where the thrusters can drive the cage to perform ground locomotion tagliabue2020shapeshifter , ornithopters with wheels for ground locomotion peterson_wing-assisted_2011 , and a transforming robot that can reorient its appendages to transition between a UGV and UAS modes sihite_multi-modal_2023 . Thrusters can be used to augment ground locomotion capabilities to assist in stabilization by using them to satisfy ground contact constraints sihite_optimization-free_2021, wang_thruster-enhanced_2025 , can also assist in jumping sihite_locomotion_2026, krishnamurthy_contact-implicit_2026 and in steep slopes pitroda_quadratic_2024, krishnamurthy_enabling_2024, krishnamurthy_wair_2026 where is not normally possible using just legged locomotion. We aim to use CCM as a control framework to create metrics for walking and flight to be used in our legged-aerial multi-modal robot. There have been many works that use Control Contraction Metrics (CCM) for either Robust or Adaptive Control manchester_control_2017, manchester_robust_2018, singh_robust_2023, zhao_tube-certified_2022, tsukamoto_learning-based_2021, tsukamoto_neural_2021 . Manchester and Slotine manchester_control_2017 introduced the idea of Control contraction metrics for a nonlinear system for universal exponential stabilizability. The control contraction metric can then be used for real-time optimization which involves finding a geodesic to the desired state from the current state and finding the control input. This problem is simpler than executing model predictive control. This work then extended to obtain Robust CCMs by using a metric to synthesis a nonlinear state feedback controller manchester_robust_2018 . This powerful tool for trajectory, while setting the foundation of our research, assumes exact model knowledge. To solve control problems at the scale of multicopters and drones, one requires careful structuring of the CCM metric and the polynomial optimization problem to bypass the computational complexity of synthesis. Singh et al. singh_robust_2023 extended this CCM synthesis with robust feedback control on multicopters and implemented this with experimental results on hardware. This was achieved using exploiting the structure of the problem and Sum of Squares Programming to obtain a metric for a high-dimensional dynamical system. Sun et al. sun_learning_2021 were able to obtain a tracking controller for different dynamical systems using contraction metrics that were learned using a Neural Network, with controller execution much faster than MPC. Exploring data-driven approaches, Tsukamoto et al. tsukamoto_neural_2021 introduced Neural Contraction Metrics (NCMs) by training LSTM networks to globally approximate these metrics. The NCM approach derives provably stable, dual estimation and control policies that are strictly optimized for disturbance attenuation. Shiromoto et al. shiromoto_distributed_2019 proposed decentralized control for large networks using contraction theory by forcing a sum-separable global metric, which guarantees stabilization around a target trajectory. Their results demonstrate that utilizing separable structures to break complex global metrics into solvable localized pieces is highly effective. While CCMs have been used to control aerial robots and other simpler systems such as inverted pendulums manchester_unifying_2018 , we also propose a way to extend this to legged robots. Quick Design Overview Consumables applied in the metal housing in standard actuators and other supporting components are considered as the bulk of mass in legged robots. Actuators compensate for major external loads, and any design flaw would lead to the concentration of forces internally and consequently yield failures. As a result, the design aims at higher safety factors and often achieve extra hardware security through massive metal housing and support parts. To avoid this problem, the fabrication of our robot took place based on embedding electronics and mechanical components precisely at the locations found by previous works. We utilize the MarkForged 3D printer in this section. In this process, the circular spline was embedded inside the actuator housings, and other components, including wave generators and flexsplines, were embedded at the subsequent steps. The actuator assembly can be seen in Fig.~ fig:actuator-assembly . The benefits of this approach are as follows. First, a considerable payload reduction can be achieved for a feasible and working platform. Second, system components can be precisely located at predetermined locations which are aimed at enhancing efficiency and reducing payload. Last, the model and robot can be matched better, which is important for model-based control design. Our legged-aerial quadrupedal robot, shown in Fig.~ fig:cover , stands at 2.5 ft (0.8 m) tall and is approximately 1 ft (0.3 m) wide. It is fabricated from reinforced thermoplastic materials through additive manufacturing and has a total weight of 12 kg. It hosts on-board power electronics and, currently, is powered using an external power supply. The robot's leg is constructed of four identical legs, where each leg has three active joints (hip frontal, hip sagittal, and knee joints), and the lower leg linkages form a parallelogram mechanism. Therefore, the robot possesses a total of twelve leg actuators. Each leg actuator is custom-made with a pancake brushless-DC motor winding from T-motor with a KV rating of 400. The motors are actuated by powerful ELMO amplifiers that are located away from the actuator and closer to the body to minimize inertia. These amplifiers are connected on an EtherCAT bus that enables high-speed bidirectional data transfer from a host computer, to command the desired joint position and receive the actual joint position from magnetic joint encoders. A Harmonic Drive set (flexspline, circular spline, and wave generator) is used for gear reduction with the following gear ratios: 30, 50, and 100 for knee, hip sagittal, and hip frontal, respectively. Some of the power components are embedded into the 3D printed parts, as shown in Fig.~ fig:actuator-assembly . The current integration has made the robot self-sustained for stable, blind walking and trotting gaits. We note that currently the platform relies on an off-board body orientation sensing system, which soon will be replaced with an on-board inertial measurement unit with negligible weight. For flight, the robot is fitted with a frame made of an aluminum hexagonal composite structure sandwiched between carbon fiber plates, which sits on a pair of carbon fiber rails. Additively manufactured motor mounts are embedded in the frame on which the propeller motor is fastened. Custom made hubs house four carbon fiber propellers at a pitch angle of 15 degrees with a diameter of 13 inches. The propeller motors

title: Real-Time Disturbance-Aware Koopman Model Predictive Control for Quadrotors in Spatially Varying Winds
summary: Reliable quadrotor flight in disturbed environments requires predictive models that remain accurate as unmodeled aerodynamic effects change during deployment. We introduce a disturbance-aware Koopman Control Family (DA-KCF) framework that preserves an offline-identified nominal model while learning only a disturbance-induced correction online. A reference-dependent KCF is first learned from simulation data and calibrated using limited hardware data. During deployment, the nominal KCF remains fixed while a lightweight residual ensemble learns a low-dimensional disturbance correction from causal state-command-state transitions. The Adaptive DA-KCF model is incorporated into MPC, where disturbance corrections are evaluated along the prediction horizon to optimize position and yaw references sent to the onboard stabilizing controller. Hardware experiments on a nano-quadrotor under uniform wind and a spatially varying wake demonstrate that online adaptation improves multi-step prediction and trajectory tracking as disturbance-induced model mismatch increases, while satisfying real-time control requirements.
full_text: Real-Time Disturbance-Aware Koopman Model Predictive Control for Quadrotors in Spatially Varying Winds Stella Kombo , Masih Haseli , Alejandro A. Stefan-Zavala , Peter I. Renn , Morteza Gharib , and Joel W. Burdick S. Kombo, M. Haseli, A. A. Stefan-Zavala, P. I. Renn, M. Gharib, and J. W. Burdick are with the Division of Engineering and Applied Science, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA. Reliable quadrotor flight in disturbed environments requires predictive models that remain accurate as unmodeled aerodynamic effects change during deployment. We introduce a disturbance-aware Koopman Control Family (DA-KCF) framework that preserves an offline-identified nominal model while learning only a disturbance-induced correction online. A reference-dependent KCF is first learned from simulation data and calibrated using limited hardware data. During deployment, the nominal KCF remains fixed while a lightweight residual ensemble learns a low-dimensional disturbance correction from causal state--command--state transitions. The Adaptive DA-KCF model is incorporated into MPC, where disturbance corrections are evaluated along the prediction horizon to optimize position and yaw references sent to the onboard stabilizing controller. Hardware experiments on a nano-quadrotor under uniform wind and a spatially varying wake demonstrate that online adaptation improves multi-step prediction and trajectory tracking as disturbance-induced model mismatch increases, while satisfying real-time control requirements. Introduction intro Autonomous aerial robots are increasingly being considered for inspection, delivery, monitoring and human mobility tasks in densely built environments~ rob . Such missions require multi-rotors to operate around buildings, above rooftops, through corridors and other confined structures while maintaining accurate trajectory tracking and satisfying state and actuation constraints. Reliable flight in these settings remains challenging since quadrotors are nonlinear, underactuated systems whose performance can degrade when aerodynamic effects are not adequately represented by the prediction or control model~ neurofly2024,erman2018 . The challenge is particularly pronounced in urban environments, where interactions between incoming flow and surrounding structures generate spatially varying wakes, vortices, recirculation zones and accelerated flows around building edges~ wind_char . Consequently, the disturbances experienced by the aerial vehicle can vary significantly along a single flight trajectory. Aerodynamic disturbances have previously been addressed at several levels of aerial-robot modeling and control. Classical approaches mainly rely on feedback to reject external disturbances and modeling errors during flight~ mellinger2011minimumsnap . Analytic aerodynamic models, such as linear/quadratic rotor-drag terms, augment nominal dynamics with low-order aerodynamic effects while remaining compatible with real-time control~ Faessler2018 . Data-driven approaches instead learn residual dynamics or full-state transition models from flight data, capturing complex effects that are difficult to model analytically. These learned effects can improve prediction and control for high-performance drone flight~ bauersfeld2021neurobem, torente, chee2022knodempc . Although such models can be identified offline and used efficiently online, their accuracy degrades when the vehicle encounters dynamics not represented in the identification data. A complementary line of work uses measured or predicted spatial flow information to aid wind-aware trajectory planning and penalize paths that enter adverse flow regions~ ware2016windfield . High-fidelity computational fluid dynamics can resolve complex urban flow structures~ galway2012urban , but their computational costs limit direct use in online prediction and high-rate control~ galway2011urbanwind . Learned flow surrogates provide a tractable alternative for wind-informed planning~ stefanzavala2026fanarray, renn2026windinformed . However, disturbed regions cannot always be avoided when geometric constraints, mission requirements or unknown wakes force the vehicle to traverse them. When this occurs, unmodeled disturbances can induce persistent mismatch between nominal predictions and the realized vehicle response, degrading tracking and stability. Adaptive, observer-based and learning-based controllers compensate for these effects by estimating disturbances, adapting model parameters or learning residual corrections online~ drewadaptivecontrol,benevides2022disturbance,neurofly2024 . For predictive control, these corrections must also be propagated over the prediction horizon without requiring online retraining of the full dynamics model. This motivates learning a nominal model offline from broad system excitation, while adapting to unmodeled disturbance-induced discrepancies during deployment. Koopman-based models provide a structured nominal predictor that can be learned offline and used efficiently online, making them potentially suitable for disturbance augmentation. By representing nonlinear dynamics through observables in a function space, finite-dimensional approximations can be incorporated into model predictive control~ williams2015edmd, korda2018koopman and have been applied to quadrotor prediction and trajectory tracking~ folkestad2022koopnet, rajkumar2025realtime . The Koopman Control Family (KCF)~ haseli2026koopmancontrol represents nonlinear and state-dependent control systems via a family of linear operators parameterized by the control input. However, existing KCF methods do not explicitly represent disturbances that arise during deployment~ haseli2025extensions . Koopman methods have also been extended to disturbance estimation and online adaptation. Disturbance-observer approaches learn disturbance models for online compensation~ jia2024evolver , while adaptive Koopman methods update residual or lifted dynamics~ singh2025adaptive,zhou2025noregret . For quadrotors, related work either switches among pre-identified Koopman models across operating conditions~ oh2024koopmanwind or augments nominal predictors with residual corrections~ todde2026residual . These approaches do not formulate online adaptation as a disturbance-dependent extension of an input-dependent KCF. This leaves open how to preserve a pretrained nominal KCF while adapting only to disturbance-induced discrepancies online within real-time predictive control, without retraining the full model. To address this gap, we introduce a disturbance-aware Koopman Control Family (DA-KCF) and apply it to real-time predictive control of multi-rotors. We first identify a nominal KCF from simulation data and calibrate it using hardware data, capturing the coupled vehicle-onboard controller response while keeping the nominal model fixed during deployment. We then adopt a structured separable approximation , where is the nominal reference-dependent KCF and is a disturbance-dependent modification. For real-time deployment, the disturbance-dependent effect is realized through a low-dimensional correction learned online and propagated through the predictive horizon, while the calibrated nominal KCF and onboard stabilization controller remain fixed. We validate the method on a nano-quadrotor under previously unmodeled aerodynamic disturbances. Experiments include figure-eight tracking in uniform fan-array flows and traversal through a spatially varying wake generated by a building-like obstacle. The results demonstrate online adaptation of the predictive dynamics, improved trajectory tracking as disturbance-induced model mismatch increases, and real-time execution within the control deadline. title: Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting
comment: Accepted at ACCV 2026 (Oral). Includes the supplementary material as appendix. Code: https://github.com/MarcelRogge/occlusion-aware-3dgs
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting grows a dense scene from a sparse initialization through adaptive density control (ADC), driven by per-Gaussian statistics gathered during rendering. These statistics pass a frustum-based visibility filter blind to occlusion: fully occluded Gaussians still count as observed, diluting the averaged gradient signal and suppressing densification precisely where geometry is occluded. We correct this with an occlusion-aware filter that restricts densification statistics to views in which a Gaussian actually contributes, and replace the criterion's raw view-count normalizer with an average-contribution one. Integrated into a StopThePop-based framework, the two together improve every image-quality metric over the occlusion-blind baseline on occlusion-heavy scenes (up to 6% lower LPIPS), at less than half the Gaussians a view-count normalizer requires. Under the longer schedules these large scenes require, the count stays bounded where most criteria diverge, and on smaller benchmarks our method stays competitive at a fraction of the competitors' count.
full_text: Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting Marcel Rogge René Schuster Didier Stricker 3D Gaussian Splatting grows a dense scene from a sparse initialization through adaptive density control (ADC), driven by per-Gaussian statistics gathered during rendering. These statistics pass a frustum-based visibility filter blind to occlusion: fully occluded Gaussians still count as observed, diluting the averaged gradient signal and suppressing densification precisely where geometry is occluded. We correct this with an occlusion-aware filter that restricts densification statistics to views in which a Gaussian actually contributes, and replace the criterion's raw view-count normalizer with an average-contribution one. Integrated into a StopThePop-based framework, the two together improve every image-quality metric over the occlusion-blind baseline on occlusion-heavy scenes (up to lower LPIPS), at less than half the Gaussians a view-count normalizer requires. Under the longer schedules these large scenes require, the count stays bounded where most criteria diverge, and on smaller benchmarks our method stays competitive at a fraction of the competitors' count. Left: top-down overview of the large alameda scene (modified reconstruction; for orientation only). Most geometry is occluded from any given position. Right: crops of the marked locations. Occlusion-blind densification (such as StopThePop) systematically starves occluded regions of Gaussians; our occlusion-aware approach resolves the missing detail. fig:teaser Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl3Dgaussians represents a milestone in 3D scene reconstruction and novel-view synthesis. It introduced a large multi-component system, with a tile-based rasterizer and adaptive density control (ADC) purpose-built for the new representation. Follow-up works improve these components largely in isolation, many focusing on ADC, which is essential for growing a dense reconstruction from the sparse initialization. However, we find that the accumulation of the densification statistics at the root of all ADC decisions has a fundamental flaw: the frustum-based visibility filter that gathers them tests only whether a Gaussian could appear in a view, not whether it actually contributes to the rendered image. A fully occluded Gaussian yields zero gradients, yet the filter still counts its view in the criterion's denominator, dragging the average down and stalling densification wherever geometry is occluded. The resulting under-densification grows with the degree of occlusion and degrades quality most where high detail and occlusion co-occur. Large, occlusion-heavy scenes such as multi-room apartments are affected most severely ( ). We correct this with an occlusion-aware visibility filter that updates a Gaussian's statistics only from views in which it is actually rendered; densification then reaches occluded regions whenever their level of detail requires it. We further find that normalizing the accumulated gradient by a raw view count does not match the contribution-weighted nature of the tracked gradients. We derive a more natural normalizer that accumulates a Gaussian's average contribution to each rendered view. To validate our occlusion-aware densification, we build a framework around StopThePop~ radl2024stopthepop that consolidates established densification improvements from separate prior methods into a strong baseline. We evaluate both changes on this baseline and directly on StopThePop. On the occlusion-heavy Zip-NeRF~ barron2023zipnerf scenes, the resulting method outperforms StopThePop on all image-quality metrics, reducing LPIPS by up to . Its Gaussian count also stays bounded under the longer schedules these large scenes require, where most competing criteria diverge. On smaller benchmarks, it performs comparably to the state of the art with up to fewer Gaussians. Our contributions are as follows: To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to replace the visibility filter itself: the frustum-based test that underlies all densification statistics. Our occlusion-aware filter updates a Gaussian's statistics only from views in which it is actually rendered, independent of the criterion built on top. We introduce a contribution-based densification criterion that is more closely related to the gradient signal used by ADC, leading to better densification decisions, demonstrated on small- and large-scale scenes. We combine both contributions with established densification improvements and other refinements into a strong framework that does not require per-scene tuning and has fewer hyperparameters ( eliminating the unstable scene extent). We will make the code available to the research community. Background and Related Work sec:related Adaptive Density Control sec:preliminaries sec:preliminaries:adc 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl3Dgaussians represents a scene as a set of 3D Gaussians, each defined by a 3D mean position, a 3D covariance matrix (parameterized by a rotation and per-axis scale), an opacity , and a view-dependent color derived from spherical harmonics~ yu2022plenoxels . For rendering, each Gaussian is projected onto the image as a 2D footprint with a screen-space mean and radius. Starting from a sparse point cloud, 3DGS grows and prunes its set of Gaussians via adaptive density control (ADC), executed every 100 iterations after a 500-iteration warm-up and disabled after the first half of training. A scene extent , computed from the training cameras, provides the reference scale for several ADC decisions. Criterion. During rendering, a frustum-based visibility filter accumulates per-Gaussian statistics: the 2D screen-space positional gradient of Gaussian in view , the screen-space radius, and a view count . At each ADC event, a Gaussian is marked for densification if its accumulated gradient magnitude, averaged over the view count, exceeds a predefined threshold ( by default). Densification. To resolve the problem of an insufficient number of Gaussians capturing a region's textural or structural detail (from here on described as under-densification), a marked Gaussian is densified in one of two modes: if it is large relative to the scene extent, it is split into two downscaled children sampled from the parent's distribution, otherwise it is cloned, duplicated, in place. Pruning. Redundant or noisy Gaussians are removed using pruning mechanisms. An opacity prune removes every Gaussian whose opacity falls below a predefined threshold ( ). A size-based prune removes Gaussians whose screen-space radius or world-space scale exceeds a fixed threshold. To clear floater artifacts, 3DGS additionally resets all opacities to near zero ( ) every iterations; important Gaussians recover quickly, floaters stay dim and fall to the opacity prune. StopThePop~ radl2024stopthepop offers a gradual opacity decay as an alternative to the drastic reset. We evaluate both as the (Reset) and (Decay) variants. Adaptive Density Control Improvements All of the following ADC improvements inherit the frustum-based visibility filter described above, which counts every in-frustum Gaussian, occluded or not. We make this filter occlusion-aware ( ). Densification Criterion. AbsGS~ ye2024absgs and GOF~ Yu2024GOF counter gradient cancellation in the accumulation, which otherwise causes under-densification of high-detail regions. PixelGS~ zhang2024pixelgs instead questions the normalization by the observation count and proposes a pixel-count-weighted mean. Grubert ~ Grubert2025improving adopt the PixelGS strategy with an ascending threshold that shifts densification earlier. Taming3DGS~ mallick2024taming3dgs replaces the threshold with a per-Gaussian multi-term score under a fixed densification budget. However, budget-controlled methods require a target count as input, a value that is not known and that a good densification criterion should find. We propose to normalize a Gaussian's accumulated gradient by the accumulated average contributions of its rendered views ( ), rather than the observation count of 3DGS or the visible-pixel count of PixelGS. We also adopt GOF's absolute-gradient signal against cancellation. Densification Step (Split Clone). GOF observes that clones remain clustered and instead samples the child's position from the parent's distribution, while ~ bulo2024revising show that the clone operation introduces an opacity bias. EFA-GS~ wang2025lowfrequencyfirsteliminatingfloating and Deng ~ deng2025improvingdensification3dgaussian drop the clone entirely, and Deng additionally propose a geometrically more meaningful split procedure. Grubert address inconsistencies in the scene-extent computation that governs some ADC decisions by also accounting for the input point cloud. Other works replace the densification step more radically~ kheradmand2024mcmc,cheng2024gaussianpro,fang2024minisplatting,wang2025steepgs . Our experiments also support dropping the clone: we notice large floater clusters due to excessive cloning on scenes where the scene extent is not well matched to the size of detail ( ). We therefore follow the split-only approach of EFA-GS and Deng , including the latter's split procedure. This removes one dependence on the scene extent. Pruning. Grubert restrict the opacity prune to Gaussians that also contribute little; EAGLES~ girish2024eagles and OC2DGS~ RoggeOC2DGS2025 prune low- or non-contributing Gaussians at intervals long enough to observe every training view; ReLaGS~ xiearafa2026relags and RadSplat~ niemeyer2025radsplat prune by maximum contribution over a full pass, at isolated points of the optimization. We prune by maximum contribution, as in ReLaGS and RadSplat, but throughout the optimization, as in EAGLES and OC2DGS. Large-Scale Scenes Large-scale scenes harbor a range of problems for Gaussian Splatting: Kerbl ~ hierarchicalgaussians24 partition them into chunks optimized individually after a coarse full-scene pass. They note problems with the regular densification regime and adopt the maximum 2D screen-space gradient as the criterion. OccluGaussian~ liu2025occlugaussian makes the partitioning occlusion-aware, clustering by what each camera sees so that no chunk contains heavy occlusions, and optimizes chunks individually before merging them. RadSplat observes that lighting variations in the Zip-NeRF dataset~ barron2023zipnerf cause 3DGS to struggle and produce overly smooth results even with an exposure-handling module. SMERF~ duckworth2023smerf performs extensive densification-related hyperparameter tuning on Zip-NeRF yet reports low Gaussian counts, indicating under-densification. Lowering the gradient threshold raises the count only at the cost of more floaters. Neither work identifies the root cause. We argue it is occlusion-blind densification (a cause that exposure correction and hyperparameter tuning leave unaddressed) and provide supporting evidence in . Unlike OccluGaussian, we do not avoid this problem by optimizing occluded regions as individual small scenes, but instead make the densification occlusion-aware, enabling a single full-scene optimization. Method sec:method We build on StopThePop~ radl2024stopthepop , a state-of-the-art Gaussian Splatting renderer whose exact per-pixel depth ordering removes popping artifacts and keeps occlusion boundaries intact. Hybrid transparency~ hahlbohm2025htgs , in contrast, sorts only the front-most Gaussians and composites all remaining ones without enforcing occlusion ordering. Leaving even fully occluded Gaussians with a nonzero contribution stands in opposition to our motivation of occlusion-aware densification. However, our method is not dependent on the per-pixel sorting of StopThePop: it relies only on the per-pixel blending weights that virtually every Gaussian Splatting rasterizer already com

title: HATCH: Hardware-Attested Task Chains for Verifiable Manipulation
comment: 2 pages, 1 table. Accepted at the 5th Workshop on Open Robotics Software, IROS 2026, Pittsburgh, PA, USA. Benchmark repository: https://github.com/shizacharania/hatch-benchmark
summary: Capability claims in robot manipulation are unverifiable, and existing leaderboards are each closed, simulated, or gameable. We propose HATCH, a robot escape room: an openly specified, physically replicable, sensor-scored, and unrehearsable benchmark. Tasks span five skill categories at three difficulty levels and are chained so that the sensor confirming one task's completion unlocks the next, turning a room into a single long-horizon evaluation. Success is confirmed by instrumentation rather than human judgment, scoring is embodiment-agnostic, and object placements are randomized by a run-day seed. Entrants submit attested self-runs (uncut video, sensor logs, and the seed), with occasional organized events for calibration. Task specifications, build guide, bill of materials, and scoring rubrics are released under an open license.
full_text: Capability claims in robot manipulation are unverifiable, and existing leaderboards are each closed, simulated, or gameable. We propose HATCH, a robot escape room: an openly specified, physically replicable, sensor-scored, and unrehearsable benchmark, released under an open license. Why Manipulation Has No Trusted Benchmark Capability claims in robot manipulation are, at present, unverifiable. Results arrive as curated demonstration videos, run on hardware no other lab owns, in environments no other lab can recreate, against self-defined success criteria. Vision and language compounded progress on shared benchmarks; ImageNet is the defining case. Manipulation never acquired one, in part because physical evaluation is expensive: hardware, resets between runs, and human labor. The leaderboards that do exist achieve at most two of the three properties a trusted benchmark requires: openness, physical evaluation, and trustworthy results. RoboLab-120~ robolab120 evaluates entrants in-house, in simulation, which resists gaming but is neither open nor physical: the entrant pool is small, and as of mid-2026, the operating vendor's own model topped the leaderboard~ paxton_leaderboards . RoboArena~ roboarena distributes real-world evaluation across volunteer institutions---an open and physical design---but its team recently disclosed that volunteer evaluators had not completed some assigned evaluations, pulling affected results and flagging low-sample entries~ roboarena_disclosure ; the failure was in the trust layer, not the robots. MolmoSpaces~ molmospaces is fully open but simulation-only, and simulated success does not certify physical capability~ rlbench . Nothing available today is simultaneously open, physical, and trustworthy~ paxton_leaderboards, paxton_progress , so we propose one that is: HATCH, a robot escape room. Benchmark Design Why an escape room. An escape room is a useful evaluation container for three reasons. First, it is bounded and exhaustively specifiable: a finite set of objects, fixtures, and sensors in a defined volume, documentable well enough for a second lab to rebuild. Second, tasks chain when assembled into a room: the sensor confirming one task's completion releases the key, code, or clue for the next, so a room is one long-horizon evaluation rather than a suite of isolated trials. A run that fails partway still yields a score, but the headline result is escape. Third, it is adversarial by construction: evaluators design the room and entrants see it for the first time at evaluation, so there is no home-field advantage and nothing to overfit. A room instance draws from a task pool of five skill categories crossed with three difficulty levels (Table~ fig:matrix ). Instrumented success. Outcomes are confirmed by sensors, not human judgment: color sensors at placement positions, a pressure plate on the checker's final square, seating sensors confirming peg insertion, and an overhead camera checking the pen-cap task. A success signal a machine emits is one a third party can audit. Selection under distractors. Tasks present candidates when only are correct, so a robot must choose, not sweep. The UV task reveals only a subset of the symbols and the photo-matching task pins 5 photographs against 10 objects. Grasping everything scores zero. Embodiment-agnostic scoring. Scoring depends only on task outcomes and elapsed time. Arms, humanoids, and mobile manipulators compete on one leaderboard; the benchmark measures what was accomplished, not what embodiment accomplished it. A room instance. A medium-level room draws one medium task per category and chains them: seating the last shape in the sorting board (spatial) releases the arrow-sequence card; the checker's final square (symbolic) trips the pressure plate that unlocks the photo-matching station (multi-step), whose completed board order opens the token jars (physical/causal); completing the numbered mat releases the poker chips (dexterous), and the final chip dropping through the slot ends the run. Each stage's sensor both scores the stage and gates the next. The run is scored as stages completed plus time, with placements randomized by a run-day seed (Sec.~III). Openness and Verification Everything required to replicate the benchmark is released in the public repository ( ) under an open license: task specifications, a room build guide with bill of materials, scoring rubrics, difficulty-level definitions, and a standard result-reporting format. Objects are commodity items and, where possible, drawn from the YCB set~ ycb , keeping rebuild cost low. The v0.1 pool holds one task per cell, enough to assemble one room per difficulty level, varied between runs by seeded placements. Growing each cell to several interchangeable tasks, so room composition is itself sampled at evaluation, is next on the roadmap, alongside automated scoring and audit tooling. Openness alone does not produce trust; verification is a spectrum of design choices. At one end sit organized events in the DARPA-challenge lineage~ darpa : high trust, low scale. At the other end sits honor-system self-reporting, which demonstrably breaks (RoboArena~ roboarena_disclosure ). We propose attested self-runs as the default middle: entrants rebuild the room from the public guide and submit uncut video, complete sensor logs, and the run-day randomization seed governing object placement. Because success is instrumented, the sensor record carries most of the trust burden, not a reviewer's eye. Occasional organized events then serve as ground-truth calibration for the self-run pool. Open Questions Treating a physical benchmark as open infrastructure imports the software community's maintenance questions regarding versioning, continuous integration, and governance into a domain where the artifact is a room. How should a physical benchmark be versioned, and what is a breaking change when old scores cannot be re-run? Who governs the task pool and audits submissions? How does the pool grow without new tasks leaking to entrants before evaluation? We offer HATCH v0.1 as a concrete first answer to the question upstream of all of these: manipulation needs a benchmark that is open, physical, and trustworthy at once, and no existing leaderboard is all three. 9 J.~X.~Yang, R.~Dagli, A.~Zook, H.~Hadfield, A.~Goyal, S.~Birchfield, F.~Ramos, and J.~Tremblay, ``RoboLab: A High-Fidelity Simulation Benchmark for Analysis of Task Generalist Policies,'' arXiv:2604.09860, 2026. title: MatchCityLoc: Aerial Localization in LoD City Models via Surface Normal Matching
summary: Autonomous Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) navigation in urban environments requires precise pose estimation. Because Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals are often unreliable in cities, visual localization serves as a crucial complement. Within this domain, textureless Level-of-Detail (LoD) city models provide a lightweight and privacy-preserving substitute for heavy 3D textured meshes. However, localizing against abstract geometry is challenging. Existing pipelines typically score 2D silhouette overlaps, which can suffer from severe geometric ambiguities. We present MatchCityLoc, a framework that shifts this paradigm to direct feature matching from a noisy 6-DoF pose prior. By extracting surface normals from the query image using a zero-shot foundation model and matching them against rendered LoD normals, we establish explicit 3D-to-2D correspondences. This enables a Perspective-n-Point (PnP) pose solve, which we iteratively refine through a render-and-match loop. Experiments demonstrate strong pose recall and accurate translation and rotation among the evaluated off-the-shelf LoD-based methods with very few renderings. By bridging the modality gap between aerial imagery and texture-free geometry, MatchCityLoc enables accurate localization using lightweight, privacy-preserving city models.

Limitations MatchCityLoc assumes distinct geometric structures and a sufficiently close full pose prior with overlapping mapped geometry. title: PLaCA: Learning Patch-Level Future Latent Change for Action Generation
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but effective manipulation also requires anticipating how the environment will change. Existing world-action models explore future image prediction and latent dynamics modeling. However, generating complete future images can be computationally expensive, while highly compressed latent representations may obscure local changes. To address these challenges, we propose PLaCA, a world-to-action framework built around future latent change. PLaCA directly predicts spatially structured patch-level future latent change from the current multimodal input, preserving local information about expected environmental changes. We introduce patch-level change-aware supervision to emphasize regions undergoing larger changes and a future-to-action interface that explicitly incorporates predicted future latent change into action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Long show that PLaCA achieves a 79.0% success rate, improving upon the Action-only baseline by 5.0 percentage points. On CALVIN, PLaCA improves the average sequence length from 2.784 to 3.564. These improvements are achieved while updating only 2.95% of the model parameters during the second training stage, demonstrating the effectiveness of future latent change modeling for downstream robotic manipulation.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but effective manipulation also requires anticipating how the environment will change. Existing world-action models explore future image prediction and latent dynamics modeling. However, generating complete future images can be computationally expensive, while highly compressed latent representations may obscure local changes. To address these challenges, we propose PLaCA, a world-to-action framework built around future latent change. PLaCA directly predicts spatially structured patch-level future latent change from the current multimodal input, preserving local information about expected environmental changes. We introduce patch-level change-aware supervision to emphasize regions undergoing larger changes and a future-to-action interface that explicitly incorporates predicted future latent change into action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Long show that PLaCA achieves a 79.0 success rate, improving upon the Action-only baseline by 5.0 percentage points. On CALVIN, PLaCA improves the average sequence length from 2.784 to 3.564. These improvements are achieved while updating only 2.95 of the model parameters during the second training stage, demonstrating the effectiveness of future latent change modeling for downstream robotic manipulation. Introduction Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models typically generate robot actions from current visual observations and language instructions~ rt12022,octo2024,rdt2025 . However, in manipulation tasks such as grasping, pushing, and placing, effective action generation requires more than understanding the current environment. A policy must also consider how its actions may change object positions, contact relations, and local environmental states. To incorporate such future information, recent studies have explored integrating world modeling with VLA policies, motivating the development of world-action modeling (WAM) ~ cen2025worldvla,WorldAgen . Existing approaches represent future information in different ways. Some predict future images or videos~ genie2024,robodreamer2024 , while others model future states or temporal dynamics in latent space~ dreamerv32025,vjepa22025 . Recent studies have further explored compact latent motion representations~ StaMo,CoWVLA,yang2026como . Latent-space modeling has become a widely adopted approach in world modeling and robot learning~ dreamerv32025,vjepa22025,CoWVLA . While pixel-level future prediction provides rich visual details, generating complete future images often involves reconstructing substantial redundant visual content, leading to additional computational costs~ ivideogpt2024,CoWVLA . In contrast, latent-space modeling avoids explicit pixel-level reconstruction, yet choosing an appropriate future representation for robotic manipulation remains an important question. For action generation, it may not be necessary to recover the complete future state or all intermediate dynamics. Instead, a policy may benefit from information about how the environment is expected to change. Recent work has shown that differences between latent states can capture information related to robot motion. StaMo~ StaMo learns highly compressed latent state representations and uses the latent displacement between states to represent robot motion. It also explores latent motion prediction for world modeling. However, latent representations differ in how they preserve spatial information. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:intro (a), when a robot places an object into a box, the changes are mainly concentrated around the robot arm and the object, while much of the background remains unchanged. Highly compressed state representations can encode such changes, but they do not explicitly preserve the correspondence between spatial locations and their latent changes. In contrast, retaining the patch-level spatial structure allows future changes at different image locations to be represented separately, as shown in Fig.~ fig:intro (b). Moreover, the magnitude of future change can vary considerably across patches, while uniform patch supervision does not specifically emphasize regions undergoing larger changes. This motivates our first research question: How can we preserve the spatial structure of future latent change and learn local changes more effectively by accounting for their different magnitudes? Another important question is how future modeling can be effectively coupled with action generation. Prior work has explored different approaches, including jointly learning future prediction and action policies within shared architectures~ WorldAgen,CoWVLA , using predicted future images or video plans to guide downstream control~ cotvla2025,videolanguageplanning2024 , and leveraging learned latent or interaction dynamics for action inference~ VideoWorld,DynBridge . These studies provide different ways of using future information to inform robotic behavior. For the spatially structured future latent change considered in this work, the predicted representation preserves local information about expected environmental changes across image regions. This motivates investigating how such spatially organized predictions can be incorporated into action representations to support action generation. We therefore pose our second research question: How can predicted future latent change be effectively used to support action generation? To address these questions, we propose PLaCA, a world-to-action framework built around future latent change. PLaCA directly predicts spatially structured patch-level future latent change from the current multimodal input and employs patch-level change-aware supervision to emphasize regions with larger changes. We further introduce a future-to-action interface that incorporates the predicted future latent change into the action representation, allowing it to directly contribute to full action-chunk generation. We evaluate PLaCA on LIBERO-Long, achieving a 79.0 task success rate. Ablation studies demonstrate that preserving fine-grained spatial structure, employing change-aware supervision, and incorporating predicted future latent change into action generation through the future-to-action interface contribute to improved downstream manipulation success rates. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We investigate patch-level future latent change modeling, which directly predicts future latent change from the current multimodal input while preserving its spatial structure, providing local future information for action generation. We propose patch-level change-aware supervision, which adjusts the supervision weights according to the magnitude of ground-truth future latent change. Ablation results show that this approach improves closed-loop manipulation performance compared with uniform patch supervision. We design an explicit future-to-action interface that incorporates the final predicted future latent change into the action representation, allowing future information to directly contribute to full action-chunk generation. Related Work World-Action Modeling Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models unify visual observations, language instructions, and robot actions within end-to-end policies, extending large-scale vision-language models toward general-purpose robotic control~ VLA,kim2024openvla,black2025pi0,rt12022,openx2024,octo2024,rdt2025 . While conventional VLAs primarily focus on predicting continuous actions or action sequences from current multimodal observations~ pi052025,gr00tn12025,smolvla2025,tinyvla2024,vlaadapter2026 , recent studies have increasingly incorporated future modeling, enabling policies to reason not only about what to do but also about what may happen after an action is executed~ cen2025worldvla,zhu2025uwm,cotvla2025,videolanguageplanning2024 . This trend has gradually extended VLA research from direct observation-to-action mapping toward joint modeling of environmental dynamics and robot behavior. One line of work models future environmental changes through image or video prediction~ ivideogpt2024 , while other approaches jointly learn future modeling and action generation~ cen2025worldvla,zhu2025uwm . WorldAgen performs future-state prediction and action prediction within a unified Transformer, allowing world modeling and policy learning to share internal representations~ WorldAgen . CoT-VLA uses predicted future images as intermediate visual guidance for subsequent action generation~ cotvla2025 . DynBridge learns interaction dynamics that connect future interaction modeling with robot control~ DynBridge , while Motus further integrates latent action modeling, world modeling, and action generation into a unified framework, using shared latent representations to characterize the relationship between robot behavior and environmental changes~ Motus . DreamVLA combines dynamic-region-guided future information with spatial and semantic cues for action generation~ zhang2025dreamvla , while Mantis learns latent visual foresight with a separate prediction head~ yang2026mantis . Collectively, these studies reflect a growing trend in which future modeling is increasingly coupled with action generation through shared or explicitly connected representations. We focus on directly predicting spatially structured future latent change and incorporating its predicted tokens into the action representation through gated cross-attention. Latent Dynamics Future image and video prediction provides a detailed description of environmental changes, but generating full future frames can be computationally expensive~ robodreamer2024,genie2024 . Recent studies have therefore explored latent state, latent motion, and latent action representations for future modeling and robot control~ bu2025univla ~ lapa2024,vjepa2024,vjepa22025,dreamerv32025 . One line of work focuses on representing dynamics in latent space. CoWVLA separates structural and motion information and learns a continuous latent motion chain to represent temporal evolution~ CoWVLA . CoMo learns continuous latent motion by combining temporal differences with contrastive learning~ yang2026como . StaMo takes a different approach by learning highly compressed latent state representations from individual observations. It shows that differences between these states contain robot motion information and can support action decoding. StaMo further uses state and motion representations as prediction targets for VLA world modeling and explores latent-motion co-training~ StaMo . These studies explore different ways to capture temporal changes in latent space, including continuous motion representations and differences between compact latent states. Another line of work investigates how latent dynamics can support action generation. VideoWorld learns discrete latent codes that represent future visual changes and uses the predicted codes together with visual information for inverse dynamics-based action decoding~ VideoWorld . Latent Bridge instead predicts continuous feature changes to update latent representations, allowing the policy to reduce repeated VLM computation during action generation~ LatentBridge . These approaches illustrate different ways of using learned latent dynamics to support action generation. Our work focuses on learning spatially structured future latent change and using the predicted representation for action generation. title: Multi-View Latent Action Pretraining for Cross-Embodiment Robot Learning from Videos
summary: Action-free videos are an appealing substitute for costly teleoperated data. Latent action models (LAMs) turn videos into a supervision signal by inferring abstract actions between frames. Existing LAMs observe a single camera view, which resolves 6D robot actions only ambiguously missing out-of-plane movements and potential occlusions. We propose a LAM that ingests synchronized multi-camera views using cross-attention to resolve depth and occlusions before compressing them into latent actions. The latent actions are fed into a policy in which a latent expert and an action expert are coupled by sequential flow matching around a frozen VLM backbone. We further evaluate in strict cross-embodiment settings where task-specific demonstrations come from other embodiments. We show that dual-view LAM pretraining improves the decodability of ground-truth 6D actions by 17% compared to single-view, while scaling single-view data by two orders of magnitude is not sufficient to fully recover out-of-plane motions. The downstream policy improves success rate by +13.5% compared to +6.2% for single-view LAM. A single cross-embodiment is sufficient for skill transfer, and adding a second viewpoint outperforms adding up to four further embodiments. The results transfer to hardware where demonstrations come from a human hand improving success rate by +20% over action-only policies in 850 rollouts. We show that video and robot data are complementary, and that benefits of learning from video are task-dependent. Website: https://learnsyslab.github.io/multiview_latent_action_pretraining/

Latent action models (LAMs) turn videos into a supervision signal by inferring abstract actions between frames. Existing LAMs observe a single camera view, which resolves 6D robot actions only ambiguously missing out-of-plane movements and potential occlusions. We propose a LAM that ingests synchronized multi-camera views using cross-attention to resolve depth and occlusions before compressing them into latent actions.
