Introduction Data availability remains a limiting factor for learning robot policies. Recent works propose leveraging action-free video data that contains semantically rich information, which can aid robots in long-term task planning. One approach infers latent actions from videos using an inverse dynamics model (IDM), and conditions a downstream policy on those latents~ schmidt2024learningactactions,bruce2024geniegenerativeinteractiveenvironments,ye2025latentactionpretrainingvideos . The latent actions are an abstract representation describing the transition dynamics in the video. Downstream policy success highly depends on how well the latent actions predict real robot actions. A number of approaches have been proposed to improve this transferability, including grounding latent actions in real robot actions or states chen2025villaxenhancinglatentaction,liang2025clamcontinuouslatentaction and visual pre-processing approaches~ nikulin2025latentactionlearningrequires,bu2026laofrobustlatentaction,bu2025univlalearningacttaskcentric . However, we show that existing single-view approaches cannot sufficiently recover the full 6D poses that define robot actions. Single views capture actions only ambiguously: out-of-plane motion is underdetermined and parts of the scene may be occluded. We therefore propose a Latent Action Model (LAM) that ingests synchronized multi-camera views and attends to image patches across viewpoints---recovering depth and occlusion a single camera leaves ambiguous---before compressing them into a latent action. We demonstrate that this spatial awareness leads to better recoverability of 6D robot actions compared to single-view approaches. Crucially, multiple views are only required during LAM pretraining to improve latent action quality, but not during the policy learning stage where only a single external camera and wrist view are used. A key advantage of learning from video is the ability to leverage cross-embodiment demonstrations, with the ultimate goal of learning from human demonstrations. Most existing works use only videos from the target robot embodiment, or leverage large-scale public datasets that confound different embodiments, tasks, and visual diversity~ ye2025latentactionpretrainingvideos,chen2025villaxenhancinglatentaction,bu2025univlalearningacttaskcentric , making performance attribution to cross-embodiment transfer difficult. We specifically evaluate our policy under cross-embodiment demonstrations, where task-specific demonstrations come from other robots in simulation or humans on hardware. We then add a small number of demonstrations on the target embodiment and investigate performance as we scale. We find that a single cross-embodiment video source already enables transfer learning both in simulation and on hardware. Adding a second viewpoint consistently outperforms adding cross-embodiments, establishing multiple viewpoints as an affordable lever for policy performance. We propose to combine our LAM with a lightweight policy training jointly on the small action-labeled dataset and the much larger video-only set using sequential flow-matching experts. The sequential design provides a strong inductive prior, enabling the action expert to effectively leverage the latent plan. We benchmark our method on LIBERO~ liu2023libero , LIBERO-Plus~ fei25libero-plus , and MimicGen~ mandlekar2023mimicgen , and a real robot using 850 rollouts. Our main contributions are: We propose an approach for multi-view IDM-style video pretraining and a downstream policy improving action-only learning by in simulation and on hardware. Training LAMs on in-domain multi-view videos raises the decodability of ground-truth actions by and policy success rate by over single-view LAMs, and outperforms large-scale single-view pretraining, which does not fully recover out-of-plane motions. We show that a single cross-embodiment already enables skill transfer, and that videos from a second viewpoint outperform adding embodiments. On hardware, dual-view pretraining improves policy success rate by , and we demonstrate skill transfer from human-only demonstrations for novel tasks. Related Work Latent Action Pretraining. Inverse-dynamics models (IDMs) for latent action learning started with LAPO~ schmidt2024learningactactions and Genie~ bruce2024geniegenerativeinteractiveenvironments . The LAPO design of coupling an IDM and FDM (forward dynamics model) forms the template of modern LAM approaches. LAPA~ ye2025latentactionpretrainingvideos adopted this for robotics by finetuning a VLM on latent actions, and subsequently adding a small MLP head to predict actions. villa-X~ chen2025villaxenhancinglatentaction uses robots' proprioceptive states and CLAM~ liang2025clamcontinuouslatentaction and LAOM~ nikulin2025latentactionlearningrequires robot actions during IDM training for physical grounding of the latent actions. However, these methods ground latent actions solely in robot data from the target platform and leave human videos entirely ungrounded. LAOF~ bu2026laofrobustlatentaction introduces optical flow as an intermediate representation to learn latent actions from videos, and UniVLA~ bu2025univlalearningacttaskcentric proposes using DINO features instead of pixels. Those methods still rely on video pre-processing from a single viewpoint, whereas we propose using multiple viewpoints to improve action recoverability. Multi-View Learning. Most robot policies operate on a single external viewpoint~ black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel,octomodelteam2024octoopensourcegeneralistrobot , although recent work shows that 3D spatial perception yields stronger manipulation capabilities~ ze20243ddiffusionpolicy,qian20243dmvp . One approach injects explicit geometric reconstructions using point clouds~ ze20243ddiffusionpolicy , depth maps~ liu2024robouniviewvisuallanguagemodelunified , or voxels. These approaches rely on auxiliary depth sensors or complex reconstruction pipelines that introduce noise. Geometric structure can be learned implicitly using multi-view supervision: RoboUniView~ liu2024robouniviewvisuallanguagemodelunified pretrains a unified view representation from multi-view images, 3D-MVP~ qian20243dmvp pretrains the visual encoder via masked autoencoding over multi-view RGB-D renderings, and CLAMP~ liu2026clamp learns visual representations through a contrastive objective. MV-MWM~ seo2023multiviewmaskedworldmodels and ReViWo~ pang2025reviwo train multi-view encoder-decoders to build viewpoint-robust world models. Concurrent work MVP-LAM~ lee2026mvplam proposes latent action alignment between multiple viewpoints. As latent action models aim to encode robot actions in 3D space, they stand to benefit substantially from 3D-aware pretraining. We propose to leverage multi-view pretraining of LAPA-style models to improve latent action learning. Cross-Embodiment Learning. Videos are a natural source for cross-embodiment learning. Demonstrations from different robots can be architecturally absorbed through per-embodiment input tokenizers~ octomodelteam2024octoopensourcegeneralistrobot , separate action heads~ black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel , or embodiment identity tokens~ nvidia2025gr00tn1openfoundation around a shared trunk. The visual gap can be closed directly by editing pixels through inpainting at test time~ chen2024miragecrossembodiment or train time~ chen2024roviaugrobotviewpoint . The same method can bridge the human--robot gap by rendering a robot at the estimated hand pose~ lepert2025phantomtrainingrobots . These methods make the mechanism of transfer interpretable, but depend on URDFs, renderers, or hand-pose estimators. XSkill~ xu2023xskillcrossembodimentskill discovers embodiment-agnostic skills from unlabeled videos. UniAct~ zheng2025universalactions decodes a vector-quantized codebook of universal behaviors, and bauer2025latentactiondiffusion contrastively aligns end-effector actions across hands and grippers. LAMs can achieve embodiment transfer from video alone without explicit reconstruction. The transfer question, however, remains confounded. Work that leverages aggregated datasets~ chen2025villaxenhancinglatentaction such as OXE~ embodimentcollaboration2025openxembodimentroboticlearning varies embodiment, task, scene, and visual diversity all at once. Those settings make it difficult to quantify cross-embodiment skill transfer. We adopt a controlled protocol in which task-specific video demonstrations stem from other robots in simulation and from human demonstrations on hardware. We seek a policy that predicts an action chunk of future actions from the current context . We learn this policy by imitation. title: RoboCasa-Shift: Stage-Aware Robustness Evaluation of Vision-Language-Action Policies in Long-Horizon Household Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) robustness is commonly summarized by aggregate task success, which obscures how individual executions change under distribution shifts and where failures emerge in long-horizon tasks. We introduce \textbf{RoboCasa-Shift}, a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 that combines controlled single-factor shifts, matched clean-perturbed rollouts in which each pair shares the same underlying settings and differs only in the target shift, and simulator-grounded stage-aware diagnostics. We evaluate GR00T N1.5 on four long-horizon tasks that pass a predefined clean-performance gate under four perturbation factors and three calibrated severity levels, including conditions that drive the evaluated policy to complete task failure, totaling 1,040 formal rollouts. Robustness responses vary substantially across factors and tasks, and increasing severity does not always produce monotonic degradation. For example, one camera condition yields $Δ\mathrm{SR}=0$ despite 8 of 80 matched episodes changing outcome. Stage-aware analysis further shows that the same end-to-end degradation can correspond to different execution-depth profiles. Camera $L_2$ and Gaussian blur $L_1$ both yield $Δ\mathrm{SR}=0.188$, yet their first-stage failure rates are 19.0\% and 36.4\%, respectively. Our findings suggest that VLA robustness should be viewed as a multi-dimensional property of execution rather than a single end-to-end performance measure, motivating evaluation protocols that jointly capture outcome degradation, paired outcome sensitivity, and failure progression. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/HaochengWang23/RoboCasa-Shift.

Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models have become an increasingly important paradigm for robotic manipulation by integrating visual observations, language instructions, and robot actions within unified policy frameworks zitkovich2023rt,kim2024openvla . Despite their growing capabilities, maintaining reliable behavior under distribution shifts remains a key challenge for deployment, as robots may encounter variations in observations, environments, and physical states that differ from those seen during training. Systematically evaluating VLA robustness under such distribution shifts is important for understanding the reliability of these models in robotic applications. Recent robustness benchmarks have expanded the evaluation of VLA policies beyond nominal task settings through diverse controlled distribution shifts and increasingly systematic evaluation protocols robocasa365,fei2025libero,wang2026libero . Despite this broader coverage, robustness is still commonly summarized at the task or evaluation-condition level through aggregate metrics such as success rate. Such summaries do not reveal how individual executions change under a distribution shift or where failures emerge within long-horizon task execution, leaving a need for more diagnostic evaluation at the execution level. Such diagnosis requires controlling episode-level variation for meaningful comparison, since clean and shifted evaluations with different task instances or initial conditions may confound episode difficulty with the target distribution shift. We therefore compare each perturbed execution with a corresponding clean execution under the same underlying task conditions, changing only the target perturbation. This counterfactual pairing provides a controlled basis for identifying episode-level outcome changes associated with the evaluated shift. Even under such controlled comparisons, a binary task outcome provides only a coarse description of failure in long-horizon manipulation. These tasks unfold through a sequence of semantically meaningful subgoals~ dai2026robomme,han2026robocerebra , so two failed executions may terminate after very different amounts of task progress. Stage-aware evaluation can therefore complement final success or failure by tracking semantic progress and identifying the first incomplete subgoal, providing a clearer view of where robustness failures emerge during execution. We introduce RoboCasa-Shift, a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365~ robocasa365 for evaluating VLA policies under controlled distribution shifts in long-horizon household manipulation, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:overview . The benchmark defines controlled single-factor shifts at multiple frozen severity levels and a matched clean-perturbed protocol for episode-level counterfactual comparison. It further incorporates simulator-grounded stage-aware diagnostics to track semantic execution progress and localize where failures emerge during long-horizon task execution. RoboCasa-Shift characterizes robustness from complementary perspectives, including end-to-end task outcomes, episode-level outcome changes, and stage-aware execution behavior. Our evaluation reveals that robustness responses vary across perturbation factors and tasks, and that increasing calibrated severity does not always lead to monotonic degradation in end-to-end performance. Aggregate success rates can also mask considerable episode-level outcome changes, while similar end-to-end degradation can correspond to failures emerging at different semantic depths of task execution. Stage-aware analysis further shows that perturbation severity can alter the semantic depth reached by failed executions, with stronger shifts in some conditions associated with earlier incomplete milestones. The main contributions of this work are as follows: We develop RoboCasa-Shift, a diagnostic robustness benchmark built on RoboCasa365 for long-horizon household manipulation. The benchmark defines controlled single-factor distribution shifts at multiple frozen severity levels under an episode-level clean-perturbed counterfactual protocol, enabling robustness changes to be examined under matched task conditions. We introduce a simulator-grounded stage-aware robustness diagnostic that complements final task success with semantic execution information. Long-horizon tasks are represented through ordered semantic subgoals evaluated by simulator-state predicates, allowing execution progress and the first incomplete subgoal to be tracked for failure localization. We conduct a controlled robustness study on four clean-qualified long-horizon RoboCasa tasks across four perturbation factors and three severity levels, jointly analyzing end-to-end task outcomes, counterfactual episode-level changes, and stage-aware execution depth. The analysis reveals robustness behaviors not captured by aggregate success alone, including heterogeneous severity responses and differences in the semantic depth reached by failed executions. Related Work Vision-Language-Action Models for Robot Manipulation sec:related_vla VLA models have emerged as a promising paradigm for robot manipulation by integrating visual perception, language understanding, and action prediction within a unified policy framework zitkovich2023rt,kim2024openvla . Building on large-scale and heterogeneous robot datasets, subsequent works have further developed generalist policies that can operate across diverse tasks, robot embodiments, and observation or action spaces team2024octo,li2026matters . Recent studies have continued to extend VLA models toward more complex sequential manipulation by improving temporal reasoning and visual grounding during task execution xiao2026ava,liu2026activevla . As VLA policies expand to diverse and complex manipulation settings, evaluating their reliability under distribution shifts becomes increasingly important. Robustness and Generalization Benchmarks for Robot Manipulation sec:related_robustness Existing robot manipulation benchmarks have increasingly emphasized generalization beyond the training distribution by evaluating policies across diverse tasks, environments, and controlled variations liu2023libero,li2024evaluating . More recent benchmarks have substantially expanded this direction by evaluating generalist robot policies under increasingly diverse and systematically controlled distribution shifts robocasa365,fei2025libero,wang2026libero . These benchmarks support systematic analysis across perturbation factors, difficulty levels, and task variations, providing broad measurements of policy robustness and generalization. However, such analyses predominantly characterize performance at the task or evaluation-condition level, providing limited information about how distribution shifts affect the semantic execution process within a long-horizon task. RoboCasa-Shift complements these efforts through controlled distribution-shift evaluation, episode-level counterfactual comparison, and semantic subgoal-aware diagnosis of robustness degradation in long-horizon execution. Long-Horizon and Compositional Manipulation Evaluation sec:related_long_horizon Recent progress in robot manipulation evaluation has extended benchmark tasks from short-horizon skills to long-horizon and multi-stage executions that require policies to coordinate multiple interactions over time li2023behavior,nasiriany2024robocasa,11444456 . Beyond increasing task horizon, several benchmarks further expose the temporal or subtask structure of manipulation tasks to evaluate capabilities such as planning, sequential reasoning, and memory-dependent execution han2026robocerebra,dai2026robomme . Despite these advances, such task structure is primarily used to characterize long-horizon manipulation capabilities themselves, while its role as a diagnostic unit for robustness under controlled distribution shifts remains less explored. RoboCasa-Shift builds on this structured view of long-horizon execution by using semantic subgoals to track execution progress and characterize the semantic depth under distribution shifts. RoboCasa-Shift Benchmark Figure~ fig:method_overview summarizes the overall evaluation pipeline. RoboCasa-Shift defines a diagnostic robustness evaluation protocol for long-horizon household manipulation. It combines clean-competence task screening, controlled single-factor shifts with frozen severity levels, and matched clean-perturbed counterfactual rollouts. RoboCasa's official task-success criterion is retained for end-to-end evaluation, while semantic subgoals tracked through simulator-state predicates provide complementary stage-aware diagnostics of execution progress. The formal study in this paper instantiates this protocol on the clean-qualified task suite described below. Task Suite sec:task_suite We screen 16 pre-frozen RoboCasa365 Composite-Seen tasks robocasa365 , with ordering and clean-performance thresholds fixed before any perturbation results are observed. To avoid conflating perturbation-induced failures with insufficient nominal task competence, we apply a predefined clean-performance screen before perturbation evaluation. Each candidate is first evaluated over 10 clean rollouts; tasks with at most three successes are excluded as clean-floor cases, while the remaining candidates are extended to 20 rollouts. We retain all and only tasks achieving at least 12/20 clean successes, resulting in the four-task formal suite summarized in Table~ tab:task_suite . The complete screening results are provided in Appendix~ app:task_selection . The reported diagnostic milestone count is used only for stage-aware analysis and is distinct from official task-structure metadata, as described in Section~ sec:stage_tracking . Controlled Distribution Shifts sec:controlled_shifts RoboCasa-Shift considers four representative single-factor shifts that preserve the task objective while perturbing distinct sources of variation in household manipulation. title: KPHarness: Co-Evolving Knowledge and Probing for Long-Horizon Gaming Harnesses
summary: A failed gaming trajectory reveals that an agent needs intervention, but not necessarily how its execution harness should change. Effective harness adaptation therefore requires gathering diagnostic evidence, rather than merely proposing alternative recovery rules. We present KPHarness, a framework that adapts the external execution harness of a frozen vision-language-action model through knowledge-probing co-evolution. Recovery knowledge supplies context-specific intervention hypotheses that guide active probing; probe outcomes reveal when these hypotheses apply and provide evidence for refining both recovery knowledge and later probe selection. This reciprocal process allows the harness to improve not only which interventions it applies, but also how it investigates failures. KPHarness separates fast policy execution from a slow research loop that translates accumulated knowledge and probing evidence into bounded harness revisions. Each revision is compared with the incumbent under matched sandbox conditions and accepted only when the paired evaluation shows improvement. Recoveries supported by further validation are retained for cross-task reuse, while immediate interaction feedback and delayed episode-success credit update action- and knowledge-probing policies during adaptation. Experiments on Minecraft tasks spanning mining, combat, and crafting show improved task coverage over bare policy execution, a manually specified fixed harness, and knowledge-only harness evolution with non-adaptive probing. Evaluation on previously unseen tasks further shows improved task completion with the evolved harness, knowledge bank, and probing policies held fixed,

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models brohan2023rt, kim2024openvla, chen2025combatvla, li2025jarvis, wang2026unified connect visual observations and language instructions with low-level control, enabling increasingly capable agents in interactive environments. Long-horizon gaming, however, exposes limitations beyond single-step action prediction. Even a capable VLA may repeatedly execute an ineffective action, fail to recover from a stalled trajectory, or overlook experience relevant to the current failure. As interaction horizons grow, performance therefore depends not only on the capabilities encoded in model parameters, but also on the external harness that governs how the model acts, probes, remembers, and recovers. Existing work improves long-horizon VLA execution through prompting, memory, recovery, and hierarchical control li2025towards, fan2025long, yang2025lohovla , but these mechanisms are often manually designed and fixed at deployment. Recent automatic harness methods instead search for prompts, tools, memory, and control logic from execution feedback lee2026meta, chen2026harnessx, lou2026autoharness . Such methods typically evaluate harness modifications through their execution outcomes. Visual gaming introduces an additional challenge: a failed trajectory often reveals what happened but not why. For example, an unsuccessful attack may result from target loss, insufficient range, an obstacle, or insufficient persistence, each requiring different recovery knowledge. Consequently, repeatedly trying harness modifications is inefficient when the underlying failure remains ambiguous. turns automatic harness evolution from outcome-driven search into evidence-guided evolution through knowledge–probing co-evolution: evolving recovery knowledge provides context-specific intervention hypotheses that can focus subsequent probing, while probe outcomes determine their applicability and provide evidence for refining both knowledge and future probe selection. These challenges motivate our central question: [ colback=white, colframe=gray, arc=3mm, boxrule=0.8pt, shadow= 0.5mm -0.5mm 0mm black!50!white ] Can transferable recovery knowledge guide what a harness should probe under ambiguous failures, while probe outcomes identify applicable knowledge and refine subsequent probing and knowledge selection? Existing harness search proposes modifications primarily from execution outcomes. In visually ambiguous environments, however, the same failure outcome may admit multiple incompatible explanations. We therefore treat harness evolution as a sequential process of hypothesis formation, active diagnosis, and empirical verification, where transferable knowledge supplies recovery hypotheses, and probing determines which hypothesis applies. We address this question with , a framework for test-time harness evolution around a frozen VLA. Here, test-time means that the VLA parameters remain fixed after training, while only the external harness evolves through environment interaction. At the fast timescale, the VLA executes actions under the current harness. When execution stalls, the harness selects a probe according to the task and failure context, executes it in the environment, and uses the resulting evidence to retrieve relevant recovery knowledge. At the slow timescale, a vision-language researcher converts this evidence into task-specific harness modifications. Candidates are compared with their incumbents through paired sandbox evaluation, and accepted modifications are subsequently assessed on disjoint holdout seeds. Immediate interaction utility and delayed episode-success credit are then used to update probe and knowledge selection. Thus, unlike outcome-driven harness search alone, learns both which intervention to apply and what to probe in order to discover it. This process creates a knowledge--probing co-evolution loop. Better probes provide clearer evidence for selecting and refining interventions, while successful interventions reveal which probes and knowledge are useful under particular task and failure contexts. Validated recoveries are distilled into transferable execution knowledge and reused on subsequent tasks, while unresolved failures and probing ambiguities are converted into targeted follow-up cases for further sandbox evaluation. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:framework , Auto-K searches for harness modifications from accumulated knowledge but does not improve its probing policy from probe outcomes. In contrast, uses subsequent interaction to update both probe and knowledge selection. Experiments on 149 Minecraft tasks show that harness evolution improves coverage over bare execution and a fixed harness, while the complete framework further improves over knowledge-only evolution without updating the underlying VLA. Our contributions are fourfold. [ leftmargin=*, topsep=2pt, itemsep=1pt, parsep=0pt, partopsep=0pt ] Evidence-guided test-time harness evolution. We identify a limitation of outcome-driven automatic harness search in visually ambiguous environments and formulate harness evolution as an evidence-guided process around a frozen VLA. Knowledge--probing co-evolution for evidence-guided search. We couple transferable recovery knowledge with active probing: knowledge provides intervention hypotheses, probes gather evidence about their applicability, and validated execution outcomes update both future knowledge and probe selection. Sandbox-grounded accumulation and transfer. Candidate harness changes are accepted only through paired environment interaction, while validated recoveries are promoted into transferable knowledge that guides subsequent tasks. Probe-driven failure-frontier expansion. We convert failure reflections and probing ambiguities into targeted follow-up cases, exposing new failure modes that guide subsequent harness evolution. Related Work Static harnesses for gaming and embodied agents. Prior work has advanced Minecraft agents through video pretraining, language-conditioned behavior learning, and unified development frameworks fan2022minedojo,baker2022video,lifshitz2023steve, cai2024minestudio,li2025jarvis . However, gaming VLAs typically produce short action segments and may lose targets, repeat ineffective actions, or fail to verify progress. External harnesses mitigate these limitations through task state, memory, action constraints, verification, and recovery. Recent embodied harnesses extend frozen VLA and world-action models through cross-stage context zeng2026helm , reusable primitives zhang2026harness , and fast--slow control gu2026harnesswam . Yet their intervention and recovery mechanisms are largely fixed before deployment. Our method instead probes ambiguous failures, acquires transferable recovery knowledge, and improves subsequent probing and knowledge selection while keeping the gaming VLA frozen. Automatic harness evolution. Early self-evolving agents primarily optimized prompts. APE and OPRO treat instruction generation as black-box optimization zhou2022large,yang2024large ; EvoPrompt and Promptbreeder use evolutionary search guo2024connecting,fernando2023promptbreeder ; and ProTeGi and TextGrad guide revisions with textual feedback pryzant2023automatic,yuksekgonul2024textgrad . DSPy and MIPRO extend optimization to instructions and demonstrations in multi-stage LM programs khattab2023dspy,opsahl2024optimizing . Recent methods further optimize broader harness components, including tools, memory, middleware, and control logic lee2026meta,chen2026harnessx,lin2026agentic,lou2026autoharness . These methods mainly target coding, textual, or programmatically verifiable environments with explicit execution feedback. Long-horizon gaming instead involves visually and temporally ambiguous failures, and proposed modifications may be difficult for a frozen VLA to execute. therefore probes the environment to identify failure contexts and applicable recovery knowledge. Interaction feedback improves subsequent probe and knowledge selection, while validated recoveries transfer across tasks. This knowledge--probing co-evolution improves both what intervention to apply and what evidence to seek. title: EventSync: Event-Driven Memory Updates for History-Dependent Manipulation
summary: History-dependent robotic manipulation requires task context and interaction history, as the current observation alone is insufficient to determine the next action. Hierarchical frameworks use task memory for high-level subgoal reasoning and low-level policies for execution. However, memory updates require accurate completion assessment: similar observations may correspond to different execution phases, and prematurely recording completion can mislead subsequent subgoal reasoning. We present EventSync, a hierarchical framework that coordinates task reasoning and action execution through event-driven memory updates. A vision-language model generates subgoals from task plans and interaction history, while a vision-language-action model executes them. A lightweight Event Monitor combines visual observations with end-effector trajectories to determine whether the current subgoal is complete. The framework records the current subgoal in its completed-subgoal history and triggers subsequent reasoning only after obtaining completion evidence. With visual history in the executor, EventSync achieves 64.5% overall success on RoboMME, exceeding the best baseline reported in the benchmark by 20.0 percentage points. Further analysis shows that this update mechanism helps build a reliable completed-subgoal history. Experiments on four real-robot tasks with different memory requirements validate the framework's effectiveness in real-world robotic manipulation.

Hierarchical frameworks use task memory for high-level subgoal reasoning and low-level policies for execution. However, memory updates require accurate completion assessment: similar observations may correspond to different execution phases, and prematurely recording completion can mislead subsequent subgoal reasoning. The framework records the current subgoal in its completed-subgoal history and triggers subsequent reasoning only after obtaining completion evidence. With visual history in the executor, EventSync achieves 64.5 overall success on RoboMME, exceeding the best baseline reported in the benchmark by 20.0 percentage points. Further analysis shows that this update mechanism helps build a reliable completed-subgoal history. Experiments on four real-robot tasks with different memory requirements validate the framework's effectiveness in real-world robotic manipulation. Introduction sec:introduction Real-world robotic manipulation often requires decisions based on previous interactions. In assembly, tidying, and everyday service tasks, earlier requirements and interaction outcomes can determine what the robot should do next~ kaelbling2013belief . History may also be needed to interpret the current phase of an ongoing operation. Such tasks are non-Markovian with respect to instantaneous observations: robots must retain task context and interpret execution history to select subsequent goals and actions~ kaelbling1998pomdp,memoryvla,sam2act,robomme . Prior work introduces memory into vision-language-action (VLA) models to use historical information~ roboflamingo,memoryvla,eventvla,nativemem , while other approaches assign task memory to a high-level reasoner that guides action execution through subgoals~ memer,tau0vla . We argue that hierarchical frameworks are well suited to history-dependent manipulation. The limited performance of hierarchical methods reported in existing evaluations~ robomme motivates us to revisit memory updates within this framework. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:motivation , an instruction issued by the high-level reasoner does not imply that the corresponding operation has been completed, and similar current poses may correspond to different execution phases. If an unfinished operation is recorded as completed, subsequent reasoning may rely on an incorrect estimate of task progress and advance to the next subgoal prematurely. For task-memory updates, completion judgments must be accurate enough to avoid premature goal transitions and timely enough to keep subsequent reasoning and actions aligned with execution progress. We propose EventSync, a hierarchical framework that coordinates task reasoning and action execution through event-driven memory updates. A Memory Reasoner built on a vision-language model (VLM) obtains a task plan and combines it with interaction history to generate subgoals, which a VLA-based Action Executor executes. EventSync maintains an event state for the current operation, and a lightweight Event Monitor with 87.39M total parameters estimates completion from visual observations and end-effector trajectories. The framework adds the current subgoal to the completed-subgoal history and triggers high-level reasoning for the next subgoal only after obtaining completion evidence. With visual history in the executor, EventSync achieves a 64.5 overall success rate on RoboMME, exceeding FrameSamp+Modul, the best baseline reported in the benchmark, by 20.0 percentage points~ robomme . Our variant without visual history in the executor achieves 94.0 on SwingXtimes, compared with the 7.3 reported for the hierarchical framework GroundSG + QwenVL~ robomme . Analysis of execution records further shows that updates guided by completion evidence help reduce premature progression and build a reliable completed-subgoal history. Experiments on four real-robot tasks further demonstrate the effectiveness of combining task-memory reasoning with event-driven memory updates. Our contributions are as follows: A hierarchical memory framework for history-dependent manipulation. We introduce EventSync, in which a high-level reasoner manages task memory and generates subgoals, a low-level policy executes actions, and an independent lightweight monitor provides completion feedback. Event-driven task-memory updates. We design a lightweight Event Monitor that combines visual observations with end-effector trajectories to assess operation completion, using the resulting evidence to trigger updates to the completed-subgoal history and subsequent high-level reasoning. Empirical evaluation in simulation and on real robots. We evaluate EventSync on the RoboMME simulation benchmark and real-robot tasks to assess its effectiveness in history-dependent manipulation, with comparisons and ablations examining the role of event-driven memory updates. Related Work sec:related_work Memory for Robotic Manipulation Research on robot memory studies how to retain task-relevant history for subsequent decisions. Existing methods preserve interaction history through recurrent states~ roboflamingo , spatial memory~ sam2act , and historical feature aggregation and retrieval~ hamlet,memoryvla . Compressed context~ contextvla,nativemem , motion trajectories overlaid on images~ tracevla , and visual evidence selected by event predictions~ eventvla further provide temporal information for action prediction. MemER~ memer retrieves historical keyframes for subgoal generation and runs reasoning asynchronously with control. RoboMME~ robomme systematically evaluates how memory representations and their integration with action policies affect history-dependent manipulation. Vision-Language Reasoning and Closed-Loop Control Language-conditioned manipulation policies combine semantic and spatial representations to map instructions to actions~ cliport,peract . Generalist robot policies and VLA models, including RT-1~ rt1 , RT-2~ rt2 , OpenVLA~ openvla , Octo~ octo , RDT-1B~ rdt1b , and the family~ pi0,pi05 , support action generation from visual observations and language instructions. High-level reasoning further organizes low-level execution through environment-grounded task planning~ saycan,palme , language-based action abstractions~ rth,hirobot , or predicted trajectories~ hamster . Programmatic control~ codeaspolicies and 3D value maps~ voxposer also provide interfaces between language requirements and robot control. Execution feedback allows subsequent decisions to adapt to actual observations. Prior work supports replanning and execution recovery through success detection and scene feedback~ inner_monologue , precondition checking~ progprompt , constraint monitoring~ doremi , and failure explanation~ reflect . title: Learning Tactile-Aware Hand Representations from Human Hand-Object Interaction Data
summary: Tactile representation learning for dexterous manipulation often requires substantial robot-side data collection, limiting its scalability across different hands and sensors. We explore whether large-scale human hand-object interaction (HOI) data can provide a useful prior for robotic tactile learning. To this end, we propose HuTact, a framework that pretrains tactile-aware hand representations from human HOI data without requiring real tactile signals during pretraining. HuTact transfers the interaction structure learned from human hand motions to robotic tactile observations and can be further adapted with a small amount of unlabeled robot interaction data. We evaluate HuTact on tactile perception and manipulation tasks, including grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and tactile-conditioned policy learning. Across these tasks, human HOI pretraining improves data efficiency and provides a strong initialization for downstream learning. Notably, with HOI pretraining followed by midtraining on unlabeled robot play data, HuTact achieves 88.26% Macro-F1 on grasp prediction using only 25\% of the labeled downstream data, comparable to training from scratch on the full labeled dataset (88.23%). These results suggest that human interaction data can serve as a scalable complementary source for robotic tactile representation learning.

These results suggest that human interaction data can serve as a scalable complementary source for robotic tactile representation learning. Introduction Tactile sensing enables humans to perceive and interact with the physical world, providing direct information about contact, force, texture, and motion that is difficult to obtain through vision alone~ dahiya2009tactile . Inspired by this remarkable human capability, tactile sensing has emerged as a critical modality for robotic manipulation, enabling robots to perceive subtle contact interactions, infer local physical properties, and regulate contact forces during complex manipulation tasks that demand precise and adaptive physical interaction~ yuan2017gelsight, taylor2022gelslim, bhirangi2025anyskin . Accordingly, a wide range of tactile sensors have been developed to capture rich information arising from physical contact, including vision-based sensors (e.g., GelSight~ yuan2017gelsight , DIGIT~ lambeta2020digit ) and magnetic-based sensors (e.g., AnySkin~ bhirangi2025anyskin , ReSkin~ pmlr-v164-bhirangi22a ). Beyond advances in tactile sensing hardware, the growing availability of large-scale tactile interaction data has further motivated learning-based approaches to extract generalizable representations from raw tactile observations~ yang2022touch . In particular, recent works have explored self-supervised pretraining using large-scale tactile interaction data collected with respective tactile sensors, learning representations that can be transferred to downstream manipulation tasks~ sharma2025selfsupervised, guzey2023dexterity, liu2024masked, fenganytouch2 . Learning generalizable tactile representations can reduce the amount of task-specific data required for downstream tasks. For vision-based tactile sensing, Feng~ propose AnyTouch~ fenganytouch , which learns transferable representations from a sensor-aligned dataset collected across multiple visuo-tactile sensors. For non-vision-based tactile sensing, Sharma~ ~ sharma2025selfsupervised apply DINO-based self-distillation to masked tactile sequences collected from a dexterous hand, while Guzey~ ~ guzey2023dexterity pretrain tactile representations using task-agnostic robotic play data. However, existing approaches for non-vision-based tactile sensors still largely require real tactile interaction data collected directly with the target robotic hand and sensing hardware. As a result, adapting representation learning to a new robotic platform or tactile sensor requires additional data collection, introducing substantial time and cost for pretraining. As an alternative, human hand-object interaction (HOI) data provide a promising source of pretraining supervision, where they contain large-scale and diverse interactions across objects, hand configurations, and manipulation behaviors~ Chao_2021_CVPR,Yang_2022_CVPR,Hampali_2020_CVPR,zhan2024oakink2 . These datasets are particularly attractive for learning transferable hand representations because they provide (1) interaction patterns that can be shared across different hand embodiments, (2) large-scale interaction data that would be costly to collect on robotic platforms, and (3) an opportunity to reduce embodiment-specific data collection when adapting to a new robotic hand. Many of these datasets also provide temporally aligned 3D reconstructions of human hands and manipulated objects, allowing fingertip configurations and their evolution during interaction to be recovered without collecting data on a robotic platform. Although HOI datasets do not contain real tactile signals, their hand--object trajectories encode spatial and temporal structure associated with physical interaction. We hypothesize that this structure can serve as a transferable prior for robotic tactile representation learning and reduce the amount of robot-side tactile data required for adaptation. In this work, our research question is: Can human hand-object interaction (HOI) data provide a transferable prior for robotic tactile representation learning? To answer this question, we propose HuTact, a framework for learning tactile-aware robot hand representations from human HOI data. Rather than attempting to reconstruct real tactile signals from human data, HuTact learns the spatial and temporal structure of hand interactions from wrist-local fingertip trajectories. To bridge human HOI pretraining and robotic tactile sensing, we separately tokenize fingertip coordinates and tactile observations, allowing the coordinate representation and shared Transformer backbone learned from HOI data to be retained while adapting the sensor-specific tactile input embedding. We further incorporate geometry-derived pseudo-contact signals as an auxiliary cue, encouraging the model to capture the relationship between fingertip coordinates and their corresponding tactile-like signals. This framework enables large-scale human interaction data to provide a transferable initialization for tactile-aware robot learning while reducing the amount of robot-side tactile data required for adaptation. To validate the effectiveness and transferability of HuTact, we evaluate it on tactile-sensitive downstream tasks, including grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and policy learning on tactile-sensitive tasks, and analyze the factors that enable transfer from human HOI data to robotic tactile sensing. In summary, our contributions are as follows: We propose HuTact, a framework that uses large-scale human hand-object interaction data to pretrain tactile-aware robot hand representations without requiring real tactile signals during the initial pretraining stage. We show that representations learned from HOI data transfer to robotic tactile perception and manipulation, improving grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and tactile-conditioned policy learning. We provide systematic analyses of the transfer mechanism through architectural ablations and data-efficiency experiments, studying the roles of temporal modeling, token separation, pseudo-contact cues, and robot-side midtraining. Our results show that HOI pretraining can substantially reduce the amount of task-specific robotic tactile data required for downstream adaptation. Related Work Tactile Sensing: Tactile sensors for robotic manipulation broadly include vision-based and non-optical sensing modalities. Vision-based sensors~ yuan2017gelsight, lambeta2020digit capture fine-grained contact geometry and have been applied to object identification~ patel2020digger , geometry sensing~ dong2017improved,taylor2022gelslim , pose estimation~ villalonga2021tactile,bauza2023tac2pose , and policy learning~ xue2025reactive,chen2026implicitrdp . However, their optical components can result in a relatively large form factor, making integration across multiple fingers challenging. Non-optical sensors instead use compact magnetic~ bhirangi2025anyskin,uskin or capacitive sensing elements~ song2026fingertip to enable distributed tactile sensing. In this work, we use the BrainCo Revo 2 hand~ brainco_revo2 , which is equipped with fingertip capacitive sensors that measure normal force, tangential force, tangential-force direction, and proximity. Tactile Representation Learning: Recent work has explored transferable tactile representations through large-scale self-supervised pretraining. For vision-based tactile sensors, objectives developed for visual representation learning~ he2022masked,oquab2023dinov2,radford2021learning have been adapted to tactile observations~ yang2024binding,liu2024masked,fenganytouch,fenganytouch2 . For skin-like tactile sensors, Sharma~ ~ sharma2025selfsupervised apply self-distillation to masked tactile sequences from a dexterous hand, while Guzey~ ~ guzey2023dexterity pretrain tactile representations using task-agnostic robotic play data. While these approaches demonstrate the benefits of tactile pretraining, they generally require interaction data collected with the target robot and tactile sensor. In contrast, HuTact initializes tactile-aware representations from human hand--object interaction data without real tactile signals. We pretrain on the spatial and temporal structure of wrist-local fingertip interactions, augmented with geometry-derived pseudo-contact cues, and subsequently adapt the representation to the target robotic tactile sensor. Robot Learning from Human Data: Human interaction data have been increasingly used to reduce robot-specific supervision for manipulation learning~ hoque2026egodex,punamiya2026egoverse,beingbeyond2025beingh0,bi2025hrdt,wi2026tactalign , by extracting hand poses, object motions, and interaction trajectories from large-scale demonstrations. HOI data have also been applied directly to dexterous manipulation: Zhao~ ~ zhao2025dexh2r retarget human hand-object interactions to dexterous robot hands and learn a residual policy for embodiment mismatch, while Zeng~ ~ zeng2026flowhoi use HOI data for vision-language-action learning. Large-scale datasets such as OakInk2~ zhan2024oakink2 , TACO~ liu2024taco , ARCTIC~ fan2023arctic , and HOT3D~ banerjee2025hot3d provide scalable supervision for learning hand--object interaction structure. HuTact differs in objective: rather than transferring human motion directly to a robot policy, we use HOI data to pretrain a tactile-aware hand representation that is subsequently adapted to real robotic tactile sensing. To our knowledge, prior work has not systematically studied large-scale HOI data as a pretraining source for robotic tactile representation learning. Methodology HuTact is designed to transfer interaction structure learned from human HOI data to robotic tactile sensing. The key challenge is that the source HOI datasets provide hand and object geometry but no real tactile signals, whereas the target robot provides sensor-specific tactile observations. We address this mismatch by factorizing the input representation into two streams: a shared wrist-local fingertip coordinate stream and a sensor-dependent contact stream. The shared Transformer backbone is pretrained on human interactions, while the sensor-specific tactile input embedding is adapted when transferring to real robotic tactile observations. title: LocoPilot: Single-Operator Bilateral Teleoperation for Loco-Manipulation Policy Learning
summary: Learning loco-manipulation policies requires demonstrations that capture coordinated base and arm motion on the target embodiment. Robot-free interfaces allow demonstrations to be collected independently of the target robot, increasing flexibility but without directly capturing platform-specific commands, proprioception, and body-mounted observations. On-robot teleoperation allows to capture these signals directly, but requires an interface capable of commanding the complete system concurrently. This paper presents LocoPilot, a single-operator bilateral teleoperation and data-collection framework implemented on a 12-DoF Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a 6-DoF AgileX Piper L manipulator, an Intel RealSense D435 wrist camera, and an Intel RealSense D405 head camera. A second 6-DoF Piper L arm, used as the leader and two handheld controllers provide simultaneous control of the base, body posture, manipulator, and gripper. The follower arm interaction forces are estimated without a dedicated force/torque sensor and rendered to the operator through a passivity-constrained haptic channel. A ROS~2 pipeline records synchronized multimodal observations together with a unified 11D action shared by teleoperation and policy deployment. Compared to prior work, LocoPilot uniquely unifies robot-in-the-loop legged data collection, force feedback without motion-capture instrumentation, and the same action interface at deployment. We evaluate the interface across multiple loco-manipulation tasks and validate the complete collection-to-deployment pipeline by fine-tuning MolmoAct2 \cite{MOLMO} on pick-and-place demonstrations and deploying on the physical robot without action retargeting or additional inverse kinematics. Code available at: https://github.com/iit-DLSLab/LocoPilot

Introduction sec:introduction Robots capable of both locomotion and manipulation extend physical interaction beyond the workspace of fixed-base manipulators. Arm-equipped quadruped robots are particularly suited to unstructured environments, where they combine legged mobility with physical interaction capabilities. Prior work has explored legged loco-manipulation through model-based whole-body control 8794273 , or learned coordination of locomotion and manipulation fu2022deep,RobotDuet . More recently, generalist models have gained increasing attention for learning manipulation behaviors from multimodal demonstrations, leveraging large-scale visual and language representations open_x_embodiment_rt_x_2023,kim24openvla,Human2LocoMan,MoManipVLA . For loco-manipulation, however, such demonstrations must capture both base and arm actions on the target embodiment. Ideally, the collection interface should therefore minimize the collection--deployment gap while preserving direct operator authority over all task-relevant commands. Existing systems trade off these requirements in different ways: Teleoperation systems place a human directly in the control loop of the physical robot, combining the operator task understanding with the constraints of the target embodiment. Leader-follower interfaces with direct joint correspondence provide intuitive control of fixed-base manipulators GELLO,Team2024ALOHA2A , while mounting the same kind of interface on a wheeled base extends the concept to mobile manipulation, recording base motion alongside bimanual manipulation fu2024mobile . XR-based systems provide more general cross-embodiment interfaces cheng2024tv,zhao2025xrobotoolkit , and DROID demonstrates the use of teleoperation for standardized large-scale data collection DROID . Immersive interfaces additionally stream the robot's own onboard imagery to the operator~ cheng2024tv , allowing real-time inspection of the visual inputs that will directly condition the downstream policy. For arm-equipped quadrupeds, previous systems have used wearable motion capture, joysticks, haptic devices, or hand gestures TeleMAN,SpaceBert,RobotTeleoperativo,quadrupedgesture . Collecting directly on the target robot reduces observation and action mismatch, but simultaneously commanding all task-relevant DoFs becomes increasingly difficult for a single operator. Robot-free interfaces make the opposite trade-off. The Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) chi2024universal records demonstrations using a sensorized handheld gripper, allowing the operator to demonstrate manipulation without the kinematic constraints of the target robot. This improves collection flexibility, but omits embodiment-specific signals such as base commands, proprioception, and body-mounted observations. Deployment therefore requires an additional mapping from demonstrated end-effector motion to the target embodiment, as in UMI on Legs UMIlegs2024 . This work aims to combine the collection-deployment consistency of on-robot teleoperation with the flexibility of learning-based interfaces for arm-equipped quadrupeds. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:system_overview , both the human operator and the learned policy act through the same loco-manipulation interface, while the resulting demonstrations are collected directly on the target platform. Achieving this requires addressing two main challenges. The first challenge is enabling a single operator to command the entire loco-manipulation action concurrently. Reaching and grasping may require the robot to translate, rotate, or change body posture while the arm is moving, so sequential base and manipulator control produces segmented demonstrations rather than the smooth continuous coordination desired from the final policy. Existing systems address this through multiple operators, wearable instrumentation, or partial autonomy, introducing additional coordination or removing task decisions from the demonstrator. To retain these decisions under single-operator control, we propose a bimanual interface design where a handheld controller is mounted on the end-effector handle of the leader arm. The dominant hand articulates the manipulator while operating the mounted controller, and the non-dominant hand provides the remaining base commands through a second controller. Together, the two interfaces provide concurrent control of planar base velocity, yaw rate, body pitch, arm configuration, and gripper aperture. Interaction forces at the follower are additionally estimated online and rendered through the leader arm, providing contact feedback without a dedicated force/torque sensor. The second challenge is maintaining consistency between collection and deployment. On a legged manipulator, high-level commands are executed through a locomotion and manipulation stack whose behavior also shapes the recorded motion. Replacing this stack at deployment can therefore shift the distribution of observations and executed motions away from the demonstrated one, even when the high-level action representation is unchanged. We avoid this by using the same 11-dimensional loco-manipulation action in both regimes and by keeping the same downstream execution modules: the locomotion policy and leg controller, the arm controller, and the gripper interface. During collection, the action is generated by the operator, whereas at deployment it is generated by the learned policy; the locomotion policy, arm controller, and gripper interface remain unchanged. Table~ tab:comparison compares LocoPilot with the closest prior systems in terms of the teleoperation and data-collection properties discussed above. The contributions of this work can be summarized as follows: A single-operator bilateral teleoperation interface for arm-equipped quadrupeds, combining concurrent base, body, arm, and gripper control with sensorless force reflection and an operator-side passivity layer. A unified 11-dimensional action interface shared between teleoperation and learned-policy deployment, with the same locomotion and manipulation controllers used in both regimes. A synchronized learning-oriented data pipeline recording multi-camera RGB-D observations, robot state, odometry, and commanded actions, validated through multiple teleoperation tasks and real-robot deployment of a fine-tuned MolmoAct2 policy. Section~ sec:teleop-brackground the teleoperation mapping and unified command. Section~ sec:Experimental_results reports the teleoperation experiments and validates the collected demonstrations through real-robot deployment. Section~ sec:Conclusion draws the final conclusions. Hardware sec:hardware Figure fig:system_overview shows both the teleoperation setup and the system being controlled. In particular, the follower platform, shown on the right, consists of a 12-DoF Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a 6-DoF AgileX Piper L manipulator and parallel gripper. Two RGB-D cameras provide complementary observations: an Intel RealSense D435 mounted near the gripper captures close-range manipulation, while an Intel RealSense D405 mounted on the quadruped head, thanks to its larger field of view, observes the wider workspace in front of the robot. This platform is the same during both demonstration collection and autonomous deployment. The leader station, on the left of Fig.~ fig:two_arm_teleop_station , is used only during data collection. It is built around a second Piper L arm serving as a leader device. A custom handle at the end-effector improves ergonomics and holds one of two Nintendo Joy-Con controllers~ nintendoJoyCon . The operator grips this handle with the dominant hand and articulates the leader arm. With the thumb of the same hand, the operator reaches the controller's analog stick and buttons, which respectively control the quadruped robot pitch and yaw rate and the episode markers, while the index finger controls the gripper through the trigger button. With the non-dominant hand the operator holds the second controller, which commands the base velocity. The configuration shown in Fig.~ fig:two_arm_teleop_station assumes a right-handed operator: for left-handed operation, a specular handle can be employed while swapping the controller assignment without changing the teleoperation scheme. To ensure visual consistency, the operator drives the robot using the exact onboard camera streams recorded for downstream policy training, displayed in real time at the leader station. title: PACT-VLA: Speculative Action-Chunk Verification with Pre-Commit Observations
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are commonly deployed with asynchronous inference in real-world settings, where the next action chunk is generated while the robot is still executing the previous one. By the time the new chunk is committed, the robot and scene have changed, so the chunk is conditioned on a stale observation and task success drops sharply as this inference delay grows. Generating multiple candidate chunks could let newer observations inform the final choice, but existing multi-candidate methods either rank candidates with the stale inference-start observation or repeatedly switch between candidates during execution, which can make the executed action sequence discontinuous. Our key insight is that inference delay can be used as decision time. While candidate generation is still underway, candidate selection can reuse the VLA itself to choose the complete action chunk that best fits a later observation. We propose PACT-VLA, a training-free framework that generates candidates from the inference-start observation and selects one using this pre-commit observation. Its scoring function, FlowRes, measures the residual between each candidate's implied flow direction and the velocity predicted by the frozen policy under the pre-commit observation, requiring no separate verifier. A pipelined implementation overlaps observation processing with candidate generation and batches scoring, so selection adds no control-step delay on the evaluated hardware. At a four-step delay, PACT-VLA improves average success by 15.0 percentage points over RTC on Kinetix and by 5.2 points over single-candidate asynchronous execution with GR00T N1.7 on LIBERO, and it further improves existing delay-robust methods. On three real-robot tasks, it raises average success from 60% to 82% over naive asynchronous execution with the same frozen $π_{0.5}$ checkpoint.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) policies~ brohan2023rt,kim2024openvla,wen2024diffusion increasingly predict action chunks rather than individual actions~ li2024cogact,liu2025rdt,black2024pi_0,team2024octo , allowing several control steps to be executed from a single policy inference and preserving temporal coherence across consecutive actions~ black2026real,zhao2023learning,kim2025fine . However, action-chunk generation is not instantaneous. While inference is running, the robot continues to act and the surrounding scene may change. Consequently, by the time a newly generated chunk is ready for execution, the observation from which it was generated may already be stale, and the chunk may no longer fit the scene~ black2026real,tang2025vlash,agouzoul2026understanding . The challenge is that action generation begins before later changes are observed. Existing approaches address this challenge in different ways. Future-state methods use information available at inference start to anticipate the conditions under which the next action chunk will be executed~ tang2025vlash . However, these methods determine the next action chunk before changes during the current inference interval are observed, so the conditions at execution may differ from what was anticipated. A natural alternative is to postpone this decision by keeping multiple candidate action chunks available until more information about the upcoming execution conditions becomes available. However, some test-time sampling methods still rank these candidates using the inference-start observation~ kwok2025robomonkey,jang2026verifier , so the final choice remains fixed before later changes are observed. DreamChunk~ chen2026dream goes further by using a learned world model to predict a trajectory for each candidate. As new observations arrive during execution, it compares them with these predicted trajectories and repeatedly reselects which candidate to follow. This allows the choice to respond to newly observed changes, but keeping the decision open during execution can cause repeated candidate switching, making the executed action sequence discontinuous, which can hurt task performance. However, sensing continues while the next chunk is being generated, so an observation arriving during inference can already be available before commitment. This leaves open whether such an observation can be used to finalize one complete action chunk before commitment, without switching between candidates during execution. Our key insight is that inference delay can be used as decision time. While candidate generation is still underway, candidate selection can reuse the VLA itself to choose the complete action chunk that best fits a later observation. We propose PACT-VLA, which realizes this principle by generating a fixed candidate pool from the inference-start observation and selecting one candidate using a pre-commit observation received shortly before execution. We introduce FlowRes, which measures the mismatch between the flow direction implied by each candidate and the direction predicted by the frozen policy under this observation. Using a pre-commit observation leaves only a short interval for candidate selection before the planned chunk switch. title: FIT-MAC: A Closed-Loop Multi-Agent Framework for Robust Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved strong performance on standard robotic manipulation benchmarks. However, their reliability can degrade substantially when task conditions deviate from the nominal setting. Perturbations in object positions and task instructions may lead to complete task failure. Existing VLA policies generally lack an explicit runtime mechanism for distinguishing these failure modes and selecting an appropriate recovery strategy. To systematically mitigate this issue, we propose FIT-MAC, a failure-aware, closed-loop multi-agent control framework for improving the robustness of VLA policies at inference time. FIT-MAC augments a VLA policy with an inference-time control layer. First, the Planner Agent parses the language instruction into a structured task specification that captures the manipulation goal and spatial constraints, and the Grounder Agent resolves each instruction-level reference to a visual target. Next, the Verifier Agent tracks phase-specific execution progress, distinguishes target-binding errors from local execution failures, and determines whether intervention is warranted. The Correction Agent then routes permitted interventions to target rebinding or bounded grasping or placement recovery, depending on the failure type. When no intervention is required, the pretrained VLA remains the default action generator. Extensive experiments on LIBERO-PRO demonstrate that FIT-MAC improves robustness across multiple VLA backbones, consistently increasing success rates and achieving state-of-the-art performance under diverse perturbations.

Code Project page: . is available at . INTRODUCTION Vision-language-action (VLA) models integrate visual perception and language understanding to generate actions for robotic manipulation. OpenVLA provides an open-source foundation for generalist robot control kim2024openvla , while uses flow matching to generate continuous actions black2025pi0 . Its successor, , further improves open-world generalization through heterogeneous co-training physicalintelligence2025pi05 . Recent models pursue complementary directions, NORA reduces the computational cost of generalist VLA policies hung2025nora , while X-VLA targets scalable cross-embodiment transfer zheng2025xvla . MolmoAct incorporates structured spatial reasoning between perception and low-level control lee2025molmoact . Other methods improve predictive modeling and long-horizon execution through world-knowledge modeling, future-goal prediction, and phase-aware policies upvla2025,dreamvla2025,longvla2025 . Collectively, these advances highlight the potential of VLA models for generalist robot control. However, strong benchmark performance does not necessarily translate into reliable execution under distribution shift. AGNOSTOS reports limited zero-shot generalization across tasks, while SAFE identifies frequent failures on novel tasks, underscoring the need for runtime failure detection agnostos2025,safe2025 . Broader evaluations show substantial sensitivity to perturbations in actions, instructions, observations, and environments robustvla2026,zhou2026liberopro . VLATest documents similar robustness gaps under variations in clutter, lighting, viewpoints, and instructions, as well as in the presence of unseen objects vlatest2025 . Adversarial evaluations further expose vulnerabilities to digital and physical perturbations advvla2025 . Together, these findings highlight the challenges of robust VLA execution. Addressing these challenges requires both reliable temporal visual evidence and effective runtime recovery. Reasoning-based video segmentation improves language-conditioned grounding by decoupling textual semantics from dynamic visual representations dang2026decoupled . At the control level, RACER combines a VLM supervisor with an actor trained on automatically generated recovery trajectories racer2025 . Sparse spatio-temporal propagation strengthens object correspondence across frames dang2026fast , while COME-robot uses execution feedback for closed-loop failure diagnosis and recovery comerobot2025 . Frame-relation mining reduces redundant memory and mitigates error accumulation dang2023efficient , whereas TCoT integrates hierarchical reasoning with global--local recovery tcot2026 . Parallel temporal--spatial memory further captures complementary motion and contextual cues dang2024temporo . We study a complementary runtime decision problem of distinguishing incorrect target binding from local execution failure and selectively applying the appropriate recovery mechanism. The pretrained VLA remains the default action generator. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:motivation , we aim to improve the robustness of pretrained VLA policies through runtime recovery without modifying the underlying policy. Our key observation is that perturbations induce distinct failure types. Target failures arise when incorrect grounding of the language-specified target object or reference relation directs the policy toward the wrong object instance before grasping. Execution failures occur when the target is correctly identified, but local control becomes unstable during grasping, transport, or placement. These failures manifest as empty grasps, failed lifts, unstable releases, or stalled execution. Distinguishing between these failure types allows an external controller to select targeted recovery mechanisms rather than apply generic retries. Building on this observation, we propose FIT-MAC, a failure-aware, closed-loop multi-agent control framework for improving the robustness of VLA policies at inference time. Specialized agents coordinate task parsing, visual grounding, execution monitoring, and recovery through a shared execution state. FIT-MAC retains the pretrained VLA as the default action generator and intervenes only when task progress, target visibility, or grasping and placement signals indicate failure. It distinguishes incorrect target binding from local execution failure and routes them to target rebinding or bounded local recovery, respectively. This design enables selective, interpretable correction while limiting disruption to nominal execution and leaving the pretrained policy unchanged. Experiments on LIBERO-Object and LIBERO-Spatial show that FIT-MAC consistently improves the robustness of OpenVLA, , and across diverse perturbations. The largest gains occur under position, task, and environment perturbations, where successful execution often requires target rebinding and stage-wise recovery. FIT-MAC also maintains high success rates under object and semantic perturbations, demonstrating its effectiveness across perturbation types. Our contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=18pt, itemsep=2pt, topsep=2pt] We propose FIT-MAC, a failure-aware, closed-loop multi-agent control framework that improves the robustness of VLA policies at inference time. Specialized agents coordinate monitoring, diagnosis, routing, and correction through a shared execution state, while the pretrained VLA remains the default action generator. We introduce a runtime verification and correction mechanism that assesses target grounding and execution progress to determine when to intervene. It distinguishes target-binding errors from local execution failures and addresses them through target rebinding and bounded local recovery, respectively. FIT-MAC achieves state-of-the-art success rates across LIBERO-PRO perturbation settings and consistently improves the robustness of OpenVLA, , and . Ablation studies further demonstrate the contribution of each component. RELATED WORK Generalist and Long-Horizon Vision-Language-Action Models. Generalist VLA models learn language-conditioned visuomotor policies from heterogeneous robotic data. OpenVLA provides an open-source autoregressive foundation model kim2024openvla . uses flow matching for continuous action generation, while improves open-world generalization through heterogeneous co-training black2025pi0,physicalintelligence2025pi05 . NORA improves inference efficiency, X-VLA supports cross-embodiment transfer through soft prompts, and MolmoAct integrates depth-aware perception, spatial reasoning, and action prediction hung2025nora,zheng2025xvla,lee2025molmoact . Recent approaches address long-horizon manipulation through hierarchical reasoning, memory, future-state prediction, and spatial representations. AtomVLA decomposes demonstrations into atomic subtasks and scores action chunks using a latent world model sun2026atomvla . LaMP incorporates a 3D scene-flow prior, R3DP introduces a real-time 3D-aware policy, and RoboTALES uses task-aligned simulated futures to guide policy learning lamp2026,r3dp2026,robotales2026 . These methods modify the policy architecture, representation, or training procedure. Perturbation Evaluation and Robust Policy Optimization. Benchmarks such as LIBERO-PRO, LIBERO-X, VLATest, adversarial VLA benchmarks, and LIBERO-RECOVER assess VLA robustness to changes in objects, positions, language, observations, and environments zhou2026liberopro,liberox2026,vlatest2025,advvla2025,liberorecover2026 . Existing methods improve robustness through perturbation-based training, post-training, uncertainty-aware action refinement, or latent world-model scoring robustvla2026,robustvla_rl2025,islam2026sureflow,sun2026atomvla . VLS instead uses a vision-language model to steer a pretrained policy at inference time vls2026 . Online Failure Detection and Agentic Runtime Recovery. Runtime recovery methods monitor execution and intervene when failures occur. SAFE, RecoveryChaining, RACER, COME-robot, and TCoT explore failure detection, recovery to resumable states, VLM supervision, execution tracing, and hierarchical recovery safe2025,recoverychaining2025,racer2025,comerobot2025,tcot2026 . GTA-VLA uses interactive visual guidance, including points, boxes, and traces, to steer VLA execution under spatial and visual ambiguity gtavla2026 . Code-based and agentic systems extend runtime recovery through execution feedback, visual verification, skill synthesis, and modular coordination fu2026capx,zhang2026rats,modularfailure2025,malmm2025,optimizedprompts2025,agenticrobot2025,robobridge2026 . Our method explicitly distinguishes target failures from execution failures and addresses them through target rebinding with closed-loop correction and bounded local grasping and placement control, respectively. The pretrained VLA remains the default action generator, and intervention is triggered only by runtime evidence of failure. METHOD sec:method Overview sec:method_overview In Figure~ fig:pipeline , we provide an overview of FIT-MAC. Given a language instruction , a visual observation , and a low-dimensional robot state , FIT-MAC augments a frozen VLA policy with an inference-time control layer. The framework comprises a Planner Agent, a Grounder Agent, a Verifier Agent, and a Correction Agent that coordinate through a shared execution state. The Planner and Grounder Agents convert the instruction into a grounded task specification, while the Verifier Agent tracks execution progress and determines whether intervention is needed. Target-binding errors trigger target rebinding, whereas local execution failures trigger bounded recovery. The pretrained VLA remains the default action generator throughout execution. Planner Agent sec:task_prompt The Planner Agent converts the language instruction into a structured task specification that guides grounding and execution. It extracts the target object, source and destination descriptions, spatial relations, and reference objects. For multi-step manipulation instructions, it organizes the required operations into an ordered sequence of subtasks. The resulting specification explicitly defines each subtask's goal and constraints for downstream agents. Execution proceeds through bounded pick-and-place attempts. title: De-Diffusing WAMs: Action-Sufficient Direct Prediction for Robot Control
summary: Cascade world-action models (WAMs) use predicted visual futures to condition robot actions, but inherit costly iterative inference from diffusion-pretrained experts. We ask what a single-step predicted future must preserve to support accurate single-step action prediction. In the evaluated WAM, resampling video noise has little effect on downstream actions, yet naively truncating both streams to one step substantially reduces task success. Video-space supervision only partially closes this gap, and a local sensitivity analysis shows that vision prediction errors have highly unequal consequences for action accuracy. These findings motivate DirectWAM, which converts pretrained video and action experts into single-step predictors without stochastic sampling through action-sufficient distillation, while retaining the explicit future-to-action cascade. After learning a one-step action model, we train the future predictor by decoding actions from its own predicted futures and backpropagating demonstration action error through the expert, with an optional future-latent reconstruction loss. The resulting objective evaluates the student-generated future through its downstream control consequences rather than relying on representation matching alone. DirectWAM achieves 97.1% average success across four LIBERO suites and 85.4% on RoboTwin 2.0, outperforming Flash-WAM at the same one-evaluation-per-stream budget. This advantage has also extended to three real-world tasks that we designed. Compared with the full iterative teacher, it reduces inference latency by $28.0\times$.
