Introduction sec:introduction Cascade world-action models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video models to predict visual futures, which then condition an inverse dynamics model (IDM) for action generation. Unlike standalone video generation, the predicted future is not the final output but an intermediate representation for robot control. This causal future-to-action relationship allows a robot policy to utilize world prior from video while retaining futures that can be decoded for inspection. However, diffusion-based video and action experts realize this computation through repeated denoising, introducing a substantial inference cost. We study how to retain the pretrained experts and explicit future-to-action interface while replacing their iterative inference procedure with direct prediction. Recent acceleration methods either modify the future-to-action interface or compress its computation. Fast-WAM retains video co-training but removes explicit future prediction at deployment~ fastwam ; Motus supports action-only inference alongside other joint and conditional modeling modes~ motus . Among methods that retain the cascade, Flash-WAM~ flashwam uses modality-aware consistency distillation to achieve one-step inference in both the video and action streams. DIDO~ dido concentrates supervision on control-relevant visual regions to learn single-step future prediction, while retaining iterative action generation. These advances establish that cascade inference can be accelerated. However, a more basic question is largely overlooked in WAM acceleration: what must a single-step future preserve to support accurate downstream action prediction? As the future serves only as an intermediate representation, the reconstruction objective of video diffusion may not naturally align with the control objective of the downstream IDM. We first disentangle the roles of stochastic sampling and iterative refinement, using LingBot-VA as our experimental instantiation. Varying only the video noise produces limited changes in downstream actions, and fixing it throughout an episode barely affects closed-loop success. Stochasticity can therefore be removed, yielding a deterministic future predictor that nonetheless still relies on the teacher's multi-step computation. Removing this iteration is non-trivial: naively reducing the steps degrades control, and learning a one-step predictor with video-space supervision recovers only part of the gap. Therefore, these results motivate learning the direct future predictor through the action model that consumes its predictions, rather than relying on video-space supervision alone. To understand how the remaining prediction errors affect control, we selectively correct components of the future-representation error under a frozen action expert. Correcting only a small, locally action-sensitive component recovers a disproportionate share of the achievable offline action-error reduction. The complementary component still contributes, but the imbalance shows that representation-error magnitude is a poor proxy for downstream importance. This motivates action sufficiency as the learning principle for single-step prediction: the predicted future should be optimized according to the action decoded from it, rather than through representation matching alone. We implement this principle in DirectWAM through action-sufficient distillation. Starting from diffusion-pretrained video and action experts, we first train a single-step action expert with the video expert fixed. We then train the single-step future predictor end-to-end through this action expert: actions are decoded from the student's own predicted futures, and the demonstration action error is backpropagated into the future predictor. An optional future-latent reconstruction loss anchors predictions to the demonstrated future. Because both objectives supervise final predictions rather than intermediate denoising states, the pretrained experts are converted into a direct cascade without the student having to reproduce the teacher's denoising trajectory. In experiments, DirectWAM achieves 97.1 average success on LIBERO and 85.4 on RoboTwin 2.0, outperforming cascade baselines at the same compute budget and substantially narrowing the single-step control gap. These gains further carry over to three real-world manipulation tasks. Inference latency decreases from 5042\,ms for the full iterative teacher to 180\,ms for DirectWAM, a speedup. Together, these results demonstrate a practical route to retaining explicit future prediction while replacing iterative diffusion inference with direct computation trained for downstream control. Our contributions are threefold: 1.5em 3pt 0pt 2pt 0pt Separating stochastic sampling from iterative refinement. We characterize their distinct roles in the evaluated cascade WAM: video-noise resampling has limited downstream effects, whereas naively truncating both streams to one step causes control drops. Action sufficiency as a learning criterion. We show that the magnitude of future-prediction error is a poor proxy for its effect on action accuracy, motivating a training objective that supervises the student-generated future through the actions it induces online. A deterministic single-step future-to-action cascade. We introduce DirectWAM, a one-step de-diffused cascade WAM that preserves explicit future prediction while achieving strong control performance both in simulation and in the real world. Related Work sec:related_work World-action models and future-conditioned control. Video-based control uses predicted observations as an intermediate representation for action generation~ unipi . Recent World-Action Models (WAMs) more tightly integrate visual dynamics and action prediction: LingBot-VA through autoregressive video--action modeling~ lingbotva , DreamZero with a video-pretrained backbone~ dreamzero , and Motus within a multi-expert architecture~ motus . Building on the cascade WAM interface, we investigate how to learn direct future prediction according to its action consequences, rather than assuming that control requires fully refined video. Distillation for efficient cascade WAMs. Consistency models and distribution matching distillation provide general routes to reducing diffusion sampling steps~ consistency_models,dmd . A distinct architectural approach, Fast-WAM, retains video co-training but removes explicit future prediction at deployment~ fastwam . We instead focus on acceleration that preserves the future-to-action cascade. Flash-WAM addresses the different noise regimes of video and action streams by assigning modality-specific consistency functions, enabling single-step inference in both streams~ flashwam . DIDO combines distribution matching with interaction-centric representation guidance for one-step video prediction, using explicit interaction representations together with visual feature alignment to preserve manipulation-relevant information~ dido . These methods demonstrate that efficient cascade WAM prediction requires more than applying a generic sampling shortcut. DirectWAM pursues the same goal of retaining useful future prediction, but defines its learning criterion through the existing action model. Control-oriented predictive representations. Predictive accuracy need not align with downstream decision quality, as studied through objective mismatch~ objective_mismatch , value-aware model learning~ value_aware , and value equivalence~ value_equivalence . Recent WAMs address related representation challenges through geometric or semantic supervision: MECo-WAM~ mecowam transfers action-relevant 4D geometric priors from a frozen VGGT~ vggt , while Robust-WAM augments video-generation-based policies with future-semantic alignment~ robustwam . GigaWorld-Policy-0.5~ gigaworld strengthens action–dynamics coupling through action-conditioned future modeling while allowing action-only inference. Our work shares the broader goal of learning predictive information useful for control, but focuses on how a predicted future should be learned when it must condition a single-step action predictor. Specifically, DirectWAM converts diffusion-pretrained experts into a deterministic single-step cascade while retaining their future-representation interface. Rather than introducing a new semantic or geometric target space, it trains the future predictor through demonstration-action error decoded from its own predictions by a learned direct action model, with optional future-latent anchoring. This places the learning criterion at the interface between the student-generated future and its action consumer, while preserving explicit future conditioning with one evaluation per stream. Rethinking Future Prediction for Cascade WAMs sec:rethinking_diffusion In this section, we systematically study the effect of the future prediction in cascade WAMs on downstream robot control. The future is not the endpoint of the model: its effect on control is mediated by the action model and should therefore be viewed from a control perspective. DOES VIDEO-SIDE STOCHASTICITY MATTER FOR CONTROL? We begin by evaluating whether the action model is sensitive to the stochasticity of future prediction. Diffusion provides the video stream with the ability to sample diverse futures under the same context, but it is unclear whether this variation is propagated into different actions. We therefore ask: does resampling the imagined future produce meaningfully different control decisions? To isolate the effect of stochastic future sampling, we fixed the action-side noise across samples, while varying only the video-diffusion noise. Thus, any variation in the generated actions is induced by changing the sampled future, rather than by resampling the action model itself. title: From Predictive Geometry to Action: Learning Complementary Predictive Representations for Embodied Manipulation
summary: Effective manipulation requires a policy to capture not only about the current scene geometry, but also about how that geometry will evolve under interaction. Existing approaches either augment policies with geometric information from current observations or introduce future prediction as auxiliary supervision, leaving open how predictive geometry should be represented for action generation. Therefore, we propose a two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations from multi-view video clips. During pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model provides dense geometric features that are compressed into predictive geometric representations and optimized to preserve scene structure and its temporal evolution. Action supervision is then applied to geometric transitions to extract a complementary motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant transitions. During downstream post-training, predictive geometry is transferred through geometry queries, while the motor representation guides intermediate features along the action-generation pathway. Future observations are used only as privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. Across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm tasks, our approach consistently improves downstream policies, including an absolute gain of 10.4 percentage points on the WidowX evaluation. We further demonstrate transfer across multiple VLA architectures and WAMs, with improvements in both future-world and action prediction. The code will be available at https://github.com/xuxiaoxxxx/CPR.

Introduction sec:introduction Anticipating how the physical world will evolve assran2025v,assran2023self under interaction is becoming increasingly important for vision-language-action (VLA) models ma2026internvla,luo2026being and world action models (WAM) li2026causal,ye2026world . Such predictive capability allows an agent to reason about the consequences of interaction, rather than mapping only its current observation to an immediate action. Yet effective manipulation requires more than temporal foresight alone: it also depends on a precise understanding of how the scene is spatially organized. Geometry specifies object layouts, spatial relationships, and robot-scene configurations, while dynamics describe how these structures evolve as an interaction unfolds. For action generation, these two aspects play distinct but complementary roles: geometry provides the spatial structure within which actions are executed, while its evolution provides cues about how the scene may change over time. This naturally raises a central question: how should geometric structure and its predicted evolution be represented so that they can more effectively support action generation? Recent efforts to incorporate geometry into predictive policy learning follow two directions. As shown in Fig. introduction , input-centric approaches sun2025geovla,spatialvla,li2026wam4d,zhang2025spatial augment observations with depth, point clouds, 3D coordinates, or pretrained geometric features. These methods improve spatial grounding, but use geometry as additional context for describing the currently observed scene and may rely on sensing or geometry-estimation pipelines. Prediction-centric approaches yang20264d,he2026elan4d,li2025spatial,li2025qdepth,su2026world instead supervise models with future RGB-D observations, future geometric states, or other world-prediction targets, explicitly exposing the policy to future scene structure. However, such targets are represented as dense observations or holistic latent states, requiring the learned representation to retain geometric information whose relevance to control may vary substantially. More broadly, these approaches primarily organize geometry to represent the scene and its evolution. They leave less explicit how action-relevant information should be distinguished from geometry needed for a coherent world representation. This creates a gap between predictive geometric modeling and action-oriented motor representation learning. A natural way to bridge this gap is to recognize that predictive geometry and action generation place different preferences on learned representations. Predictive geometric modeling benefits from preserving a sufficiently complete and coherent account of scene structure. Action generation, in contrast, benefits from emphasizing geometric variations that are informative for motor commands while reducing the influence of static or action-irrelevant scene content. Rather than forcing these roles to be served in exactly the same representation, we introduce two complementary representations with distinct but related purposes: a predictive geometric representation that provides a compact and structured description of scene geometry and its evolution, and a motor representation that emphasizes action-aware information from geometric transitions. The former provides structured predictive context, while the latter focuses this predictive information toward control. Building on this observation, we propose the two-stage framework, which learns complementary predictive representations (CPR) from large-scale heterogeneous interaction videos open_x_embodiment,jin2026umi,Libero,goyal2017something,chen2025robotwin and transfers them to downstream policies. As illustrated in Fig.~ introduction , our framework first constructs a predictive geometric representation from dense geometric features and then extracts action-aware information from the temporal evolution of scene geometry across video clips, providing complementary guidance for downstream action generation. Specifically, as shown in Fig. fig2 , during representation pretraining, a frozen 3D foundation model~ wang2025vggt extracts dense geometric features from multi-view video observations, which are progressively compressed by a hierarchical query-based encoder into compact temporal states. Geometry reconstruction, masked representation prediction, and geometric transition prediction encourage the predictive geometric representation to preserve scene structure while capturing its evolution over time. We then apply action supervision to transitions between consecutive predictive geometric states, yielding a motor representation that emphasizes action-relevant geometric transitions. The predictive geometric representation therefore captures structured information about the evolving scene, while the motor representation focuses on transitions that are more directly informative for action. During post-training, as shown in Fig. fig3 , these two representations are transferred through role-specific supervision pathways. Dedicated geometry queries are trained to infer the predictive geometric representation from current-time inputs, while intermediate features along the action-generation pathway are aligned with the motor representation. Importantly, future observations and the pretrained representation model are used only to construct privileged supervision during training and are not required at inference time. We evaluate CPR on both multiple VLA architectures and WAM across diverse simulated and real-world manipulation benchmarks, demonstrating consistent improvements across different robot embodiments and action-generation paradigms. Our contributions are summarized as follows: [leftmargin=1.2em, itemindent=0pt] We identify complementary roles for predictive geometric and motor representations in predictive policy learning: predictive geometric modeling benefits from preserving structured scene geometry, while action generation benefits from emphasizing control-relevant geometric transitions. We develop a two-stage framework that learns and transfers these complementary predictive representations. Hierarchical geometric tokenization and predictive objectives learn geometric states, while action supervision extracts action-aware information from their transitions; the two representations are transferred through geometry-query and motor-alignment pathways. Extensive experiments across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv, and real-world bimanual and single-arm manipulation tasks demonstrate consistent improvements across policy architectures and robot embodiments. CPR yields a 10.4 absolute gain on the WidowX evaluation and improves future-world and action prediction in WAM. Related Work Predictive Representations for VLA and WAM. Predictive modeling provides VLA models and WAMs with foresight beyond the current observation. Existing approaches introduce future information either through observation prediction or compact predictive representations. Observation-level methods predict future RGB observations, videos, or world states to support action generation~ zhang2025dreamvla,lv2025f1,yuan2026fastwam,agarwal2026cosmos , while latent-space approaches compress future information into compact conditions or visuomotor representations~ xu2026futurevla,su2026world,sun2026vla . Recent methods~ lee2026mu_0,yan2026robust,lee2026act,wang2026robointer1,li2025cronusvla,chen2025internvla,instructvla,ding2026skillplug , also explore structured predictive signals such as dynamic, spatial, or semantic information to connect VLMs or world modeling with control. However, existing methods vary in how geometric structure and action-relevant temporal transitions are organized. Our work focuses specifically on predictive geometry: we learn a structured representation that preserves scene geometry and its evolution, and derive a complementary motor representation from geometric transitions. Geometric Learning for Robotic Manipulation. Geometric information has been increasingly incorporated into robotic policies to improve spatial grounding. Input-centric approaches spatialvla,sun2025geovla,bhat20253d,zhang2025spatial,huang2025roboground,li2026robointer,yang2026robo3r augment current observations with depth, point clouds, 2D or 3D coordinates, or spatial features, providing direct access to the geometry of the observed scene. More recent prediction-centric approaches li2025qdepth,he2026elan4d,yang20264d,su2026world instead use geometric or spatiotemporal prediction as auxiliary supervision, including depth prediction, robot trajectories, and 3D motion representations. These approaches demonstrate the value of geometry for predictive policy learning, but geometric structure and action relevance may favor different types of information: preserving scene geometry requires broad structural fidelity, whereas action generation benefits from transitions that are informative for motor behavior. Our work addresses this distinction by learning complementary predictive geometric and motor representations, and transferring them separately to downstream policies through dedicated interfaces. Method sec:method We present a two-stage framework for learning complementary predictive representations and transferring them to downstream policies. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig2 , during (i) Complementary Predictive Representation Pretraining, continuous multi-view video clips are first converted into compact predictive geometric representations that preserve the spatial structure of the scene while capturing its temporal evolution. We then use the transitions between these predictive geometric representations, together with temporally aligned action supervision, to extract action-aware information into a complementary motor representation. During (ii) Representation-Guided Policy Post-training, as shown in Fig. fig3 , the predictive geometric representations and motor representations are transferred to the policy through two dedicated supervision pathways. Geometry queries are trained to infer structured predictive geometric information from current-time inputs, while intermediate features along the action-generation pathway are aligned with the motor representation. title: Reasoning as a Distribution: Generative Plan Latents for Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies increasingly reason before acting, but existing reasoning models compress this intermediate decision into a single representation. When several plans are valid, this commitment hides alternatives that could otherwise be selected or revised. We introduce the Generative Plan Latent (GPL), which represents the reasoning state as a low-dimensional conditional distribution over plans, such as which object, grasp, or route to use. This makes the reasoning state addressable: without retraining the VLA, plans can be sampled (coverage), selected on request (steering), and reweighted by deployment outcomes (outcome adaptation). We test all three on SimplerEnv manipulation with $π_0$, and extend the analysis to RoboCasa, LIBERO, and a maze domain. Steering the plan raises the fraction of executions that follow the request from 0.48 to 0.94, while the same guidance on the native action distribution shows no reliable gain. Finally, we show that an explicit plan is most useful when it carries decision information not already determined by the observation.
full_text: Introduction sec:introduction Vision–Language–Action (VLA) policies increasingly place a reasoning stage between perception and action Zawalski24-ecot,hao2024training,bai2026latent, huang2026thinkact,huang2026fast , and this intermediate state empirically improves policy success rate. This intermediate state is attractive because it can separate what the robot decides to do from the motor trajectory that realizes that decision. Yet existing reasoning models represent this state as one vector per observation. This raises the question: should a model expose one committed decision per observation, or a distribution over valid ones? The distinction matters whenever the observation leaves more than one decision valid. Consider a robot facing two identical cubes, with an instruction that names neither: nothing favors one target over the other. The same ambiguity is pervasive in everyday tasks: whether to pick up a can or push it aside, how to grasp a mug, or which route to take. A reasoning state that must produce a single decision necessarily collapses these alternatives. Averaging them may yield an invalid plan between the cubes; choosing one avoids this failure but still hides the equally valid alternative. The missing property is therefore not simply validity, but a representation that preserves the alternatives so they remain accessible at inference time, allowing preferences or outcomes to dynamically select the most viable strategy at deployment without retraining ( ). We call a reasoning state addressable when, at inference time, the policy can be: sampled to obtain distinct valid decisions (coverage), conditioned to select among them a single decision (steering), and reweighted by outcome to adapt the decision in closed-loop (outcome adaptation). The limitation of prior designs is therefore a lack of addressability. This is not the usual action-multimodality problem: robot learning has already developed generative action models precisely to avoid averaging incompatible motor trajectories ( ). The unresolved question is whether the upstream decision should itself also be represented as a distribution. We introduce the Generative Plan Latent ( ), which replaces a deterministic plan readout with a conditional distribution \(p_ (z c)\) of plans given a VLA representation . This distribution can be sampled, steered toward a requested mode, and reweighted from deployment experience, all without retraining the underlying VLA. We show that the plan provides a substantially stronger handle than the action distribution for expressing an external preference. Under matched executors, selecting a requested plan increases the fraction of executions that follow it from 0.48 to 0.94, whereas applying the same inference-time intervention to 's native action distribution yields no reliable improvement. Because these alternatives remain explicit, deployment outcomes can also change which plans are preferred without updating the plan generator or VLA. This benefit is conditional: an explicit plan can influence behavior only when it carries decision information that the executor cannot already recover from the observation. We call this the redundancy principle. In a controlled test, changing only the demonstrations to reduce this redundancy increases the plan-selection effect from +0.19 to +0.65. Finally, these capabilities do not depend on hand-designed plan coordinates: they persist when the plan representation is learned directly from demonstrated behavior. Our contributions are: We identify the decision bottleneck as a distinct locus for multimodality in VLAs and define addressability, the capacity to preserve alternative decisions so they can be sampled, selected, and revised. Matched plan- and action-level interventions show that the decision bottleneck provides the stronger handle for controlling behavior. We introduce , a distribution over task-level plans, instantiated by a rectified-flow head and integrated into with frozen base weights and a small adaptation. We propose the redundancy principle: an explicit plan should affect behavior only when it carries decision information not already determined by the observation. Related Work sec:related Reasoning in VLAs. Recent VLAs increasingly insert an intermediate reasoning stage between perception and action. Embodied Chain-of-Thought (ECoT) Zawalski24-ecot makes this reasoning explicit in language, grounded in robot-relevant quantities such as subtasks, objects, and motion; other approaches move this computation into continuous hidden states huang2026thinkact,huang2026fast,bai2026latent,tur2026rdvla . CoT-VLA zhao2025cot instead samples visual subgoals as sequences of future frames, yielding a visual chain-of-thought in pixel space rather than a compact plan representation. Despite these different representations, continuous action-domain reasoners typically expose a single intermediate state per observation ( ), rather than an explicit distribution over alternative decisions. Continuous and generative latent reasoning. Continuous reasoning was first studied in the language domain: Coconut hao2024training feeds hidden states back into the model as continuous thoughts, while generative approaches place a distribution over the reasoning state ye2024diffusion,huang2025reinforcing,kang2026ladirlatentdiffusionenhances,tu2026latent . STAR-LDM lovelace2025stopthinkautoregress similarly samples a latent reasoning state that is injected as soft tokens before generation. These works establish continuous and stochastic reasoning for text. Latent plans and generative planning. Sampling latent plans to condition low-level control is well established in robot learning lynch2019learning,lynch2021language,mees2022hulc . Higher-level policies can search these spaces rosete2022tacorl , while LDCQ venkatraman2024reasoning learns a multimodal distribution over latent skills and selects among them with a value function. Trajectory-level generative planners janner2022planning,ajay2023is combine sampling with test-time guidance, while SuSIE black2024zero and UniPi du2023learning generate visual subgoals for downstream control. Generative actions and adaptation. Generative action models florence2022implicit,lee2024behavior,chi2025diffusion and flow-based VLAs black2024pi_0 already represent multimodal motor behavior. Flow-reversal and noise-space methods wagenmaker2025steering,tang2026improving,lu2026unisteerunifiednoisesteering steer these action distributions, while verifier-based selection kwok2025robomonkeyscalingtesttimesampling , rejection-based post-training tan2025interactive , reinforcement-learning-style updates chen2025conrft,li2025simplevla , and failure- or energy-guided action generation zheng2026failing,song2026omniguide use feedback to improve behavior. Together, these lines of work provide intermediate reasoning states, generative latent plans, and multimodal action distributions, but leave open where multimodality should reside in a reasoning-augmented VLA. Method: The Generative Plan Latent sec:method The change relative to a standard VLA. A modern VLA may already be generative at the action level; our method does not replace that machinery. Instead, we insert a generative variable upstream of the action model, at the point where the task-level decision is represented. traces the resulting pipeline: the frozen VLA backbone reads the observation and instruction into a conditioning vector, the generative plan latent samples and projects the task-level decision from that conditioning, and the action expert consumes the projected plan alongside fresh observations to act at every step. Problem setting. Let denote an image observation and a language instruction. A pretrained VLA backbone maps them to a conditioning representation . We define a plan as a low-dimensional representation of the decision required by the task as opposed to the motor trajectory that accomplishes it. Generative plan model. We model the conditional plan distribution with rectified flow liu2023flow,lipman2023flow . With , and for a plan extracted from a demonstration, a velocity field is trained with At inference we draw from the prior and integrate with the Euler method to obtain ; because this takes only a handful of integration steps rather than a token-by-token decode, one latent-plan draw costs roughly \(80 \) less than one sampled reasoning chain in a matched comparison on the same conditioning and backbone (ECoT-VLA, Zawalski24-ecot ). A projector maps the sampled plan to soft tokens inserted into the executor prefix, the plan interface, after which the executor predicts its action chunk using its native action objective. Steering. Suppose a user specifies a desired plan property , such as which object to grasp or which route to follow. We train a lightweight noise-conditioned classifier on intermediate noisy plans along the flow path and bias the velocity field with its score during inference: where controls guidance strength. Setting recovers the original plan distribution while increasing moves probability mass toward the requested mode, and neither the plan generator nor the VLA is retrained when the command changes ( ). Outcome adaptation from experience. Steering assumes that the desired plan property is specified externally; outcome adaptation instead uses feedback obtained after deployment, while keeping the plan generator fixed. Let \(z^ (1) , ,z^ (K) p_ (z c)\) be candidate plans and let \(s(c,z)\) denote a deployment-time score, with larger values preferred. Outcome adaptation reweights the plan prior toward high-scoring candidates: where \( 0\) controls how strongly deployment feedback modifies the plan prior. The score \(s\) is deliberately generic, and we evaluate two broad classes of scoring mechanisms (formalized in ). A learned critic trains a parametric model \(s(c,z)=g_ (z)\) to predict rewards directly from accumulated \((z,r)\) deployment rollouts, where \(r\) is the deployment outcome associated with \(z\). Alternatively, when a task partitions into discrete modes, a non-parametric reward table simply assigns a candidate plan the historical average reward of its corresponding mode, requiring zero training floating-point operations (FLOPs). Rather than greedily executing a single top-scoring draw, both methods reweight the discrete candidate pool with Boltzmann weights; reported performance is the resulting expected outcome. Both scoring mechanisms can continuously absorb new deployment experience to update their estimates, while the generative prior \(p_ (z c)\) and the underlying VLA remain completely fixed. Adapting a pretrained VLA. While the GPL is designed to augment any modern pretrained VLA, we instantiate our primary architecture using . To integrate the generative plan without disrupting the underlying capabilities of the backbone, we add a projector and a low-rank adapter (LoRA) hu2021lora to the action expert. This adapter is trained purely through the native action objective of the VLA without requiring an auxiliary plan-imitation loss. To ensure the executor remains robust, we use classifier-free guidance (CFG) ho2022classifierfreediffusionguidance , so we randomly drop plan tokens during training. We evaluate against three strict baselines: the unmodified stock , a plan-less control (which uses our adapted weights but omits the plan at inference), and a dedicated no-plan adapter trained at an identical budget. Full details are in . Three Capabilities of an Addressable Plan sec:experiments Setup. We deploy our method across two distinct executor pipelines. To isolate reasoning from execution confounds and enable extensive ablation matrices, we first use a learned soft-token executor featuring a frozen perception backbone and a flow action head trained from scratch. For external validity, we then evaluate on a pretrained VLA ( or ), adapted as described in . Coverage: Representing the Full Decision Space subsec:coverage Coverag

title: Perceives but Doesn't Brake: A Perception-Action Binding Gap in Reasoning Driving VLAs
summary: Reasoning-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) driving models can perceive and reason about safety-critical hazards yet fail to translate that evidence into safe actions. We characterize this failure as a perception-action binding gap: hazard information is available inside the model but exerts insufficient control over trajectory generation. Using matched simulated counterfactuals and logged driving replay, we show that in-path hazards are actually encoded in the visual representation, but longitudinal plans are dominated by ego-speed history and respond only weakly to hazard proximity or the model's own reasoning trace. Further analysis shows that the trajectory generator is capable of braking but sometimes fails to do so due to the perception-action binding gap. Without retraining or modifying any weights, we inject a hazard-conditioned energy into the frozen flow-matching sampler of Alpamayo-1.5, restoring the missing coupling at generation time. With exact obstacle geometry, guidance cuts footprint intrusion from 58.1% to 14.5% and recovers safe braking whenever sufficient stopping distance remains, eliminating collisions entirely in our braking-relevant closed-loop battery. It also reverses the diagnosed dependence of the plan, from tracking ego speed to responding to obstacle range. These results separate hazard perception from hazard control in driving VLAs, show that unsafe behavior can arise even when the model has both the evidence and the ability to act on it, and propose a simple fix for bridging this binding gap.
full_text: Reasoning-augmented vision-language-action (VLA) driving models can perceive and reason about safety-critical hazards yet fail to translate that evidence into safe actions. We characterize this failure as a perception--action binding gap: hazard information is available inside the model but exerts insufficient control over trajectory generation. Using matched simulated counterfactuals and logged driving replay, we show that in-path hazards are actually encoded in the visual representation, but longitudinal plans are dominated by ego-speed history and respond only weakly to hazard proximity or the model's own reasoning trace. Further analysis shows that the trajectory generator is capable of braking but sometimes fails to do so due to the perception-action binding gap. Without retraining or modifying any weights, we inject a hazard-conditioned energy into the frozen flow-matching sampler of , restoring the missing coupling at generation time. With exact obstacle geometry, guidance cuts footprint intrusion from 58.1 to 14.5 and recovers safe braking whenever sufficient stopping distance remains, eliminating collisions entirely in our braking-relevant closed-loop battery. It also reverses the diagnosed dependence of the plan, from tracking ego speed to responding to obstacle range. These results separate hazard perception from hazard control in driving VLAs, show that unsafe behavior can arise even when the model has both the evidence and the ability to act on it, and propose a simple fix for bridging this binding gap. Introduction sec:intro Reasoning-augmented vision--language--action (VLA) models are increasingly designed to do more than map observations directly to actions: they perceive the scene, produce an explicit reasoning trace, and then generate a driving trajectory. This architecture suggests a natural safety premise: if the model correctly identifies a hazard and reasons that the vehicle should respond, that evidence should influence the resulting action. However, on simulated scenes containing a stationary obstacle in the ego lane, a state-of-the-art reasoning VLA~ alpamayo2025r1 generates trajectories that enter the obstacle footprint on 58.1 of samples, and its selected actions collide with a reconstructed version of that obstacle in most closed-loop rollouts, even though a comfortable stop was still possible. Crucially, the failure does not arise because the hazard is absent from the model. The obstacle is recoverable from the visual representation and is often explicitly identified in the model's own reasoning, yet neither source of evidence exerts sufficient influence on the generated longitudinal plan. Instead, the plan remains strongly governed by the supplied ego-speed history. We call this dissociation between accessible hazard evidence and its influence on action a perception--action binding gap ( ); here perceives means recoverable from the model's representation (formalized as availability, ), not awareness. This distinction matters because an unsafe action can have at least three different causes. First, the relevant hazard may not be represented at all (availability). Second, the trajectory generator may be incapable of producing an appropriate response even when the hazard is known (action-side sufficiency). Third, the evidence may be available and a safe action may be expressible, but the evidence may have insufficient action authority: changing the hazard does not sufficiently change the generated plan. These cases imply different remedies, yet standard driving metrics typically conflate them. We disentangle them with matched simulated interventions that vary visual hazard content, obstacle range, ego-speed history, and textual reasoning while holding competing inputs fixed. Hazard information is available throughout, yet longitudinal behavior is far more sensitive to ego history than to the hazard itself, under closed-loop control in AlpaSim/NuRec alpasim_2025 as well as open-loop scoring. Next, we ask whether the missing coupling can be restored without retraining the policy. We inject a differentiable hazard energy into the frozen flow-matching sampler of , steering trajectory generation during flow integration while leaving all model parameters unchanged. Supplied exact obstacle geometry, this reduces footprint intrusion from 58.1 to 14.5 and changes the governing dependence of the generated plan: trajectory reach becomes primarily responsive to obstacle range rather than ego speed. Controlled CARLA sweeps further show that the remaining failures are those in which insufficient stopping distance remains. Finally, we ask how far this intervention can be driven by signals already present in the frozen model, rather than by privileged geometry. Lightweight readouts of the visual cache estimate both when an in-path hazard is present and where it lies. The key is to preserve the spatial structure needed for that estimate: on sites held out in both geometry and appearance, a spatially aware readout reduces footprint intrusion from to , approaching the obtained with exact geometry, with no measured reach loss on matched clear scenes. Thus, much of the safety constraint needed to restore perception-action binding is already recoverable from the model's own representation. Autonomous binding is therefore feasible within the evaluated visual domain, while robust semantic triggering under domain shift remains open. Our contributions are threefold. First, our primary contribution is to identify and causally diagnose a perception--action binding gap in a reasoning driving VLA. Across logged driving, matched counterfactuals, and closed-loop replay, we separate hazard availability from action authority and show that longitudinal planning is dominated by ego-speed history; to our knowledge, this is the first causal, rather than correlational, separation of hazard availability from action authority in a reasoning driving VLA. Second, we show that the missing coupling can be enforced at inference time without retraining. A differentiable hazard-conditioned energy steers the frozen flow-matching sampler toward safe braking and, when supplied an accurate constraint, shifts the plan's dependence from ego speed toward obstacle range, demonstrating action-side sufficiency. Third, we show why standard logged evaluation can miss such a failure. Because a binding gap is a failure of hazard-conditioned action response rather than average prediction quality, standard logged evaluation can miss it: safety-critical states in which a moving ego must brake for a stationary in-path obstacle are rare because human drivers typically avoid them. Related Work sec:related Ego-State Shortcuts and Driving Evaluation Prior work shows that open-loop driving benchmarks can be solved surprisingly well from ego dynamics alone~ zhai2023admlp , and that planners remain nearly unchanged under severe visual corruption while responding strongly to ego-velocity perturbations~ li2024ego . These findings establish an ego-state shortcut but do not distinguish whether visual evidence is absent from the representation or present yet uncoupled from action. Reasoning and Video--Action Driving Models Recent driving policies increasingly couple visual observations, language or reasoning, and action generation. combines chain-of-causation reasoning with a flow-matching trajectory expert~ alpamayo2025r1 ; predicts language-level driving decisions~ senna2024 ; combines language, perception, navigation, and explicit ego state~ shao2024lmdrive ; and is a language-free video--action policy without explicit ego-state input~ bartoccioni2025vavim . Reasoning--Action Faithfulness Prior work shows that stated reasoning and executed behavior can disagree, including within the same model family~ cotfaithful2026av , and that embodied reasoning faithfulness can be improved with learned critics~ pinocchio2026 . These studies show language and action can diverge, but do not separate hazard availability from whether it exerts causal authority over the trajectory. Inference-Time Guidance for Generative Policies Gradient guidance can steer pretrained diffusion and flow samplers during generation without retraining~ dhariwal2021diffusion,lipman2023flow,guidedflows2023 ; runtime reasoning--action alignment has also used sample-and-rerank schemes~ dowhatyousay2025 . We use guidance as a diagnostic intervention rather than proposing a new control mechanism: by granting a safety constraint direct authority during sampling, we test whether the frozen generator can produce a response that its native conditioning fails to elicit. Background sec:setup Model and Evaluation Instruments We evaluate ~ alpamayo2025r1 frozen and zero-shot, preserving its native input and ego history conditioning. The flow-matching trajectory expert generates a 6.4\,s trajectory; unless otherwise noted, we sample trajectories per state. All instruments study the same critical state: an approaching ego vehicle facing a stationary in-path obstacle. Logged scenes From held-out US test clips of the NVIDIA PhysicalAI-AV set~ nvidia2025physicalai , we select states where ego speed is at least 4\,m/s and a stationary object lies 8--45\,m ahead in the ego corridor, using only contemporaneous labels and never the driver's future trajectory, yielding states from clips. These states form a nominal diagnostic set, not a hazard benchmark: the objects are predominantly vehicles parked at the curb, no braking is required of the ego, and at the model's native input its plans enter the footprint on only of samples. We use these scenes only to measure which input variable the plan's forward reach tracks. Designed hazards in controlled simulation Using CARLA~ dosovitskiy2017carla through Fail2Drive~ fail2drive2026 , we construct matched-despawn pairs: identical sites, rendering, ego motion, history, and native four-camera temporal input, differing only in whether the stationary obstacle is present, isolating the causal effect of hazard content. Hazards span six object kinds at 8--30\,m. We report two populations: seen sites ( hazard and 24 empty scenes over six sites, evaluated leave-one-site-out) and new sites ( and 12 over six disjoint sites held out in both geometry and appearance). Unless stated otherwise, 95 confidence intervals (CIs) are site-clustered bootstraps ( ). Closed-loop replay In AlpaSim/NuRec, we test repeated replanning with the native four-camera controller, using two stimuli. In the static one we re-pose a reconstructed vehicle 40\,m ahead in the ego lane and freeze it, paired with its unedited reconstruction as control; 24 of 27 candidate scenes completed both rollouts. In the dynamic one, we instead use a lead vehicle already present in the simulation. For each of 38 scenes in which this vehicle remains ahead of the ego in the same lane, we compare two matched rollouts: in the Drives on control, it continues along its logged motion, while in the Stops condition, we stop it at a pose it actually occupies in the logged scene. Thus, unlike the static stimulus, no vehicle is inserted or repositioned; only the lead vehicle's subsequent motion is changed. For the static stimulus, placing the obstacle 40\,m ahead only initializes the encounter: the policy then replans repeatedly as the ego approaches it. Crucially, the failure occurs while braking is still physically feasible. At the relevant replanning states, the obstacle is 8--24\,m ahead and stopping would require only 0.35--1.4\,m/s of deceleration. Metrics sec:metrics Our primary open-loop metric is footprint intrusion: the fraction of sampled trajectories whose swept ego footprint intersects the obstacle's. We also report forward reach, the distance traveled before rest (or over the full horizon), and minimum clearance, the smallest separation between swept ego and obstacle footprints, signed negative when they overlap. For close-range CARLA experiments, near-stop denotes forward reach below 8\,m.

title: PanoGraphGS: Unifying Panoptic Segmentation and Hierarchical 3D Scene Graphs with Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D scene graphs support language-guided navigation by organizing physical entities and their containment and spatial relations into hierarchical maps. Building such structured maps requires a scene representation that consistently distinguishes semantic regions and object instances across viewpoints. To this end, we present PanoGraphGS, a unified framework that integrates panoptic 3D Gaussian representation learning with hierarchical 3D scene graph construction. The framework learns semantic and instance features on shared Gaussian geometry. Prototype-based semantic learning and association-based instance learning produce consistent panoptic predictions across viewpoints. The learned representation supports novel-view panoptic segmentation and direct Gaussian-level panoptic decoding. A semantic-aware scene graph module further recovers a floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy with containment and spatial relations. We further release NaviGS, a real-world dataset for panoramic scene understanding. The dataset provides 3DGS, mesh, RGB, semantic, and depth data. For 3D scene graph identification, PanoGraphGS outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline in object-node accuracy by more than 50\% points on average across Replica and NaviGS. PanoGraphGS also achieves state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods in 2D panoptic segmentation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of PanoGraphGS in both hierarchical 3D scene understanding and 2D panoptic segmentation. The project website is available at: https://github.com/gaojh0333/PanoGraphGS.

For 3D scene graph identification, PanoGraphGS outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline in object-node accuracy by more than 50 points on average across Replica and NaviGS. PanoGraphGS also achieves state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods in 2D panoptic segmentation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of PanoGraphGS in both hierarchical 3D scene understanding and 2D panoptic segmentation. The project website is available at: . INTRODUCTION Panoptic 3D scene reconstruction is fundamental to language-guided robotic navigation. Successful navigation requires embodied agents to recognize semantic categories, maintain persistent instance identities, and reason about spatial organization in a globally consistent map. Such tasks require reasoning over nested containment and spatial relations. A 3D scene graph formalizes this organization by representing physical entities as nodes and their containment and spatial relations as edges~ armeni2019scenegraph,wald2020learning3dssg . 3D Dynamic Scene Graphs~ rosinol20203ddsg , Hydra~ hughes2022hydra , and HOV-SG~ werby2024hovsg , have advanced structured spatial mapping. However, these pipelines commonly rely on per-pixel RGB-D observations or depth-derived geometry. Incomplete or noisy depth can degrade object-extent estimation, cross-view association, room partitioning, and spatial-relation inference. Moreover, existing methods typically construct scene graphs and dense panoptic representations separately, requiring an additional stage to associate panoptic predictions with graph entities. These limitations motivate a unified 3D representation that preserves geometry, semantic categories, and persistent instance identities while being learned directly from multi-view RGB observations. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233dgs provides such a representation through explicit, spatially anchored Gaussian primitives and differentiable rendering. Visibility-aware rendering lifts multi-view semantic and instance supervision into a shared 3D field. The learned features can be rendered for novel-view panoptic prediction or decoded directly from Gaussians for 3D entity abstraction. Unified-Lift~ zhu2025unifiedlift learns Gaussian- and object-level representations from multi-view segmentation cues. More recently, GaussianGraph~ wang2025gaussiangraph extends 3DGS toward scene graph generation by clustering Gaussian primitives and associating them with CLIP features and spatial relations extracted from 2D foundation models. However, its reasoning mainly focuses on object-level spatial relations and relies on high-dimensional vision--language features for semantic association, while clustering may discard fine-grained spatial information. Explicit identification, matching, and hierarchical association across the floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy remain unaddressed. Consequently, dense panoptic prediction and hierarchical scene organization remain loosely integrated. Establishing globally consistent panoptic predictions within a Gaussian representation therefore presents two challenges. First, viewpoint-dependent visibility and occlusion produce nonuniform multi-view supervision. Second, the same physical object may receive different view-local pseudo-instance identifiers across views, causing conflicting identity supervision without cross-view association. Gaussian-level labels also do not explicitly encode the floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy or its containment and spatial relations. Recovering this structure requires joint reasoning over Gaussian semantics, persistent instance identities, and reconstructed geometry. To address these challenges, we propose PanoGraphGS, an end-to-end framework that integrates panoptic 3D Gaussian representation learning with hierarchical 3D scene graph construction. PanoGraphGS jointly learns semantic and instance features anchored to shared Gaussian geometry. The semantic branch combines residual feature projection and category prototypes with confidence-weighted supervision, while the instance branch associates view-local pseudo-labels with persistent Gaussian instance identities to ensure consistent object correspondence across views. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:resthome15 , the resulting panoptic Gaussian representation supports both panoptic segmentation and direct Gaussian-level decoding. The semantic-aware hierarchical reasoning module combines structural semantics with Gaussian geometry to recover the floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy and its containment and spatial relations, enabling structured spatial queries such as locating the bed1 in the living room on floor1. CLIP~ radford2021clip is further used to assign functional categories to rooms. Our main contributions are: We propose Prototype-Based Semantic Learning, which jointly optimizes 2D rendered and 3D Gaussian features in a unified semantic space, overcoming the limitation of optimizing features in only the 2D or 3D domain. We propose Association-Based Instance Learning, which associates view-local instance masks with persistent identities for cross-frame consistent panoptic prediction, with confidence-aware supervision reducing the impact of unreliable labels. We propose a semantic-aware hierarchical 3D scene graph construction method that organizes learned panoptic Gaussians into a floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy without additional training or RGB-D inputs. We achieve state-of-the-art performance in both 2D panoptic segmentation and 3D scene graph construction. RELATED WORK sec:related_work 3D Gaussian Segmentation 3DGS-based segmentation has progressed from open-vocabulary semantics and instance grouping to panoptic understanding. Open-vocabulary methods embed vision--language features into 3D Gaussian primitives. LangSplat~ qin2024langsplat learns language-aligned Gaussian features, while OpenGaussian~ wu2024opengaussian and OVGaussian~ chen2025ovgaussian extend this paradigm to point-level open-vocabulary segmentation. Mask-lifting methods transfer 2D masks and instance information into Gaussian representations. Gaussian Grouping~ ye2024gaussiangrouping learns identity-aware Gaussian features for object grouping, while Unified-Lift~ zhu2025unifiedlift combines Gaussian- and object-level representations with association learning for 3D instance segmentation. More recently, PLGS~ wang2025plgs jointly learns semantic and instance attributes from multi-view supervision, and PanoSLAM~ chen2025panoslam integrates panoptic Gaussian learning with sequential RGB-D mapping. Similarly, PanoGS~ zhai2025panogs combines open-vocabulary semantics with instance segmentation, while PanopticSplatting~ xie2025panopticsplatting introduces query-guided cross-view label refinement for panoptic segmentation. Despite these advances, existing methods mainly focus on novel-view panoptic prediction, with feature optimization restricted to either the 2D or 3D domain. In contrast, PanoGraphGS jointly optimizes 2D and 3D features, enabling both panoptic segmentation and direct Gaussian-level decoding. Hierarchical 3D Scene Graphs Armeni et al.~ armeni2019scenegraph first organize buildings, rooms, and objects into a multi-layer graph, while 3DSSG~ wald2020learning3dssg learns object relations from indoor reconstructions. 3DDGS~ rosinol20203ddsg integrate geometry with objects, places, and agents, Hydra~ hughes2022hydra enables online hierarchical mapping, and HOV-SG~ werby2024hovsg introduces an open-vocabulary floor-room-object hierarchy. GaussianGraph~ wang2025gaussiangraph novelly constructs structured scene graphs directly from Gaussians. However, these approaches commonly rely on per-pixel RGB-D observations for geometry and primarily focus on object-level recognition. In contrast, PanoGraphGS leverages learned semantic and instance features together with Gaussian geometry to recover a hierarchical floor-room-stuff-object scene graph with explicit containment and spatial relations without training. title: VLA-Retain: Benchmarking Cross-Dimension Effects of Vision Tuning in VLAs
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer knowledge from large-scale pretraining into robot control, but their manipulation performance remains sensitive to changes in observation conditions, which recent work addresses by fine-tuning the visual module on target-domain data. However, it remains unclear how such adaptation affects robustness beyond the target condition, as existing robustness benchmarks only evaluate models without fine-tuning and adaptation studies only report the target gain. Measuring this cross-dimension effect requires separating target gains from off-target changes, isolating adaptation effects from architectural differences, ruling out generic forgetting, and comparing tuning choices. Therefore, we introduce VLA-Retain, a benchmark that compares five open VLA models, tuned on Camera-view or Sensor-noise data, with their own base checkpoints on LIBERO-Plus dataset spanning seven perturbation dimensions. Our study reveals four findings. First, targeted vision tuning is not local, and its target gain does not predict retention. Mean off-target gain is negative in 8 of 10 model--domain configurations. Under Camera-view tuning, X-VLA gains $69.4$ percentage points on the target but loses $4.6$ points on average elsewhere, whereas OpenVLA-OFT gains $39.3$ and $1.4$ points, respectively. Second, these regressions are not explained only by performance loss on the same tasks without perturbations. Third, broader training coverage raises overall gain over target-specific training but does not eliminate dimension-level regressions. Fourth, tuning strategies are model-dependent, as DELTA-style feature preservation raises X-VLA's mean off-target gain to $+1.2$ points but lowers OpenVLA-OFT's to $-23.1$. Overall, these findings show that target-domain success alone is insufficient and highlight cross-dimensional retention as a key criterion for targeted VLA adaptation.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations, language instructions, and robot state to executable actions, transferring large-scale visual and semantic knowledge into robot control~ brohan2023rt2,driess2023palme,openx2023,kim2024openvla . This provides a scalable route toward general-purpose manipulation, but deployment conditions rarely match those seen during training, as camera placement changes, sensors become noisy, illumination and backgrounds vary, objects appear in new layouts, and operators phrase the same goal differently. Current VLAs remain sensitive to these shifts~ simplerenv2024,fei2025liberoplus , so a deployed model must be adapted to new conditions. Reliable deployment therefore requires adapting to the new condition while retaining robustness to the other conditions the robot continues to encounter. Existing studies address this requirement from two directions. First, robustness benchmarks~ fei2025liberoplus,zhang2025vlaarena,wang2026liberox evaluate fixed models under controlled perturbations, showing that robustness varies across visual, spatial, linguistic, and task-level dimensions and thereby guiding model selection. Second, targeted adaptation studies fine-tune the chosen model's vision encoder on target-domain data to recover robustness to a selected shift. li2025generalizable recover camera-view robustness through low-rank visual updates, while VLAGuard~ yin2026vlaguard and Structure-Aware Robust Fine-Tuning~ zhang2026sarf defend against physical attention hijacking by tuning only the vision encoder. Since model selection cannot cover every shift, targeted vision tuning offers a more practical adaptation strategy. However, this strategy overlooks how tuning for one shift affects robustness to non-target perturbations. Targeted adaptation studies report only the target-domain gain, and robustness benchmarks evaluate only models without such tuning, so neither reveals how the adaptation itself changes robustness under the remaining conditions. This matters because the adapted visual representation feeds the same frozen downstream components under every condition. Tuning it for one domain can thus change behavior under unseen shifts in language, object layout, or sensor noise, while target-domain success or an aggregate score can hide such regressions. Measuring such cross-dimension effects poses four challenges. First, adaptation effects are multi-dimensional, so neither target-only nor aggregate evaluation suffices. Second, VLA architectures differ in baseline robustness, so absolute post-tuning scores mix adaptation effects with differences in their starting points. Third, an off-target regression may reflect generic forgetting or task sampling rather than perturbation-specific interference. Fourth, adaptation has a large design space spanning data coverage, tuning scope, and retention methods, whose effects may vary by model. We introduce , a paired benchmark designed to address these challenges (Figure~ fig:benchmark_overview ). To expose multi-dimensional effects, it evaluates every base--tuned pair on the same 10,030 episodes~ fei2025liberoplus including seven perturbation dimensions and reports target, mean and worst off-target, and overall gains separately. To isolate adaptation effects, it compares five open VLA models, each tuned on Camera-view or Sensor-noise data, with their own base checkpoints fine-tuned on LIBERO~ liu2023libero . To test alternative explanations, it adds original-LIBERO controls and paired cluster-bootstrap intervals. To cover the design space, it varies training-data coverage across all five models and tuning strategy on two representative architectures. We use to answer the following four questions. Does targeted vision tuning affect off-target robustness? Yes, and the change is usually a regression. Mean off-target gain is negative in 8 of 10 model--domain configurations, and language and object-layout success decline in 9 of 10, although only the visual module is updated. The target gain does not predict these effects: under Camera-view tuning, X-VLA improves target success from to but loses percentage points on average across off-target dimensions, whereas OpenVLA-OFT improves from to while gaining points. Are these regressions explained by forgetting of the original tasks? Not fully. Success on the same tasks without perturbations declines by at most points for every checkpoint except NORA-1.5 after Camera-view tuning. After subtracting this change, every Camera-view-tuned model and four of five Sensor-noise-tuned models still regress on at least one off-target perturbation. Does broader training coverage prevent them? No. Mixed training over the complete training set gets a higher overall gain than either target-specific setting for all five models, yet every model still regresses on at least one dimension. Can alternative tuning strategies control them? Not consistently across models. Weight interpolation improves retention on both evaluated models but reduces the target gain, and the preferred tuning scope differs between them. In particular, DELTA-style feature preservation raises X-VLA's mean off-target gain from to points but lowers OpenVLA-OFT's from to . These results show that target-domain evaluation is valid but incomplete, as the same update can also affect off-target performance. By treating each tuned model as a paired change across seven robustness dimensions, separates target gains from changes elsewhere and makes cross-dimensional retention measurable. Targeted VLA adaptation should therefore be evaluated jointly by target improvement, off-target retention, and overall performance. Related Work sec:background Targeted adaptation of VLA models. VLA models map images and language instructions, optionally together with robot proprioception, to discrete action tokens or continuous action chunks~ brohan2023rt2,driess2023palme,openx2023 . Modern systems differ in their visual backbones, multimodal trunks, and action decoders~ kim2024openvla,kim2025oft,black2025pi05,zheng2025xvla,hung2025nora,ma2026internvla , but all rely on a visual representation that is consumed by downstream reasoning and action components. Parameter-efficient adaptation, including LoRA~ hu2022lora , makes it practical to update this pathway while freezing most of the VLA. Recent robustness methods use such visual updates to correct spatial misalignment under camera changes or defend against physical attention hijacking~ li2025generalizable,yin2026vlaguard,zhang2026sarf , establishing that adaptation improves the target condition. does not challenge these target-domain gains, it asks what the tuning update changes elsewhere. Retention under model adaptation. Retention methods constrain adaptation by keeping the tuned model close to a pretrained solution. WiSE-FT interpolates pretrained and fine-tuned weights to improve robustness~ wortsman2022robust , while DELTA preserves task-relevant source representations during transfer~ li2018delta . Our setting differs from sequential task learning because the manipulation tasks remain fixed while adaptation targets a specific observation shift in the shared visual pathway. We therefore evaluate retention across deployment conditions rather than by accuracy over a sequence of learned tasks, and Section~ sec:mitigation tests whether such retention methods control cross-dimension effects in VLAs. VLA robustness benchmarks. Existing benchmarks expose complementary limitations of VLA models. SimplerEnv~ simplerenv2024 studies simulation-based evaluation for real-robot setups, while LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025liberoplus extends LIBERO's~ liu2023libero manipulation tasks with seven controlled perturbation dimensions. VLA-Arena~ zhang2025vlaarena organizes evaluation by task structure, language, and visual difficulty, and LIBERO-X~ wang2026liberox introduces hierarchical tests of spatial generalization, object recognition, and instruction understanding. VLM4VLA~ zhang2026vlm4vla uses a common action design to isolate how VLM choice and embodied capabilities affect downstream control, identifying the visual module as a central bottleneck. These works characterize the robustness of fixed models, backbones, or generalization regimes, whereas measures how perturbation-specific vision tuning changes that robustness by pairing every fine-tuned model with its own base model. title: RLSplat: Resource-Linear Budget Control for Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (FF3DGS) reconstructs 3D scenes from images in a single forward pass, making it well-suited to applications that must operate within limited resource budgets. To further improve its practicality, recent budget-controllable FF3DGS methods allow the number of Gaussians to be adjusted at inference, so that the output meets a given storage limit or rendering-latency constraint. However, these methods overlook the cost of inference itself: to produce a representation with the target number of Gaussians, they first predict a dense set of Gaussians and then prune or select from it, requiring nearly constant latency and peak memory regardless of the budget. We therefore propose RLSplat, a resource-linear budget-controllable FF3DGS framework whose representation size, inference latency, and peak memory all decrease linearly as the Gaussian budget is reduced. Instead of pruning or selection, RLSplat learns a Gaussian allocation policy that distributes the budget across local scene regions, so that exactly the requested number of Gaussians is generated. These Gaussians are then refined through resource-linear Gaussian decoding, in which each Gaussian attends only to nearby Gaussians found via an efficient hierarchical neighbor search, so that the decoding cost decreases linearly with fewer Gaussians. In zero-shot evaluation, RLSplat outperforms prior budget-controllable methods at every budget, surpassing the strongest baseline even with 4$\times$ fewer Gaussians, while running up to 4.1$\times$ faster with 9.6$\times$ less peak memory at low budgets.

Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233dgs has become a leading representation for photorealistic, real-time novel view synthesis, supporting applications from AR/VR~ qian2024gaussianavatars,jiang2024vrgs to robotics~ keetha2024splatam,matsuki2024gsslam and digital content creation~ tang2024dreamgaussian,chen2024gsgen . Its explicit form further allows it to serve as a 3D scene representation for downstream models, such as 3D vision-language models~ li2025scenesplat,thai2025splattalk . Since per-scene optimization of 3DGS takes minutes to hours and requires many calibrated views, feed-forward 3DGS (FF3DGS) methods instead predict Gaussians in a single forward pass~ charatan2024pixelsplat,chen2024mvsplat , and recent variants even operate directly on uncalibrated images~ jiang2025anysplat . Owing to this fast and readily available reconstruction, FF3DGS has become a practical choice for applications that build 3D scene representations on the fly. Early FF3DGS methods~ charatan2024pixelsplat, chen2024mvsplat, ye2024nopo simplify the problem by allocating a fixed number of Gaussians to each input pixel, which allows the feed-forward network to be trained effectively. However, this pixel-aligned design produces many redundant Gaussians, since Gaussians from overlapping views become increasingly redundant as more views are added. To address this redundancy, query-based methods~ an2025c3g,itkin2026globalsplat decode a fixed set of learnable query tokens into Gaussians. Yet neither approach can adjust the number of Gaussians without retraining. This lack of controllability makes it difficult to adapt to the diverse resource budgets encountered in real-world deployment. To address this, recent works have proposed Gaussian budget-controllable methods. Given a Gaussian budget , EcoSplat~ park2025ecosplat first predicts one Gaussian per pixel and keeps the Gaussians with the highest opacity. Splat~ kim2026f4splat instead predicts Gaussians at multiple scales and selects the Gaussians. However, these methods overlook the computational cost of inference itself. Both methods first predict a much larger set of candidate Gaussians before reducing them to , so their inference latency and peak memory remain nearly constant regardless of the budget, as shown in (b) and (c). We therefore propose RLSplat, a budget-controllable FF3DGS framework that is resource-linear: both its representation size and inference cost scale linearly with the budget . Given uncalibrated images and a budget , a geometry backbone encodes the images into anchor tokens, each representing a local 3D region of the scene. To obtain a compact representation, we formulate Gaussian generation as an allocation problem rather than pruning or selection: we predict how many Gaussians to assign to each anchor's region, summing to . Since these discrete allocations are non-differentiable and can only be evaluated by rendering the resulting Gaussians, we model this prediction as a Gaussian allocation policy and train it with policy optimization, using Group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO)~ zheng2025gspo with rendering quality as the reward. Given the allocation, each anchor token spawns as many Gaussian tokens as its allocated count, yielding a total of Gaussian tokens. To efficiently decode these tokens into the final Gaussians, we introduce a resource-linear decoder. It refines each Gaussian token through local cross-attention over its nearest Gaussian tokens, which we find with an efficient hierarchical neighbor search. Whereas global self-attention over all tokens costs , each token here attends to only neighbors, so the decoding cost is and scales linearly with the Gaussian budget ( (c)). As a result, RLSplat achieves higher quality than prior budget-controllable methods at every budget ( (a)), while its peak memory and latency decrease with the budget. At 2K Gaussians, it achieves higher PSNR than F Splat while using 9.6 less peak memory ( (b)) and running 4.1 faster ( (c)). In summary, our contributions are as follows: We identify that existing budget-controllable FF3DGS methods control only the size of the output, not the cost of producing it, and introduce RLSplat, a resource-linear FF3DGS framework in which the number of Gaussians, inference latency, and peak memory all decrease linearly as the budget is reduced. We formulate Gaussian generation as an allocation problem and learn a Gaussian allocation policy via policy optimization that places exactly Gaussians where the scene needs them, together with a resource-linear decoder whose cost decreases linearly as the budget decreases through local cross-attention and an efficient hierarchical neighbor search. consistently outperforms prior budget-controllable methods across all budgets. At a budget of 2K Gaussians, it improves PSNR by 0.9 dB over F Splat while using 9.6 less peak memory and running 4.1 faster. Related Work -Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233dgs represents a scene with explicit Gaussian primitives and achieves real-time rendering, but requires time-consuming per-scene optimization from many calibrated views. Feed-forward 3DGS (FF3DGS) methods instead predict Gaussians in a single forward pass, from a single image~ szymanowicz2024splatter or from a few posed views~ charatan2024pixelsplat,chen2024mvsplat,xu2025depthsplat,zhang2024gs . Building on 3D foundation models~ wang2024dust3r,leroy2024mast3r,wang2025vggt , recent methods further remove the need for known camera poses~ ye2024nopo,smart2024splatt3r,huang2025spfsplat,jiang2025anysplat . Most of these methods predict one Gaussian per pixel or per voxel, so the number of Gaussians is determined by the input resolution and the number of views rather than by the scene content. This leads to redundant Gaussians in overlapping and textureless regions, and the number of Gaussians cannot be specified directly. and Gaussian budget-controllable FF3DGS. For per-scene 3DGS, many works aim to represent a scene with fewer Gaussians without sacrificing quality, either by pruning redundant Gaussians~ fan2024lightgaussian,lee2024compact,papantonakis2024reducing or by deciding where to place Gaussians under a fixed or constrained budget during densification~ fang2024mini,mallick2024taming,kheradmand20243d . These methods, however, rely on iterative per-scene optimization. In FF3DGS, C3G~ an2025c3g and GlobalSplat~ itkin2026globalsplat decode a fixed set of learnable query tokens into compact sets of Gaussians, whose size is determined by the architecture. EcoSplat~ park2025ecosplat and Splat~ kim2026f4splat instead accept a target count at inference, by keeping the Gaussians with the highest budget-conditioned opacity and by selecting one of multiple scales per region, respectively; both derive the output from a dense set of candidates. ZipSplat~ veicht2026zipsplat , developed concurrently with our work, controls the number of Gaussians by clustering visual tokens at inference. In contrast, we learn to allocate exactly the requested number of Gaussians and decode only those, so that our inference cost scales with the budget. optimization. Policy gradient methods~ williams1992reinforce,schulman2017ppo optimize non-differentiable, discrete decisions from a scalar reward, and have been applied to generative vision models, to align diffusion models with reward functions~ black2024ddpo . Group-relative variants such as GRPO~ shao2024deepseekmath and GSPO~ zheng2025gspo remove the need for a learned value function by normalizing rewards within a group of samples, and have become standard for fine-tuning large language models. In particular, GSPO defines the importance ratio from the likelihood of the whole sequence rather than of individual tokens, and clips it at the sequence level. We adopt this approach to learn Gaussian allocation, treating an allocation as a sequence of Gaussians and using rendering quality as the reward. Method sec:method We present RLSplat, a feed-forward 3DGS framework whose Gaussian count and inference cost are both controlled by a single budget . Rather than pruning or selecting from a dense set of Gaussians, formulates Gaussian generation as allocation: a Gaussian allocation policy decides how many Gaussians each local region of the scene receives ( ), and a resource-linear decoder generates the allocated Gaussians and efficiently refines them with local cross-attention ( ). We begin with an overview ( ) and conclude with the training procedure ( ). Overview of sec:problem Given uncalibrated context images and a target Gaussian budget , predicts a set of 3D Gaussians along with the context camera parameters : Here, the 3DGS attribute consists of a 3D center, opacity, scale, rotation, and color coefficients. As illustrated in , a geometry backbone~ burzio2026dvlt encodes the images into anchor tokens . These anchors serve as the foundational sites from which the 3D Gaussians are spawned. To use the limited budget effectively, \ adaptively distributes the Gaussians across these anchors. Specifically, a Gaussian allocation policy assesses the local significance of each anchor to predict a discrete allocation that strictly sums to the budget ( ), and we optimize this policy via reinforcement learning ( ). Next, a resource-linear decoder instantiates exactly Gaussian tokens at each anchor.
