title: Plausible Future, Wrong Choice: Steering World-Action Models toward Intended Future
summary: World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied generalist policies by jointly modeling future world evolution and robot actions across diverse manipulation tasks. However, representing diverse futures is only the first step: a capable WAM must also generate futures that match the requirements of the current task and execution progress. In long-horizon manipulation where similar observation-action segments occur across different tasks and stages, existing approaches may generate locally plausible yet misdirected rollouts to drift toward wrong task stage, i.e., a phenomenon we term Stage Confusion. To address this problem, we propose TaskWAM, a closed-loop, stage-aware framework that represents fine-grained task requirements with Mode Tokens and tracks execution progress with State Tokens, forming a structured task state to steer world--action generation toward intended future. We further introduce StageBench, a controlled multi-stage manipulation benchmark with parameterized stage variations and automated evaluation.Extensive experiments on both simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks demonstrate that TaskWAM effectively reduces confusion and achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, TaskWAM provides strong plug-and-play transfer across heterogeneous WAM architectures and robot embodiments, including single-arm robots, dual-arm grippers, dexterous hands, and humanoid robots.
full_text: World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for embodied generalist policies by jointly modeling future world evolution and robot actions across diverse manipulation tasks. However, representing diverse futures is only the first step: a capable WAM must also generate futures that match the requirements of the current task and execution progress. In long-horizon manipulation where similar observation-action segments occur across different tasks and stages, existing approaches may generate locally plausible yet misdirected rollouts to drift toward wrong task stage, , a phenomenon we term Stage Confusion. To address this problem, we propose TaskWAM, a closed-loop, stage-aware framework that represents fine-grained task requirements with Mode Tokens and tracks execution progress with State Tokens, forming a structured task state to steer world--action generation toward intended future. We further introduce StageBench, a controlled multi-stage manipulation benchmark with parameterized stage variations and automated evaluation. Extensive experiments on both simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks demonstrate that TaskWAM effectively reduces confusion and achieves competitive performance with state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, TaskWAM provides strong plug-and-play transfer across heterogeneous WAM architectures and robot embodiments, including single-arm robots, dual-arm grippers, dexterous hands, and humanoid robots. Project Page: Introduction sec:intro Recently, World-Action Models (WAMs) bi2026motus,ye2026dreamzero,li2026lingbotva,yuan2026fastwam,chen2026lawam have shown promise for embodied generalist policies by jointly modeling future world evolution and robot actions, with the goal of supporting diverse manipulation tasks in everyday environments zhu2025uwm,li2025uva,li2026lingbotva . However, modeling diverse futures is only the first step. Once models are capable of representing multiple possible futures, the next challenge lies in generating future that is consistent with the task requirements and execution context. Existing WAMs typically infer stage progression implicitly from task instructions, observations, and execution histories lin2026jepawamlearningvisionlanguageactionpolicies,zhao2026sgwamselfguidedworldmodeling . This becomes particularly challenging in long-horizon household manipulation, where similar observation-action interactions can correspond to different next stages depending on fine-grained task requirements, , ordering, timing, repetition, or embodiment assignment, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:teaser (Top left). Consequently, WAMs may generate futures that are visually plausible and physically feasible, yet lead execution to the wrong stage. We refer to this failure as stage confusion in world-action modeling (hereafter, stage confusion). A few recent WAMs yang2026memorywam,cai2026ahawam have explored longer-term history modeling, but stage confusion is not merely a memory-length problem, leaving two key challenges: (1) similar interaction histories may still require different next stages, making instruction-specific guidance essential for resolving stage ambiguity; and (2) simply extending history introduces substantial redundant context, which can obscure critical execution cues for stage tracking while increasing the architectural burden of WAMs. To address these challenges, we propose TaskWAM, a closed-loop, stage-aware framework that explicitly grounds world-action generation in both task requirements and execution progress for long-horizon manipulation. Specifically, we introduce Structured Task-State Grounding with two complementary representations: Mode Tokens retrieve mode representations from a learnable mode codebook and ground them with text context to encode fine-grained execution requirements, while State Tokens track execution progress through causal temporal modeling of closed-loop action-observation transitions. We further propose Task-State Conditioned Future Steering, which steers future prediction by inject the structured task state into world and action generation through attention conditioning and residual flow correction. TaskWAM thus bridges diverse future modeling and intended future generation, offering two main advantages: (i) future generation grounding in closed-loop robot-environment interaction; (ii) plug-and-play steering mechanism applicable across heterogeneous WAM backbones. Additionally, existing benchmarks mees2022calvin,NEURIPS2023_8c3c6668,chen2025robotwin2,ICLR2026_a05003fd has mainly evaluated tasks in relatively independent settings, lacking sufficient data and evaluation protocols to assess this capability. To support systematic evaluation, we further introduce StageBench, a controlled multi-stage manipulation benchmark built on LIBERO NEURIPS2023_8c3c6668 and RoboTwin chen2025robotwin2 . StageBench constructs overlapping observation-action trajectories across tasks and execution stages by varying stage compositions and orders, covering visual grounding, sequential reasoning, embodiment coordination, etc. Extensive experiments in simulation and diverse real-world robotic tasks demonstrate that TaskWAM significantly reduces stage confusion and improves multi-stage manipulation over state-of-the-art methods. We further validate its generalization on RoboTwin 2.0 benchmark chen2025robotwin2 and its plug-and-play applicability across heterogeneous WAM architectures. Moreover, our method can be applied across diverse robot embodiments, including single-arm robots, dual-arm grippers, dexterous hands, and humanoid platforms. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We identify stage confusion in world-action modeling, where WAMs generate locally plausible yet stage-inconsistent futures under overlapping observation-action trajectories. We propose TaskWAM, which explicitly grounds world-action generation in task requirements and execution progress through Structured Task-State Grounding and task-state-conditioned future steering for stage-consistent future generation. We introduce StageBench, a controlled multi-stage manipulation benchmark that systematically constructs overlapping trajectories through parameterized task-stage variations and provides automated stage-aware evaluation. Extensive experiments across simulation and real-world tasks demonstrate that TaskWAM significantly reduces stage confusion and improves multi-stage manipulation across heterogeneous WAM backbones and diverse robot embodiments. Related Work sec:related_work -Action Models. Generalist robot learning aims to develop unified policies that can handle diverse manipulation tasks within a single model. Vision-Language-Action models physicalintelligence2025pi05,nvidia2026gr00tn17 have advanced this direction by scaling language-conditioned robot policies. World-Action Models (WAMs) bi2026motus,zhu2025uwm,ye2026dreamzero,li2026lingbotva,yuan2026fastwam, cai2026ahawam,chen2026lawam further extend this paradigm by jointly modeling future observations and robot actions. Recent studies explores inference-time imagination, world-action information exchange, and more efficient generation schedules ye2026dreamzero,li2026lingbotva,yuan2026fastwam , such as DreamZero ye2026dreamzero and LingBot-VA li2026lingbotva . However, existing WAMs still typically learn world-action futures from unified conditioning contexts lin2026jepawamlearningvisionlanguageactionpolicies,zhao2026sgwamselfguidedworldmodeling , leaving stage progression to be inferred implicitly from instructions, observations, and histories. Consequently, a predicted future can remain locally plausible while leading the robot to the wrong stage, , plausible future, yet wrong choice. In contrast, TaskWAM explicitly grounds future generation in task requirements and execution progress, targeting stage confusion in long-horizon manipulation. Context Modeling. Temporal context has been widely used to support long-horizon decision making in language modeling dai-etal-2019-transformer , navigation Fang_2019_CVPR , video generation Henschel_2025_CVPR , and robot manipulation pmlr-v205-guhur23a . Existing robot policies incorporate history through temporal abstraction Belkhale-RSS-24 , visual memory pmlr-v267-fang25c , retrieval ShahR-RSS-26 , or explicit state representations chung2026memorystate . However, task instructions and longer histories is insufficient to guarantee that task requirements remain effective throughout execution; policies may still rely on easier visual-action correlations lin2026jepawamlearningvisionlanguageactionpolicies,zhao2026sgwamselfguidedworldmodeling . Moreover, longer execution contexts often contain redundant information, which can dilute critical execution cues while increasing design complexity and computational cost ICLR2026_9da515b1 . Rather than extending raw history, TaskWAM extracts progress-relevant evidence from causal action-observation transitions for explicit execution tracking. -Horizon Multi-Stage Manipulation. Long-horizon household tasks are common in daily life and remain a key challenge for reliable robot deployment pmlr-v205-li23a . A common characteristic of these tasks is that similar observation-action interactions often recur within the same scene across different tasks and execution stages ICLR2026_a05003fd . Reliable execution therefore requires robots to distinguish such overlapping trajectories and complete the required stages in demanding order~ mees2022calvin,pmlr-v205-li23a . However, prior work has largely learned and evaluated tasks in relatively isolated settings OpenX24 , leaving this capability underexplored. In this work, we target this setting with a stage-aware approach and introduce a controlled multi-stage benchmark for systematic evaluation. TaskWAM Framework sec:method Problem Formulation sec:problem_setup Confusion. For task , we denote a rollout by , where is segmented into a stage sequence . At the transition from stage , let denote the observed execution history and the subsequent stage. Two stage-transition points and may have similar local histories, , but require different subsequent stages, . WAMs may generate a locally plausible future yet advances execution to the wrong stage, which we refer to as Stage Confusion. It typically occurs in two cases: Cross-task confusion, where the model continued toward a wrong stage from another task, , , ; Within-task confusion, where the model mistakes similar stages within the same task for one another, leading to stage repetition or skipping, , , . -State Grounding for Future Generation. Stage progression depends on two complementary task factors: task requirements specify how execution should proceed, while closed-loop interaction history provides evidence of the progress achieved so far. We represent them as an explicit task state , where encodes fine-grained task requirements grounded in instruction , and tracks execution progress from history . We condition future world evolution and robot actions on this structured state: Our goal is to explicitly model stage progression in world-action generation rather than leaving it to be implicitly inferred from an unstructured conditioning context. Overview TaskWAM grounds world--action generation in task requirements and execution progress to reduce stage confusion. As illustrated in Figure~ fig:taskwam_overview , it consists of two core components: (1) Structured Task-State Grounding constructs Mode Tokens through codebook retrieval and text grounding, and State Tokens through interaction aggregation and causal temporal encoding; and (2) Task-State Conditioned Future Steering incorporates the resulting task state into backbone conditioning and velocity predictions, steering generation toward the intended future. title: World2HOSI: A Multi-Expert Harness for Long-Horizon Human-Object-Scene Interaction Generation
summary: Long-horizon human-object-scene interaction (HOSI) is central to embodied AI, animation, and game development. Existing human-object interaction (HOI) and human-scene interaction (HSI) models excel in their respective domains, but none alone covers tasks requiring multiple interaction skills. Training unified HOSI models is hindered by scarce and costly data. We introduce World2HOSI, a multi-expert orchestration harness that generates continuous HOSI data from 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes and natural language instructions. Our key insight is that long-horizon HOSI hinges not on a stronger single model but on orchestration. Given a shared, structured scene state and an orchestration harness grounded in it, existing experts can jointly accomplish tasks beyond the reach of any of them alone. World2HOSI realizes this insight as a closed loop around a persistent scene state built from decoupled background and object assets. A harness plans action stages over this state, invokes experts via their native conditioning interfaces, and writes each action's effects back, so that every invocation is grounded in the evolving world. To reduce physical artifacts, bounded residual optimization and contact-driven physics simulation further ensure the physical plausibility of human motion and object manipulation, respectively, while preserving interaction intent. Experiments and a perceptual user study show that World2HOSI achieves the best task completion and interaction quality on the evaluated HOSI tasks, while generating more diverse data.
full_text: Long-horizon human–object–scene interaction (HOSI) is central to embodied AI, animation, and game development. Existing human-object interaction (HOI) and human–scene interaction (HSI) models excel in their respective domains, but none alone covers tasks requiring multiple interaction skills. Training unified HOSI models is hindered by scarce and costly data. We introduce World2HOSI, a multi-expert orchestration harness that generates continuous HOSI data from 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes and natural language instructions. Our key insight is that long-horizon HOSI hinges not on a stronger single model but on orchestration. Given a shared, structured scene state and an orchestration harness grounded in it, existing experts can jointly accomplish tasks beyond the reach of any of them alone. World2HOSI realizes this insight as a closed loop around a persistent scene state built from decoupled background and object assets. A harness plans action stages over this state, invokes experts via their native conditioning interfaces, and writes each action's effects back, so that every invocation is grounded in the evolving world. To reduce physical artifacts, bounded residual optimization and contact-driven physics simulation further ensure the physical plausibility of human motion and object manipulation, respectively, while preserving interaction intent. Experiments and a perceptual user study show that World2HOSI achieves the best task completion and interaction quality on the evaluated HOSI tasks, while generating more diverse data. Project Page: nintreesssss.github.io/World2HOSI . Introduction sec:introduction =-1 Human-centric 3D scene understanding connects renderable environments with embodied AI training. Beyond high-fidelity reconstruction, it captures natural interactions with static scenes and their objects, termed human-object-scene interaction (HOSI). Such motion data support training and evaluation in computer graphics, embodied AI, and agent learning, but remain scarce. GRAB~ GRAB:2020 , BEHAVE~ bhatnagar22behave , and TRUMANS~ jiang2024scaling capture human motion together with objects or scenes to support interaction learning. Yet costly motion capture struggles to cover increasingly diverse indoor layouts, object combinations, and multi-stage tasks. This motivates using existing scene and motion resources to produce richer HOSI data. =-1 Generative models offer an alternative route to data synthesis. BEDLAM~ Black_CVPR_2023 shows that networks trained entirely on synthetic data can achieve state-of-the-art human pose and shape estimation. InHabit~ kister2026inhabit leverages interaction priors in image foundation models to synthesize 3D human poses in scenes, benefiting downstream tasks such as contact estimation. For 4D interactions, existing models offer complementary capabilities: human-scene interaction (HSI) models condition motion on static furniture geometry, while human-object interaction (HOI) models coordinate humans and dynamic objects~ Kimodo2026,zhao2023synthesizing,hoifhli . However, individual models lack the full chain of capabilities required for long-horizon HOSI. For example, ``move the chair and then sit down'' combines dynamic manipulation with static interaction, and requires subsequent motion to reflect the chair's new location. Either capability alone is insufficient. A unified HOSI generator can broaden this capability coverage, but doing so requires training data spanning diverse combinations of actions, objects, and scenes, which remain scarce. InfBaGel's hybrid-data training indirectly reflects the scarcity of these data~ zou2026infbagel . If an additional unified generator needs to be trained for data production, this reintroduces dependence on the very data that are extremely scarce. Orchestrating complementary experts through conditioning interfaces is therefore essential to expanding task coverage without additional motion-generator training. =-1 Therefore, our goal is to generate text-guided, long-horizon 4D interactions in realistic reconstructed scenes by coordinating motion experts. We build on 3D Gaussian Splatting(3DGS), whose rich appearance provides renderable worlds for data synthesis~ kerbl3Dgaussians . But the central question is not only how to render realistic scenes and simply concatenate expert outputs, but how the scene representation gives each expert the right conditions as earlier actions change the world. A scheduler is required to connect task intent to a shared scene state that persists across expert invocations. =-1 Realizing this goal presents three related challenges. First, native 3DGS is primarily a visual representation, typically static and monolithic, which fails to provide separated object identities required for planning and manipulation, thereby hindering a closed loop scene state update~ hu2026worldact,gaussian_grouping . Second, converting natural language into executable actions requires spatial understanding and long-horizon planning. Instructions often leave objects and execution order unspecified, requiring decomposition based on spatial relationships and action preconditions. Third, expert models differ in their capabilities and motion boundaries. A shared textual goal alone is insufficient for them to disambiguate their respective roles and produce a continuous sequence. =-1 We introduce World2HOSI, a stage-based orchestration harness for long-horizon HOSI data synthesis. Its organizing principle is a closed loop between a structured scene state and experts that read and update it. An Interactive Scene Package (ISP) maintains object assets and evolving spatial relationships. We use a large language model (LLM) to decompose instructions into a structured script of ordered actions, compiled into numerical conditions at each stage, thereby enabling task-specific expert models to generate corresponding motion segments. Finally, when physical execution is needed, a physics optimizer applies residual corrections for physical plausibility. Object transformations are written back to the ISP to condition subsequent tasks. Experiments show the highest task completion and interaction quality on the evaluated tasks and greater data diversity. A user study confirms that participants prefer our interactions over existing methods. In summary, our contributions are threefold: =-1 We present the first multi-expert orchestration harness for long-horizon HOSI data synthesis. This framework resolves stages against this state and compiles expert-specific conditions, enabling complementary capabilities to be used without training an additional unified motion generator. =-1 We introduce a structured scene-state substrate for 4D HOSI generation, linking renderable scenes, object interaction geometry, and persistent object identities so that heterogeneous experts share a consistent account of the world. =-1 We establish a closed-loop generation mechanism that carries state across motion boundaries and writes action outcomes back to the world, allowing subsequent targets to follow the environmental changes induced by earlier actions. Related Work sec:related-work =-1 From Renderable Scenes to Interactive Worlds. 3D Gaussian Splatting supports high-quality reconstruction with an explicit Gaussian representation~ kerbl3Dgaussians , providing visually realistic 3D environments. Making these visual assets interactive additionally requires object-level editability. WorldAct uses object segmentation and geometry construction to make objects in monolithic 3D worlds independently editable and manipulable~ hu2026worldact . InteriorGS provides indoor Gaussian scenes with semantic annotations and structural information~ InteriorGS2025 , while SAGE-3D builds on these assets to provide mesh representations~ miao2026towards . Together, these efforts supply assets for scene understanding and interaction research. EgoSim~ hao2026egosim maintains an evolving 3D world state for egocentric interaction video generation. InHabit demonstrates the potential of reusing foundation-model priors for automated scene-related human data synthesis, although its outputs are primarily static poses~ kister2026inhabit . This motivates using generative priors to construct scene-related human data. =-1 Human Object and Scene Interaction Generation. HSI and HOI methods develop different motion priors. HSI methods use static environments as geometric constraints, progressively combining obstacle-avoiding navigation with furniture interactions such as sitting and lying down. DIMOS~ zhao2023synthesizing is a representative example. Complementing this line, MDM~ tevet2023human uses diffusion for text-conditioned human motion generation. OmniControl~ xie2024omnicontrol and Kimodo~ Kimodo2026 further support control signals including text, full-body keyframes, and 2D paths, providing priors for diverse motion along specified routes. =-1 HOI methods focus on coordination between humans and movable objects. OMOMO~ li2023object synthesizes full-body manipulation from object trajectories, using intermediate hand positions to strengthen hand-object contact constraints. CHOIS~ li2023controllable jointly generates human and object motion from text, initial states, and sparse object waypoints, using sampling guidance to improve contact consistency. HOI-FHLI~ hoifhli further integrates navigation and manipulation generation into a single system, providing more comprehensive priors for long-horizon manipulation. PrimHOI~ jia2025primhoi composes reusable contact primitives for complex HOI. =-1 These conditioning interfaces allow World2HOSI to treat existing models as an orchestrated capability set. A high-level planner decomposes tasks, invokes models, and coordinates outputs. Compatible experts can introduce new capabilities without requiring one base model to master every locomotion and interaction type. =-1 Joint Human-Object-Scene Interaction Generation. Several methods pursue joint HOSI generation. HOSIG~ yao2026hosig incorporates scene constraints into navigation and fine-grained manipulation, InteractMove~ cai-etal-2025-interactmove addresses interactions in scenes with movable objects. InfBaGel~ zou2026infbagel updates dynamic scene perception during generation and mitigates data scarcity through hybrid training on HOI and HSI data. These methods highlight environmental changes and data coverage as central issues. Physical imitation and reference-trajectory refinement~ wang2023physhoi,xu2025intermimic,zhao2026real2sim further provide contact-driven execution for kinematic sequences, allowing them to satisfy dynamics constraints. However, these methods all face data scarcity, which also limits the generalization of their learned priors. Method sec:method =-1 World2HOSI is a multi-model orchestration framework that generates human-object-scene interactions from 3D Gaussian scenes and text instructions, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:pipeline . World2HOSI closes the loop around a persistent scene state. (a) The ISP organizes background and object assets. (b) Task Planner grounds each action stage in the current state. (c) Experts generate motion, whose outcomes update the ISP before the next invocation. (d) Optional physics-based refinement supports contact-driven execution. State write-back keeps subsequent targets consistent with earlier actions. fig:pipeline Interactive World Representation sec:world =-1 Representation. Native 3DGS provides a renderable collection of Gaussians~ kerbl3Dgaussians , but not the object-level structure needed for task planning, interaction, and state memory. So we introduce the Interactive Scene Package (ISP), a unified structure with persistent object identities. Each object has visual assets, local collision geometry, semantic labels, a world transformation, and physical properties. title: SuperMimic: Scaling Humanoid Whole-Body Control with One Differentiable World Model
comment: Accepted at CoRL 2026 (Oral). Project website: https://supermimic.github.io
summary: Tracking large human-motion datasets has become the dominant route to general, expressive humanoid whole-body control, but scaling across many motions is expensive. Current pipelines use model-free reinforcement learning, either merging per-motion specialists through lossy distillation, or brute-forcing a single policy with cluster-scale compute. SuperMimic amortizes learning across all motions with one differentiable world model of their shared dynamics, fit from logged transitions of a standard rigid-body simulator. The world model and the tracking policy train together in one loop, and backpropagation-through-time over short imagined rollouts gives the policy analytic gradients. Fast imagined rollouts and analytic gradients make policy learning efficient. In 3 hours on a single GPU, SuperMimic surpasses the return of a state-of-the-art motion tracker baseline trained for 7 days on 128 GPUs. It reduces GPU-hours by more than $1000\times$ and fails on only 25 of 129,514 benchmark motions, versus 179 failures for the baseline. After 9.8 hours on two GPUs, SuperMimic achieves zero failures. From 1 to 264 hours of motion, the world model's prediction error stays stable, and GPU-hours to a target return grow slowly. Our policy transfers to a physical Unitree G1 across diverse and acrobatic motions. SuperMimic removes compute as the bottleneck to scaling humanoid whole-body control, making it practical to measure motion-tracking scaling laws.
full_text: Experimental Results We show that SuperMimic scales favorably relative to PPO pipelines, identify the world-model properties behind this scaling, demonstrate transfer on a real Unitree~G1, and report a preliminary study of downstream goal interfaces. The simulator is MuJoCo Warp, a GPU implementation of MuJoCo~ todorov2012mujoco . All our reported costs are measured on NVIDIA~H100 ( SXM5) GPUs of Lambda on-demand instances. We ran several random seeds and found training very stable, which we attribute to the dense reward that motion tracking gives at every step. The figures therefore do not report seed variation. Normalized return, return for short, is the undiscounted sum of the per-step reward over the full episode, divided by the largest value this sum can take. A policy that terminates early therefore scores low. Real-robot transfer sec:real-robot One general motion tracker deploys on a real Unitree~G1 without per-motion tuning (Figure~ fig:acrobatics ). The four motions cover locomotion (a skipping jump), contact-rich whole-body motion with the torso and limbs on the floor (a side roll), and acrobatics (a flip and an in-place flip). Downstream tasks: RL encoder vs.\ distillation baseline sec:downstream SuperMimic trains downstream goal encoders jointly with the motion-tracking interface, sharing one decoder and world model (Appendix~ app:unified ). Our study of downstream interfaces is preliminary. We train one velocity encoder on a velocity-tracking reward through the world model. We compare it with a distillation baseline: a velocity encoder trained on the motion-tracking reward, with commands read from the reference motions. Figure~ fig:downstream evaluates both on 672 step responses spanning the velocity space (Appendix~ app:velocity ). The RL encoder has the lower steady-state error on 650 of them, and the distillation encoder on 15. Only the distillation encoder falls, on seven fast turns with almost no motion-library data.

title: AgenticRoboRL: Bringing Coding-Agent Post-Training to Agentic Robotics
summary: Agentic robotics systems combine planners with robot harnesses to perform complex manipulation tasks. Recent work improves these systems through better harnesses and external memory, but relies on powerful closed-source models as planners and does not improve the planners' own capabilities. In contrast, coding agents have improved substantially by post-training the model itself. We therefore investigate whether post-training can also improve robot planners. However, applying it across robot harnesses requires accommodating different execution mechanisms, including VLA skill invocation and control-code generation. To this end, we introduce AgenticRoboRL, a framework for post-training robot planners across different harnesses. The training recipe combines supervised fine-tuning with multi-turn reinforcement learning. To accommodate different execution mechanisms, harness-specific adapters connect recorded planner interactions with task outcomes, enabling a common RL training pipeline while keeping execution components fixed. On LIBERO-PRO, AgenticRoboRL raises the success rate of a 9B-parameter planner from 18.1% to 71.0% without external memory, approaching the 72.1% achieved by Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory. These results demonstrate post-training as an effective approach for improving robot planners. We will release the framework and trained planner checkpoints.
full_text: Agentic robotics systems combine planners with robot harnesses to perform complex manipulation tasks. Recent work improves these systems through better harnesses and external memory, but relies on powerful closed-source models as planners and does not improve the planners' own capabilities. In contrast, coding agents have improved substantially by post-training the model itself. We therefore investigate whether post-training can also improve robot planners. However, applying it across robot harnesses requires accommodating different execution mechanisms, including VLA skill invocation and control-code generation. To this end, we introduce , a framework for post-training robot planners across different harnesses. The training recipe combines supervised fine-tuning with multi-turn reinforcement learning. To accommodate different execution mechanisms, harness-specific adapters connect recorded planner interactions with task outcomes, enabling a common RL training pipeline while keeping execution components fixed. On LIBERO-PRO, raises the success rate of a 9B-parameter planner from 18.1 to 71.0 without external memory, approaching the 72.1 achieved by Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory. These results demonstrate post-training as an effective approach for improving robot planners. We will release the framework and trained planner checkpoints. Introduction sec:intro =-1 Agentic robotics systems can perform complex manipulation tasks by combining a planner with a robot harness. The planner invokes VLA skills~ harnessvla or generates control code~ codeaspolicies,capx , observes the execution results, and decides what to do next over multiple rounds of interaction. Recent work has improved performance by refining robot harnesses and storing experience from task exploration in external memory~ harnessvla,baton , with coding agents such as Codex and Claude Code~ codex,claudecode serving as planners. However, these approaches primarily leverage existing planner capabilities and strengthen the support available to the planner. We explore a complementary direction: enhancing planners’ own capabilities to improve the performance of agentic robotics systems. For coding agents, enhancing the model's own capabilities through post-training, including supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, has proven highly effective~ swegym,swesmith,skyrlagent . These advances raise a natural question: Can the post-training methods used for coding agents also improve the performance of Applying these methods to robot planners is complicated by the fact that robot harnesses differ in how they carry out a planner's response. In some harnesses the planner calls learned VLA skills, and a VLA policy executes each call. In others the planner writes control code over perception and control APIs, and a motion controller executes it. Harnesses also differ in what feedback they return to the planner and in how they decide whether the task has succeeded. Training planners across harnesses therefore requires a single pipeline that supports these different execution mechanisms. To realize such a pipeline, we introduce , a framework for post-training robot planners across different harnesses (Figure~ fig:teaser ). The training recipe combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with multi-turn reinforcement learning (RL). SFT trains the planner on successful demonstrations, providing a starting point for RL. During RL, we train on recorded planner requests and responses, while harness-specific adapters associate these interactions with episode outcomes. This allows the same RL pipeline to support VLA skill invocation and control-code generation without changing their execution interfaces. In both stages, only the planner is optimized, while the underlying execution components remain fixed (Figure~ fig:framework ). We evaluate the pipeline across these two execution mechanisms using a 9B planner. With RPent~ harnessvla , a harness that invokes VLA skills, SFT improves success on LIBERO-PRO from 18.1 to 65.1 , and RL further raises it to 71.0 , without external memory. The same checkpoint achieves 72.2 on LIBERO-Plus~ liberoplus without additional training, compared with 19.2 for the original model. With the CaP-X harness~ capx , post-training improves success from 2.7 to 28.5 . These results establish post-training as an effective approach for improving agentic robotics systems. Our contributions are threefold: 0pt 0pt To our knowledge, is the first general post-training framework to agentic robotics systems. first fine-tunes the planner on successful demonstrations and then refines it with RL, updating only the planner while keeping execution components fixed. Lightweight harness-specific adapters link each recorded planner call to its episode outcome, so the harnesses do not need a shared low-level action representation. Strong empirical results and an open release. With , a 9B planner improves from 18.1 to 71.0 on LIBERO-PRO without external memory. This nearly matches Codex (GPT-5.5) with external memory (72.1 )~ harnessvla . With the CaP-X harness, it improves from 2.7 to 28.5 . We will release the framework and trained planner checkpoints. Related Work sec:related Robot harness agents. Language models can guide robot behavior by selecting learned skills or generating programs over perception and control APIs~ saycan,codeaspolicies,progprompt,voxposer,robocodex . In this organization, the planner chooses how to use the available capabilities, while the harness executes its decisions and returns observations. Execution feedback and reusable skill libraries support interaction over multiple turns~ innermonologue,voyager . Hierarchical systems place a language-level reasoning model above a learned low-level policy~ rth,hirobot . Recent harnesses expose these capabilities to coding agents: Harness VLA combines a frozen VLA with analytic primitives and task memory~ harnessvla , while CaP-X provides interfaces for generating executable control code~ capx . General-purpose coding agents have also been applied to manipulation without robot-specific training~ aor,agentaspolicy . Other systems improve perception, memory, safety, or skill libraries around the planner~ roboharnessk1,baton,dynaharness,mtp,skillcomposer . A concurrent training-free approach, RV-ICL, provides on-demand access to a hierarchy of demonstration-video keyframes and clips~ rvicl . instead improves the planner through SFT and multi-turn RL while reusing the harness's Training planners for embodied agents. RL has been used to improve language and vision-language planners in embodied environments~ embodiedplannerr1,era,robogptr1,reinforcedreasoning,dreamplan . CaP-RL applies RL to a code model that generates a complete control program in a single turn~ capx . In contrast, trains planners that interact with the harness over multiple turns, and it applies to harnesses based on VLA skills as well as to harnesses based on control code. Closer to our supervised stage, Robo-Harness K1 and World Action Agent train 9B students on teacher trajectories collected within their respective harnesses~ roboharnessk1,worldactionagent . These methods use supervised training to transfer the capabilities of stronger agents. REAL combines SFT with online RL for mobile manipulation, using a rule-based planner for supervision and a shaped reward~ real . instead uses teacher-agent trajectories followed by multi-turn RL with task success as the sole reward. It adapts teacher supervision when the teacher and student have different prompts, tools, or access to memory. =-1 Post-training of tool-using agents. Coding-agent training commonly combines supervision from successful teacher trajectories~ swegym,swesmith,r2egym with multi-turn RL on verifiable outcomes~ skyrlagent . Related approaches extend to search and computer-use agents~ searchr1,opensearchvl,uitars2,computerrl . Frameworks including Agent Lightning and LEGO-RL separate agent execution from model optimization and construct training data from recorded interactions~ agentlightning,agentlightningv1,legorl . builds on this approach for robot harnesses: a proxy records planner calls, and harness-specific adapters associate them with episode outcomes. This interface accommodates different execution mechanisms without requiring a common low-level action representation. AgenticRoboRL Framework sec:method Overview and Problem Setup post-trains the planner of a robot agent while reusing its harness's execution components. The planner produces harness-native responses, including structured tool calls in RPent, the harness released with Harness VLA~ harnessvla , or executable Python code in CaP-X~ capx . The harness executes these commands and returns observations and execution feedback for subsequent decisions. We update the planner, not the perception modules, motion planners, or VLA executors it invokes. Figure~ fig:framework summarizes the training pipeline: teacher supervision initializes the planner, and multi-turn interaction supplies task outcomes for reinforcement learning (RL). Let specify a task and its initial-state configuration. At turn , the harness constructs the actual model context from the task, observations, and preceding responses: Here includes prompt construction, tool specifications, and history processing. A response is a complete model-generated token sequence, potentially containing reasoning, text, tool calls, or control code; it is not a single low-level robot action. A trajectory contains the successive model requests and responses together with their execution outcomes. Our objective is denotes the training task/initial-state distribution. This objective describes the terminal-success reward used in our main RL configuration, without intermediate rewards or a length penalty. Training Infrastructure Recording the actual model interaction. Because VLA skill invocations and generated control programs differ in representation and execution granularity, we place the shared RL interface at the model-call boundary rather than the low-level action boundary. During RL, the training unit is a recorded planner request, not a simulator step or a reconstructed full transcript. A recording proxy captures each request's context, generated token IDs, and rollout log-probabilities at the model-serving boundary, following recent agent training frameworks~ agentlightning,legorl,polar . Images and tool specifications are retained where applicable. This matters because a harness may prune images, omit previous reasoning, or otherwise transform its history between requests. The trainer checks its rendered prompt against the recorded prompt tokens; mismatched samples receive zero optimization weight. Training therefore uses the inputs associated with each sampled response rather than assuming that a final transcript reproduces them. Connecting interactions to outcomes. A harness-specific adapter reports, for every episode, five fields: the task, the initial-state identifier, the attempt index, the reward, and a validity flag. The first two define the group used for within-group comparison; the validity flag separates task failures, which remain reward-zero episodes, from infrastructure failures, which are excluded from optimization. Recorded model calls are then matched to their episode, and the pipeline checks record completeness and policy version before any sample is built. The adapter is plain conversion code with no learnable parameters: it provides a common training representation without imposing a common robot execution interface, and it does not alter the harness's tools, prompts, or control loop. Appendix~ app:adapters lists the fields for our two harnesses. Policy-versioned rounds. Each round collects episodes under fixed planner weights, constructs training samples from the recorded interactions, and updates the planner before the next collection round. title: Physical Canvas: A Vision Tactile World Model For Robot Policy Evaluation And Learning
summary: Evaluating and post-training robot policies through physical interaction is costly and difficult to scale, motivating action-conditioned world models as interactive simulators. However, visually plausible predictions can misrepresent contact dynamics, providing unreliable feedback for policy evaluation and learning. We introduce PhysCanvas, a state-consistent visuo-tactile world model for contact-rich robot manipulation. PhysCanvas unifies multi-view RGB, tactile images, marker displacement, task state, and actions within a unified vision space. All modalities share a video VAE and pretrained generative backbone, allowing optical touch to reuse visual and temporal priors. Motion images derived through forward kinematics and camera projection provide spatially aligned action conditioning, while an initial RGB anchor and updated reference observations guide sequential generation. Our consistency-aware post-training uses the frozen Scene Reward Model, Modality Reward Model, and State Reward Model to supervise scene preservation, visual-tactile compatibility, and agreement with real task outcomes. The resulting world model supports closed-loop policy rollouts for evaluation and provides imagined interactions and rewards for GRPO policy updates. Across four real-world manipulation tasks, when policies are rolled out in the world model, State Reward Model supervision increases the arithmetic mean of task-wise Pearson correlations between world-model and real-world success rates from 0.602 to 0.885. Policy post-training in the reward-guided world model further increases $π_{0.5}$'s mean real-world success rate from a 59.1% SFT baseline to 70.8%. These results demonstrate the value of unified multimodal modeling and consistency-aware post-training for robot policy evaluation and learning. Project page: https://zebinx.github.io/PhysCanvas_HomePage/.

Introduction sec:introduction Robot world models predict how environments evolve in response to actions, offering low-cost, reproducible interactions for policy evaluation and learning~ ha2018worldmodels,wu2023daydreamer,wang2026interactive . Contact-rich manipulation requires both visual observations of scene dynamics and tactile feedback about contact changes~ yuan2017gelsight,lambeta2020digit,lee2020making,guzey2024seetotouch . A world model that captures these complementary signals and their associated task outcomes could reduce the need for repeated physical trials. Recent action-conditioned video models combine pretrained generative priors with action representations to support interactive prediction, policy evaluation, and learning in imagination~ wu2026imac,wang2026interactive,yang2026rise . Existing visuo-tactile models, however, typically require a dedicated tactile encoder and a custom interface for injecting tactile features into a general backbone~ zheng2026omnivta,ma2026feelworld . Adapting to new tactile data or sensor configurations may therefore require retraining, limiting generality and complicating the pipeline. Meanwhile, token-wise reconstruction supervision emphasizes local fidelity and can miss high-level semantics such as task success. Reliable rollouts thus require visual observations, tactile feedback, and predicted task outcomes to describe the consequences of the same action; inconsistencies can mislead policy optimization~ yang2026mirabench,jiang2026wovr . For example, after an object slips, predicting stable tactile contact or eventual success is semantically inconsistent despite visually plausible frames. The challenge is to build a reusable multimodal model while preserving scene, cross-modal, and task-outcome consistency for policy evaluation and learning. We investigate two questions: (1) Can a simple, general mechanism encode heterogeneous modalities in a shared space? (2) Can high-level semantics be injected into the world model without additional networks? =10000 =10000 =10000 =1em To address this challenge, we introduce , a world model with state consistency for visual and tactile prediction, robot policy evaluation, and learning. places multiple modalities in a shared generative space and uses consistency supervision during post training to preserve the interaction dynamics and task outcomes induced by actions, providing interactive, coherent observations. Specifically, places multiview RGB, tactile images, marker displacement, and task state on a unified canvas predicted by a shared video VAE and generative backbone, allowing optical touch to reuse pretrained visual and temporal priors~ wan2025 . Actions are encoded as spatially aligned motion images through forward kinematics and camera projection~ wu2026imac , while an initial RGB anchor and updated references guide sequential generation. During post training, the frozen Scene Reward Model, Modality Reward Model, and State Reward Model enforce scene preservation, visual and tactile compatibility, and agreement with real outcomes, including both success and failure. The resulting model supports evaluation in a closed loop and supplies imagined interactions and rewards for GRPO policy updates~ shao2024deepseekmath,rlinf . We evaluate on four real-world manipulation tasks: test-tube placement, bottle-cap unscrewing, block relocation, and Rubik's Cube manipulation (Figure~ fig:task_tactile_overview ). When policies are rolled out in the world model, post-training improves the Pearson correlation between their world-model and real-world success rates on every task, increasing the arithmetic mean of task-wise correlations from to . Each task includes nine evaluation batches spanning ACT, FM, and ~ zhao2023act,lipman2023flowmatching,black2025pi05 ; the batches are evaluated at different times, and each task receives equal weight in the summary. Policy optimization through reward-guided imagined interactions further improves the mean real-world success rate of by percentage points over SFT, from to across the four tasks. These results demonstrate utility for reliable evaluation and policy improvement. Our contributions are threefold: (1) a unified canvas space that jointly models vision, touch, task state, and actions using a shared video generation framework; (2) consistency-aware post-training that constrains generated interactions through scene, modality, and task-state supervision; and (3) a framework for policy evaluation and learning in imagination, evaluated on real robots. Pretrained video priors~ ho2022videodiffusion,blattmann2023alignlatents,wan2025 and embodied action conditioning~ jiang2025evac,wu2026imac improve controllability, while unified architectures connect video prediction with policy modeling~ bi2026motus,kim2026cosmospolicy . Extending these visual simulators to contact-rich manipulation also requires predicting the tactile observations on which policies act. Imagined rollouts also support policy evaluation and learning~ ha2018worldmodels,hafner2020dreamer,hansen2024tdmpc2,hafner2025dreamerv3,wang2026interactive,jiang2026wovr , making reliable action consequences and task outcomes essential. Recent work studies long horizon consistency and simulator validity~ gigaworld2026,yang2026mirabench , or improves generation through reward based optimization~ bardhan2026persistent,wang2025alignavideo . brings these requirements to joint visual and tactile prediction through scene and task state consistency supervision, and evaluates generated rollouts against real policy outcomes. The shared visual VAE and video denoiser then model aligned sensory futures, with explicit supervision of visual and tactile agreement. title: S$^3$E-Det: A Strict Spatial-Spectral Equivariant Detector for Multispectral Object Detection
summary: Multispectral object detection requires detectors to exploit material-dependent spectral responses while maintaining consistent localization under geometric variations. Existing MOD detectors learn discriminative spectral representations, yet lack a unified mechanism that preserves spectral order, adapts spectral-context fusion across pyramid levels, and regulates geometric responses under rotation. To address these limitations, we propose S$^3$E-Det, a strict spatial-spectral equivariant detector that couples ordered spectral modeling with transformation-consistent prediction. Spectral Order-aware Sampling Calibration (SOSC) imposes local order constraints on input-derived spectral features through first-order variation, while Common-Differential Equivariant Fusion (CDEF) adapts spectral-context aggregation across pyramid levels. A compact Geometric Alignment Head (GAH) reconciles invariant and equivariant output properties within a unified prediction stage. Across MODA, HOD3K, and DroneVehicle, S$^3$E-Det combines high detection accuracy with a compact parameter footprint and reduced rotation-induced variation. Code is available at https://github.com/Riiluo/S3E-Det.

title: SGLDet: Spectral-aware Global-Local Dynamic Modeling for Multispectral Aerial Object Detection
summary: Multispectral aerial object detection aims to exploit spectral-spatial cues to address object detection challenges in complex aerial scenes. Existing methods mainly focus on spectral-spatial decoupling and object-aware spectral-spatial fusion to improve spectral utilization. However, two critical issues remain underexplored: 1) severe foreground-background imbalance caused by large scene coverage hinders reliable object recognition; 2) aerial objects exhibit substantial local variations in scale, orientation, and structure, which hinder accurate localization. To address these issues, we propose SGLDet, a spectral-aware global-local dynamic modeling framework for multispectral aerial object detection, which is motivated by the observation that object semantics are jointly determined by global spectral consistency and scene context, while precise localization requires dynamic feature modulation conditioned on the input spectral and spatial properties. To realize these properties, SGLDet consists of three coordinated components: a Spectral-driven Global Dynamic Modeling module that aggregates spectrally related features across the scene via similarity-guided sparse matching; a Multi-scale Global Context Integration module that constructs a compact scene memory for scene-guided contextual reasoning; and a Spectral-aware Input-dependent Calibration Aggregation module that performs expert-kernel aggregation with scene-guided spectral-spatial calibration to enable adaptive local feature modulation. Extensive experiments on MODA, HOD3K, and DroneVehicle demonstrate that SGLDet achieves superior performance with competitive computational cost. Code is available at https://github.com/Riiluo/SGLDet.

Multispectral aerial object detection aims to exploit spectral--spatial cues to address object detection challenges in complex aerial scenes. Existing methods mainly focus on spectral--spatial decoupling and object-aware spectral--spatial fusion to improve spectral utilization. However, two critical issues remain underexplored: 1) severe foreground--background imbalance caused by large scene coverage hinders reliable object recognition; 2) aerial objects exhibit substantial local variations in scale, orientation, and structure, which hinder accurate localization. To address these issues, we propose SGLDet, a spectral-aware global--local dynamic modeling framework for multispectral aerial object detection, which is motivated by the observation that object semantics are jointly determined by global spectral consistency and scene context, while precise localization requires dynamic feature modulation conditioned on the input spectral and spatial properties. To realize these properties, SGLDet consists of three coordinated components: a Spectral-driven Global Dynamic Modeling module that aggregates spectrally related features across the scene via similarity-guided sparse matching; a Multi-scale Global Context Integration module that constructs a compact scene memory for scene-guided contextual reasoning; and a Spectral-aware Input-dependent Calibration Aggregation module that performs expert-kernel aggregation with scene-guided spectral--spatial calibration to enable adaptive local feature modulation. Extensive experiments on MODA, HOD3K, and DroneVehicle demonstrate that SGLDet achieves superior performance with competitive computational cost. Code is available at . Multispectral aerial object detection, spectral-aware modeling, global-local dynamic modeling. Introduction sec:intro erial object detection is a fundamental task in remote sensing, with applications in urban management, traffic surveillance, maritime monitoring, and disaster response. Most existing methods rely on RGB inputs, whose limited spectral representation often struggles under illumination changes, occlusions, and background interference, especially when objects resemble surrounding regions. Multispectral images (MSIs) provide richer spectral responses across multiple wavelengths and thus offer complementary cues beyond spatial appearance, making them a promising information source for aerial object detection. Existing methods for multispectral aerial object detection (MAOD) mainly either decouple spectral and spatial information for separate modeling or strengthen adaptive spectral-spatial fusion for target perception he2023object, han2025moda, xu2026dahnet . However, because these methods mainly focus on local spectral-spatial interaction and emphasize feature enhancement within limited receptive fields, they remain inherently insufficient for resolving global semantic ambiguity in complex real-world aerial scenes. Concretely, aerial images usually cover large spatial extents, and aerial objects often appear at small scales and are embedded in complex scenes. In MODA~ han2025moda , for example, objects occupy only 0.15 of the image area on average, resulting in severe foreground--background imbalance, so local spectral--spatial cues alone are often insufficient for reliable recognition. Fortunately, MSI data provide a clue that is difficult to obtain from RGB imagery: objects composed of similar materials often exhibit consistent spectral signatures even across distant spatial locations, while scene context can further suppress visually confusing background regions. As shown in~ (a), linking distant regions with similar spectral responses can reinforce objects with ambiguous local appearances while suppressing visually similar but spectrally distinct background responses. Scene context further resolves the remaining semantic ambiguity. These observations indicate that robust MAOD should integrate scene-wide spectral relations with scene-level context to better resolve semantic ambiguity in aerial scenes. Motivated by this observation, we introduce two complementary designs for global reasoning in multispectral aerial object detection. The first is a Spectral-driven Global Dynamic Modeling (SGDM) module, which retrieves spectrally similar responses through similarity-guided sparse matching to encourage semantically coherent representations for spectrally similar objects. The second is a Multi-scale Global Context Integration (MGCI) module, which consolidates cross-scale evidence into a compact scene memory and enhances scene-guided contextual reasoning through contextual retrieval. However, resolving global semantic ambiguity is still insufficient for MAOD. Aerial objects often vary substantially in scale, orientation, and structure, whereas standard convolutions apply fixed kernels and receptive fields to all inputs. This mismatch makes it difficult to produce object-aligned responses in cluttered backgrounds, as shown in~ (b). Local dynamic modulation therefore complements global reasoning by improving object localization. To address this issue, we further introduce a Spectral-aware Input-dependent Calibration Aggregation (SICA) module, which performs scene-dependent dynamic feature modulation through input-adaptive expert aggregation with spectral--spatial calibration for precise localization. Together, SGDM, MGCI, and SICA constitute SGLDet, a spectral-aware global-local dynamic modeling framework for multispectral aerial object detection. Overall, SGLDet unifies global spectral dependency modeling, scene-guided contextual reasoning, and scene-dependent local feature modulation within a single framework. To evaluate the proposed method, we conduct extensive experiments on three benchmark datasets: MODA~ han2025moda , HOD3K~ he2023object , and DroneVehicle~ dronevehicle . The results demonstrate that SGLDet achieves superior detection performance with competitive computational cost. As shown in~ , SGLDet achieves stronger detection performance on both MODA and HOD3K with comparable computational cost. The main contributions are summarized as follows: We propose SGLDet, a spectral-aware global-local dynamic modeling framework for multispectral aerial object detection that unifies global spectral dependency modeling, scene-guided contextual refinement, and scene-dependent dynamic local modulation. We develop a spectral-driven global reasoning design coupling similarity-guided sparse retrieval with scene-guided refinement, strengthening semantic consistency across spectrally similar objects and alleviating global semantic ambiguity in aerial scenes. We develop a spectral-aware input-dependent calibration aggregation mechanism with input-adaptive expert aggregation and spectral--spatial calibration for accurate localization under local variations. Related Work sec:related_work Object Detection in Aerial Images sec:rw_aerial Object detection in RGB images has achieved remarkable progress in recent years, driven by advances in single-stage~ tian2019fcos , two-stage~ Cascade , and Transformer-based detectors~ deformable-detr . In aerial imagery, however, objects frequently appear with arbitrary orientations, necessitating specialized representations beyond horizontal bounding boxes. Two-stage approaches such as RoI Transformer~ roi_trans address rotation through region transformation, while single-stage oriented detectors such as R3Det~ yang2021r3det , S ANet~ han2021align , Oriented RepPoints~ oriented-reppoints , and CFA~ cfa improve oriented localization and dense object modeling. More recently, LSKNet~ Li_2024_IJCV and Strip R-CNN~ yuan2025strip explore large-kernel designs to better capture broader spatial context in remote sensing scenes. Beyond geometric modeling, recent aerial detectors further improve dense-instance perception through stronger spatial context modeling and feature aggregation~ Li_2024_IJCV, yuan2025strip, wu2025measuring . However, these methods primarily rely on RGB spatial features and therefore remain limited when objects share similar visual appearances with cluttered backgrounds. Multispectral Object Detection sec:rw_mod Leveraging information from continuous spectral bands, multispectral imagery holds significant potential for scene characterization and interpretation~ hong2021spectralformer . However, due to the limitations of multispectral image acquisition and resolution, datasets and methods for multispectral object detection remain relatively scarce. Multispectral data usually exhibit high correlation and redundancy among adjacent bands, and early studies mainly focused on pixel-level analysis such as spectral matching or anomaly detection, rather than object-level localization. Yan et al.~ yan2021object explored spectral image object detection at the object level. He et al.~ he2023object proposed S2ADet and the HOD3K dataset, introducing a two-stream architecture that separately extracts spectral and spatial features before aggregating dual detection branches. Han et al.~ han2025moda further introduced MODA and proposed OSSDet to enhance target perception and suppress background interference through spectral-spatial interaction and object-aware cues. Xu et al.~ xu2026dahnet subsequently proposed DAHNet, which decomposes multispectral data and aggregates complementary spectral-spatial representations through cross-domain synergistic attention. Despite these advances, spectral information is still mainly used as an auxiliary cue for local feature enhancement through dimensionality reduction or channel reweighting, rather than as a global semantic prior for unifying materially consistent objects across the scene he2023object, han2025moda, xu2026dahnet . Spatial-Spectral Feature Learning sec:rw_ss Spatial-spectral feature learning has been extensively studied in multispectral image analysis, where the primary objective is to jointly model spectral correlations and spatial context for pixel-level discrimination. Early deep learning methods applied 2D CNNs to extract spatial features from individual bands or reduced representations, while 3D CNNs were later introduced to capture inter-band dependencies through volumetric convolutions. Despite these advances, most spatial-spectral learning paradigms are designed for classification or restoration rather than accurate instance-level localization in aerial detection. When extended to object detection, spatial-spectral learning remains relatively underexplored. Existing methods usually treat spectral cues as auxiliary signals in feature fusion he2023object, han2025moda, xu2026dahnet , so most strategies still operate at the local feature level without explicit modeling of global dependencies or adaptive local aggregation for object-specific variations across aerial scenes. SGLDet follows a global-to-local design to jointly address semantic ambiguity and localization challenges in complex aerial scenes. title: Decoupling Action from Egocentric Observation for World Simulation
comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026, Project page: https://ego-act.github.io/, Code: https://github.com/mayuelala/EgoACT
summary: Egocentric action transfer aims to decouple the semantic action from egocentric observations and reproduce them in new visual contexts, enabling scalable world simulation, embodied policy learning, and robotic data generation. Existing approaches to transferring actions rely on condition-guided video generation, which converts the observation video into explicit geometric controls (e.g., hand poses or meshes) to drive synthesis. However, these methods introduce geometric estimation errors, making it difficult to preserve physically plausible interactions when transferred to new scenes. Alternatively, motion transfer methods directly extract motion patterns from the observation video, yet motion-level features alone cannot encode rich contact dynamics, frequently leading to severe hand structural collapse and implausible contact layout. To address both limitations, we present EgoACT, a test-time framework for egocentric action transfer that operates directly on the denoising process of video diffusion models without requiring additional geometric estimators. EgoACT uses Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring to stabilize reference-consistent hand-object structure in the early denoising stage, and Sparse Correspondence Calibration to refine reliable local correspondences in the mid-to-late denoising stages. Together, these two components preserve transferable action semantics while improving temporal coherence and interaction realism. We further establish EgoActionBench, a benchmark for evaluating action preservation, visual quality, and hand-object plausibility across diverse egocentric manipulation scenarios. Experiments show that EgoACT generates more coherent and physically plausible interaction videos than strong baselines.

Introduction sec:introduction Egocentric action transfer aims to decouple the semantic action from egocentric observations and reproduce it in new visual scenes, enabling scalable world simulation, embodied policy learning, and robotic data generation. The core challenge is to decouple what action is being performed from how the current scene happens to look, so that the interaction logic, including contact transitions, object responses, and coordinated hand-object dynamics , can be faithfully reproduced in novel scenarios. Existing approaches to transferring egocentric actions are predominantly formulated as condition-guided video generation~ xing2024make,zhao2023controlvideo,wang2024motionctrl . These methods first convert an observation video into explicit geometric controls, such as keypoints, hand poses, or mesh sequences~ ge2018hand,xiao2024spatialtracker,hu2025depthcrafter , and then force the target video to follow these extracted conditions. However, these methods rely on accurate geometric estimation and inevitably introduce external errors into the generation process. When transferred to a new scene, the injected geometric controls cannot guarantee physically valid interactions (Fig.~ fig:intro_motivation ). An alternative line of work, motion transfer~ pondaven2025video,ma2026fastvmt,ling2024motionclone , sidesteps explicit geometric estimation by extracting and replaying motion patterns directly from the observation video. While this avoids estimator-induced errors, motion-level features alone cannot encode the rich contact dynamics inherent in egocentric manipulation. These methods frequently suffer from severe hand structural collapse and implausible contact layout (Fig.~ fig:intro_motivation ). To address this, instead of hard-copying sparse geometric structures or replaying raw motion from an observation video, we aim to extract the transferable semantic action from an egocentric observation and use it to synthesize a new interaction video under a different visual realization. This setting asks the model to preserve the interaction logic behind the motion, including contact timing, object response, and coherent hand-object coordination, rather than the observation appearance or exact geometric condition. In this work, we present EgoACT, a test-time action transfer framework for egocentric world simulation. We observe that egocentric action transfer faces two major failure modes during generation. First, hand-object structural collapse often occurs in the early denoising stage, where action guidance can distort hands, objects, and contact geometry before a stable interaction layout is formed. Second, physically unrealistic interaction can still appear even when visible motion is roughly aligned, because local correspondences, contact timing, and object responses may drift in later denoising stages. To address these challenges, EgoACT combines two complementary test-time refinements. Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring (VSA) stabilizes early denoising by preserving reference-consistent hand-object structure, while Sparse Correspondence Calibration (SCC) refines mid-to-late denoising by correcting reliable local correspondences around interaction regions. Beyond the method, we establish EgoActionBench, a benchmark for evaluating egocentric action transfer. EgoActionBench contains 350 egocentric manipulation videos covering diverse interaction categories, object types, hand configurations, and scene layouts. It evaluates not only visual fidelity, but also action preservation, temporal coherence, and hand-object interaction plausibility. Experiments on EgoActionBench show that EgoACT produces more coherent transferred actions and more plausible hand-object interactions than strong baselines, supporting the effectiveness of our formulation. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We analyze the challenges of egocentric action transfer and propose EgoACT, a test-time action transfer framework that decouples transferable action semantics from observation visual appearance without additional training. Technically, we introduce Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring and Sparse Correspondence Calibration, which respectively address hand-object structural collapse and physically unrealistic interaction. We establish EgoActionBench, a benchmark for evaluating egocentric action transfer comprehensively, and conduct extensive experiments that support the effectiveness of our formulation and method. Related Work Motion Transfer. Motion transfer aims to synthesize novel videos by preserving reference motion dynamics, requiring effective decoupling of spatial appearance and temporal motion. Early works~ guo2023animatediff, xing2024make, xing2024dynamicrafter, feng2025dit4edit, zhao2023controlvideo, wang2024motionctrl, zhang2025framepainter rely on explicit control signals, which demand large-scale annotations and substantial computation. Consequently, recent diffusion models shift toward implicit control, employing either parameter-efficient tuning~ zhao2024motiondirector, jeong2024dreammotion, ren2024customize, wu2024motionbooth or inference-time motion extraction~ hu2024motionmaster, qiu2024tfb, qiu2025duet, qiu2025DBLoss, qiu2026dag, yesiltepe2024motionshop, geyer2023tokenflow, qi2023fatezero, ling2024motionclone, xiao2024video . However, these frameworks primarily target 3D U-Nets~ blattmann2023align . As models evolve toward Diffusion Transformers (DiTs)~ peebles2023scalable with fully coupled 3D attention, traditional methods relying on explicit spatio-temporal separation become difficult to apply. Recent DiT-based adaptations explore attention flow optimization~ pondaven2025video , parameter-efficient tuning~ abdal2025dynamic , temporal kernel encoding~ shi2025decouple , and streamlined extraction~ ma2026fastvmt . However, these methods still focus primarily on visible motion transfer, while egocentric action transfer requires preserving contact transitions and hand-object dynamics. -Centric Video Generation. Recent advances in diffusion have increasingly pushed generative video models toward the paradigm of video world modeling~ brooks2024sora, bruce2024genie, hu2023gaia , where the goal is to capture not only visual appearance but also the underlying dynamics and interactions of the physical world. Some works~ li2026mask2iv, zhang2025vhoi, HOIGen address interactive manipulation video generation by introducing structured interaction signals to improve controllability and physical plausibility. Methods such as Mask2IV~ li2026mask2iv and VHOI~ zhang2025vhoi leverage mask trajectories or keypoints to guide fine-grained interactions. Other approaches incorporate more explicit control cues or geometric priors, such as InterDyn~ akkerman2025interdyn , GenHSI~ li2026genhsi , and ZeroHSI~ li2024zerohsi . EgoSim~ hao2026egosim and Hand2World~ wang2026hand2world further introduce egocentric conditioning or structured world representations to enhance interaction realism and consistency. Despite these advances, existing methods largely rely on external condition estimators~ ge2018hand, xiao2024spatialtracker, hu2025depthcrafter to guide the generation of physically consistent interaction videos, which limit practical application. In contrast, we propose EgoACT, which enhances interaction consistency without requiring external estimators, enabling more robust interaction world modeling. Method sec:method Given an egocentric manipulation video that demonstrates a source action, egocentric action transfer aims to synthesize a new video that preserves the transferable action semantics while allowing the visual realization to change. The transferred signal should not be limited to visible hand displacement, but should also retain the underlying interaction logic, including contact transitions, object response, and coordinated hand-object dynamics. In this section, we first discuss the motivation and key challenges of egocentric action transfer in Sec.~ subsec:motivation . We then introduce Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring (VSA) in Sec.~ subsec:VSA , which stabilizes the global hand-object structure during the early denoising stage. Finally, we present Sparse Correspondence Calibration (SCC) in Sec.~ subsec:scc , which refines local temporal correspondences in the mid-to-late denoising stages. Motivation subsec:motivation Egocentric action transfer requires the model to transfer the semantic action from a reference egocentric observation while synthesizing a new interaction video under a different visual realization. Consistent with the discussion in Sec.~ sec:introduction , this setting is difficult because the model must preserve the interaction logic behind the motion rather than simply reproduce visible hand displacement. We focus on two failure modes that commonly appear during generation: -object Structural Collapse. Explicit condition guidance usually converts the reference video into geometric controls, such as keypoints, hand poses, or mesh sequences, and then forces the generation process to follow these controls. Although this can preserve coarse motion, it is fragile in egocentric manipulation, where hands are frequently occluded, distorted by perspective, and tightly coupled with objects. Noisy or distribution-mismatched controls can over-constrain the early denoising trajectory, leading to broken fingers, distorted hands, collapsed objects, or implausible contact geometry. title: CLOSER: Evidence-Aware Active Visual Verification for Embodied Object-Goal Navigation
summary: Object-goal navigation (ObjectNav) requires an embodied agent to find an instance of a specified category in an unseen environment and stop near it. The agent typically relies on an object detector but must judge online from a limited egocentric video stream, sometimes a single frame, whether a detected candidate is the target. Detectors often confidently mistake similar objects, such as a sofa for a bed, and stopping at a false positive fails the episode. Prevailing systems also approach candidates greedily, leaving them occluded or partially observed. We present CLOSER, an evidence-aware active verification framework that treats stopping as closed-loop evidence acquisition, coupling vision-language model (VLM) verification with active perception. CLOSER fine-tunes an open-source VLM to label each view of a candidate tracked across frames as target, non-target, or uncertain, selects complementary views with an embedding-based diversity gate, and fuses their per-view probabilities with a lightweight network. If the fused judgment remains uncertain, a diffusion policy drives the agent toward the candidate using only the tracked mask and depth until the decision becomes decisive. CLOSER runs locally and plugs into existing ObjectNav systems without retraining them. On Gibson and Habitat-Matterport 3D, it raises average success rate by 3.6 points and success weighted by path length by 2.0 points, showing that verifying evidence before committing improves embodied navigation.
