Object-goal navigation, embodied AI, spatial reasoning, scene understanding, vision for robotics, object detection and recognition. Introduction bject-goal navigation (ObjectNav) is a fundamental task in embodied AI~ 11098567 in which an agent searches an unseen environment for an object of a specified target category and stops near it~ chaplot2020semexp,fukushima2023omt . To find the target, the agent must explore the environment efficiently and infer where the target is likely to be located. When an object resembling the target comes into view, the agent must further judge whether it is the target. ObjectNav therefore demands both efficient exploration and reliable perception from its online egocentric video stream, and remains a challenging problem despite extensive study~ sun2024objectnav_survey . To meet these demands, prevailing modular systems adopt an exploration strategy to search promising regions and an off-the-shelf object detector to recognize the observed objects~ chaplot2020semexp,zhou2023esc,yokoyama2024vlfm . Whenever a candidate for the target category is detected, the agent must decide from limited local observations whether the candidate is the target and hence whether to stop; in the worst case, only a single partial view is available. Since the episode ends once the agent stops, a wrong stop cannot be corrected, and this stopping decision has been identified as a major bottleneck of modular systems~ song2023dita,ratenav2025 . Although modern open-vocabulary detectors such as YOLO-World and Grounded-SAM~ cheng2024yolo,ren2024grounded achieve high recall on common indoor categories, they frequently mistake semantically similar objects for the target. For example, a sofa observed from a distance may be detected as a bed (Fig.~ fig:teaser ), and a stool partially occluded by a table may be detected as a chair. Such confusers are often detected with tight bounding boxes and high confidence, so raising the confidence threshold removes true targets before it removes these errors. Therefore, each detected candidate needs to be further verified before the agent commits to a stop. To this end, recent systems introduce a closed-source vision--language model (VLM) such as GPT-4o-mini as a verifier that confirms or rejects each detected candidate~ zhu2025strive . Such a model provides open-world visual reasoning that the detector lacks, and can reject confusers even when the detection confidence is high. However, the verifier is accessible only through a remote API, which incurs per-query cost and latency and leaves its weights unavailable for local adaptation. A smaller open-source VLM avoids these constraints, yet its verification accuracy drops markedly on hard cases such as distant or partially occluded confusers. Moreover, existing verifiers are binary and must decide even when the current view supports neither confirmation nor rejection. Such a forced decision may stop the agent at a non-target or reject a candidate that a closer view could confirm. Recent work has proposed ternary uncertainty scores and explicit outcomes~ qasknav2026,vlnnf2026 , but neither mechanism moves the agent to acquire more views of the candidate for verification. In this paper, we propose CLOSER (Closed-Loop Observation Sensing for Embodied veRification), an evidence-aware active verification framework in which the agent decides whether to stop by reasoning over the visual evidence on a candidate and acting to improve it. Our key insight is that a reliable stopping decision depends not only on what the candidate appears to be but also on whether the available views suffice to identify it, and this sufficiency depends on the spatial relationship between the agent and the candidate, including its distance, viewing angle, and degree of occlusion. The agent therefore commits to a decision only when the evidence suffices and otherwise approaches the candidate to acquire more informative views (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). Realizing this closed loop poses two challenges. First, the agent must learn when its evidence is insufficient, which confidence cannot reveal since distant or occluded views often yield confident predictions. Second, it must learn how to reach a more informative view without a complete map of the unseen environment. To learn when the evidence is insufficient, CLOSER fine-tunes an open-source VLM with LoRA~ hu2022lora to assess both the identity of the candidate and the sufficiency of each view. During navigation, CLOSER tracks the candidate across egocentric frames with ByteTrack~ zhang2022bytetrack and caches complementary views of it, and a lightweight MLP fuses the per-view assessments of the VLM to decide whether the evidence suffices. To learn how to reach a more informative view, CLOSER imitates an expert that plans maximum-clearance paths along the Voronoi medial axis of the complete map and smooths them into B\'ezier trajectories, so that walls are less likely to occlude the candidate along the way. To eliminate this dependence on the map, we distill the expert trajectories into a Diffusion Transformer policy~ chi2023diffusion_policy,peebles2023dit that conditions only on the tracked candidate mask and depth, which encode the distance and visibility of the candidate relative to the agent. As the agent follows this policy, verification and active perception form a closed loop, in which every view cached along the trajectory refines the assessment and the approach phase ends as soon as the evidence supports a decision. CLOSER is invoked only when a candidate for the target category is detected and leaves the exploration and mapping components of existing ObjectNav systems unchanged. It can therefore be inserted into these systems as a plug-in verification layer without retraining them. The main contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: We propose CLOSER, a plug-in layer for existing ObjectNav systems that formulates the stopping decision as an active verification problem. Closer judges not only whether a candidate is the target but also whether its views suffice for that judgment, and it drives the agent to acquire more views by approaching the candidate when the current views are insufficient. Since a confident prediction on a distant or occluded view can be wrong, we design the verifier in Closer to assess the sufficiency of each view in addition to the identity of the candidate. We fine-tune an open-source VLM for this assessment under a closed-source VLM teacher and train a lightweight MLP that fuses the assessments of complementary views into a single decision. We train a map-free approach policy by distilling an expert into a Diffusion Transformer that generates a trajectory toward the candidate from its tracked mask and depth. To keep the candidate in view throughout the approach phase, the expert plans each path along the Voronoi medial axis of the free space for maximum clearance from walls and smooths the path into a B\'ezier trajectory. Simulation experiments confirm that CLOSER improves ObjectNav performance. Across diverse ObjectNav systems on Gibson, HM3D v1, and HM3D v2, CLOSER improves success rate (SR), with an average gain of 3.6 points and a maximum gain of 4.9 points. CLOSER also improves success weighted by path length (SPL) by 2.0 points on average. Related Work sec:related_work Object-Goal Navigation and Target Verification subsec:rw_objectnav Existing ObjectNav methods range from end-to-end reinforcement learning, which learns continuous environment representations with multi-step look-ahead planning~ chen2024think or agent-centric relation graphs that encode object layout and target distance~ hu2024acrg , to modular pipelines that combine semantic mapping with goal selection~ chaplot2020semexp,fukushima2023omt and zero-shot variants~ sun2024objectnav_survey , supported by large-scale simulators~ yadav2023hm3dsem . Recent methods use vision--language models to score exploration frontiers~ yokoyama2024vlfm or large language models to prioritize search regions~ zhu2025chatnav,cao2025cognav ; E BA~ shi2025e2ba further fuses LLM commonsense scores with geometric costs through particle filtering and uses a cascaded discriminator to decide when to backtrack. These advances concentrate on where to explore, and a separate mechanism is still required to verify whether a detected candidate is the target. For the stopping decision, DITA~ song2023dita decouples depth-based termination from the navigation policy, RATE-Nav~ ratenav2025 models spatial regions to trigger stopping, and ACRG~ hu2024acrg encodes the depth-derived agent--target distance into the policy. Classical pipelines verify candidates with detector confidence thresholds~ chaplot2020semexp , which fail under partial observability~ rememNav2026 . Memory~ fukushima2023omt,rememNav2026 and blacklist mechanisms~ yin2025unigoal improve decision consistency, SPENav~ yuan2026spenav filters task-irrelevant objects with room-guided semantic priors, and recent systems query a closed-source VLM to verify each candidate~ zhu2025strive . For image goals, RSRNav~ qin2026rsrnav reasons about the spatial relationship between the goal and the current observation through direction-aware correlation and remains robust when the goal viewpoint differs from the test viewpoint. Beyond binary decisions, QAsk-Nav~ qasknav2026 and VLN-NF~ vlnnf2026 introduce ternary uncertainty scores and an explicit outcome, while IEVE~ lei2024ieve and DRIVE-Nav~ gao2026drivenav verify potential targets by keypoint matching and cross-frame VLM inspection. However, these systems either depend on closed-source VLM APIs or do not collect further observations when the evidence on a candidate is insufficient. In CLOSER, verification runs on local hardware, and the agent approaches a candidate with insufficient evidence to acquire additional views. Vision--Language Model Adaptation and Chain-of-Thought Reasoning subsec:rw_vlm Large VLMs can be adapted by training only a small fraction of their parameters, either a lightweight query module with the image encoder and language model frozen~ dai2023instructblip or low-rank updates such as LoRA~ hu2022lora , and EverWalker~ li2026everwalker

title: CoGaussian: Open-Vocabulary Gaussian-based Collaborative 3D Scene Understanding
summary: Collaborative perception enables agents to retrieve the scene semantics and geometry beyond the field of view of any individual agent. This broader scene understanding enhances transportation safety and improves efficiency in multi-robot systems. However, existing collaborative semantic occupancy methods rely on dense 3D voxel annotations and are limited to recognizing objects within a predefined set of semantic classes. To overcome these limitations, we present CoGaussian, an open-vocabulary Gaussian-based collaborative semantic occupancy prediction framework. CoGaussian represents a scene as a set of foundation model-aligned sparse 3D Gaussians, which serve as a compact representation for communicating and fusing geometric and semantic information across multiple agents. On the Semantic-OPV2V benchmark, our method outperforms existing open-vocabulary single-agent approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of open-vocabulary collaborative scene understanding.
full_text: Collaborative perception enables agents to retrieve the scene semantics and geometry beyond the field of view of any individual agent. This broader scene understanding enhances transportation safety and improves efficiency in multi-robot systems. However, existing collaborative semantic occupancy methods rely on dense 3D voxel annotations and are limited to recognizing objects within a predefined set of semantic classes. To overcome these limitations, we present CoGaussian, an open-vocabulary Gaussian-based collaborative semantic occupancy prediction framework. CoGaussian represents a scene as a set of foundation model-aligned sparse 3D Gaussians, which serve as a compact representation for communicating and fusing geometric and semantic information across multiple agents. On the Semantic-OPV2V benchmark, our method outperforms existing open-vocabulary single-agent approaches, highlighting the effectiveness of open-vocabulary collaborative scene understanding. INTRODUCTION Collaborative perception enables local agents to exchange information that may be occluded or beyond their field-of-view, improving geometric and semantic understanding of their environment, and enabling safer and more reliable decision making in autonomous driving and robot navigation. Semantic occupancy prediction (SOP) is a representative and challenging task in 3D spatial understanding, which aims to predict voxel-wise occupancy status and semantic class. Recently, 3D Gaussian-based methods~ 3dgs have been shown to be effective for SOP. The GaussianFormer family~ gaussianformer, gaussianformer2, zhao2025gaussianformer3d, gaussianworld represents scenes as 3D Gaussians, supervised by dense occupancy labels. VOGS-CP~ vogs-cp extends GaussianFormer to collaborative SOP which communicates Gaussian primitives between neighboring agents. However, these methods are limited to predicting semantics within a closed vocabulary and heavily rely on densely annotated 3D occupancy labels that are expensive to obtain. Vision foundation models (VFMs), such as DINO~ dinov2 and CLIP~ clip have demonstrated strong open-vocabulary capabilities in 2D perception. In addition, Talk2DINO~ barsellotti2025talkingdinobridgingselfsupervised and DINO.txt~ dinotxt further align 2D VFM features with natural language. Building on the above VFMs, GaussTR~ gausstr represents scenes as a set of sparse open-vocabulary 3D Gaussians that are predicted in a feed-forward manner and can be queried via natural language. The Gaussians are encoded with geometry and semantic information by splatting into 2D views and aligning rendered features with foundation model-derived depth~ metric3dv2 and semantics~ clip, dinov2 . However, GaussTR is designed for single-agent perception and cannot leverage information that is visible only to neighboring agents. Based on these observations, we propose CoGaussian, the first open-vocabulary multi-robot collaborative perception framework. We represent scenes as sets of sparse VFM-aligned 3D Gaussians, which also serve as the communication primitives among agents. We also explore and develop three different algorithms to aggregate and fuse information from neighboring agents. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: Open-Vocabulary Collaborative Perception: We propose CoGaussian, the first framework for open-vocabulary collaborative perception (e.g. 3D semantic occupancy prediction) in outdoor environments. Multi-Robot 3D Gaussian Representation: We develop a foundation model-aligned 3D Gaussian representation for collaborative perception, along with fusion strategies to enhance information transfer among agents. Zero-Shot Benchmarking: We evaluate CoGaussian on the Semantic-OPV2V~ opv2v,cohff dataset in a zero-shot manner. Without any task-specific supervision, our approach achieves impressive performance for semantic occupancy prediction, highlighting the potential for open-vocabulary collaborative perception. Method sec:method We represent a scene as a sparse set of 3D Gaussians with associated DINOv2~ dinov2 features. Predicted Gaussians are splatted back into the source camera view and supervised by DINOv2~ dinov2 features and Metric3Dv2~ metric3dv2 monocular depth. During inference, semantic class logits are computed as similarity between the predicted Gaussian features and Talk2DINO~ barsellotti2025talkingdinobridgingselfsupervised text embeddings for each class. While this approach is effective for datasets with limited camera overlap, such as in the nuScenes dataset nuscenes , it is suboptimal for multi-agent perception, where independent supervision fails to exploit overlapping observations across agents. title: Differentiable Task-Driven Coded Aperture Camera Design with 3D Gaussian Scene Representations
summary: Camera design heavily influences perception task performance, yet cameras are typically designed by domain experts through costly experimentation, in isolation from the tasks they serve. Existing joint-design methods either rely on differentiable simulation limited to pre-captured 2D images, restricting them to optics or image-processing pipeline design, or use non-differentiable camera simulators optimised with derivative-free or reinforcement-learning methods that scale poorly with the number of design parameters. We present a differentiable framework for jointly designing complex camera systems and downstream perception tasks. We use it to design two coded-aperture depth-from-defocus cameras, a monocular and a stereo configuration, by jointly optimising the coded aperture mask, camera parameters, and a depth estimation network end-to-end. Our framework represents scenes with 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructed from real-world captures, providing a differentiable image formation process for gradient-based optimisation over design spaces intractable for prior differentiable approaches. Results demonstrate that our differentiable method improves over existing coded aperture design and non-differentiable camera design baselines, offering a step forward in automated and principled camera design for autonomous systems.
full_text: Camera design heavily influences perception task performance, yet cameras are typically designed by domain experts through costly experimentation, in isolation from the tasks they serve. Existing joint-design methods either rely on differentiable simulation limited to pre-captured 2D images, restricting them to optics or image-processing pipeline design, or use non-differentiable camera simulators optimised with derivative-free or reinforcement-learning methods that scale poorly with the number of design parameters. We present a differentiable framework for jointly designing complex camera systems and downstream perception tasks. We use it to design two coded-aperture depth-from-defocus cameras, a monocular and a stereo configuration, by jointly optimising the coded aperture mask, camera parameters, and a depth estimation network end-to-end. Our framework represents scenes with 3D Gaussian Splatting reconstructed from real-world captures, providing a differentiable image formation process for gradient-based optimisation over design spaces intractable for prior differentiable approaches. Results demonstrate that our differentiable method improves over existing coded-aperture design and non-differentiable camera design baselines, offering a step forward in automated and principled camera design for autonomous systems. Introduction diff-sec:intro The quality of camera captures directly governs the performance of downstream perception tasks, yet different autonomous systems require different camera designs to suit their tasks: autonomous vehicles need wide field of view (FoV) and high dynamic range, medical imaging needs fine resolution and colour fidelity, and robotics needs reliable depth and colour sensing. Hence, cameras should be designed in a task-specific manner. Many works jointly optimise imaging systems and perception tasks via differentiable simulation and gradient-based optimisers~ sitzmann2018end, chang2018hybrid, tseng2021differentiable, ikoma2021depth, cote2023differentiable, yang2023image, ghanekar2024passive . However, their reliance on pre-captured 2D image datasets prevents generalisation to broader design problems such as FOV, resolution, multi-camera configurations, or unconventional architectures, limiting them to designing parts of the camera system (e.g., optics or the image signal processing pipeline) rather than full camera systems. Other works design full camera systems using 3D simulation environments, but treat the simulator as a non-differentiable black box, relying on reinforcement-learning~ klinghoffer2023diser or derivative-free~ yan2025tacos, tiwary2025if, yan2026joca optimisers that ignore gradient information and must optimise for long iterations. This becomes prohibitively inefficient as the number of design parameters grows, particularly for high-dimensional parameters such as a coded aperture mask. In this work, we propose a differentiable method for jointly designing complex camera systems and downstream perception tasks (Figure~ diff-fig:key_figure ), using 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d for scene representation and differentiable image formation. This enables gradient-based optimisation of optics, sensors, and placement while retaining the capacity to model complex, unconventional camera systems beyond the reach of prior differentiable methods. Since 3DGS scenes can be reconstructed from real-world captures, our method trains on both rendered and captured data; discrete parameters such as the coded aperture mask and sensor selection are optimised via a continuous-relaxation surrogate gradient. We demonstrate scalability to high-dimensional design spaces by jointly optimising a coded aperture mask with the remaining camera parameters and a depth-from-defocus perception task, for both single-camera and stereo configurations, analysing the resulting design trade-offs, an analysis made possible by our 3DGS-based representation and largely overlooked in prior coded aperture work. In summary, our contributions are: [noitemsep,topsep=0pt] We introduce a differentiable framework that jointly optimises camera systems and their perception networks using 3DGS scenes reconstructed from real-world captures. We use this framework to design both monocular and stereo coded aperture cameras, via a depth-from-defocus network augmented with a frequency injection module and extended to the stereo setup. We systematically compare against existing camera design approaches and demonstrate significant improvements (e.g., up to 65 lower all-in-focus (AiF) LPIPS and 13 lower depth RMSE compared to the strongest baseline in the monocular setup), and analyse the design trade-offs between camera parameters, aperture masks, and task performance. This work provides a unified, differentiable framework that bridges scene representation, image formation, and perception, enabling systematic study of how camera design choices affect downstream task performance. Related Work diff-sec:lit Task-Driven Camera Design Designing cameras for perception tasks improves performance, though many approaches rely on non-differentiable simulators. Early work used renderers such as ISET~ Wandell2024ISET3D, Wandell2024ISETCam to prototype cameras and manually tune parameters against task outcomes~ blasinski2018optimizing, liu2019system, liu2019soft, weikl2021end, liu2023using , trading laborious manual iteration for lower development cost. Later work automates this with reinforcement-learning~ klinghoffer2023diser, hou2023optimizing or evolutionary~ yan2025tacos, yan2026joca, tiwary2025if methods that bypass large networks for faster, more data-efficient optimisation. Treating the simulator as a black box, however, makes these methods inefficient with high-dimensional or numerous parameters such as a coded aperture mask, which our method handles efficiently via gradient-based optimisation while retaining full camera system support. Another line of work instead leverages differentiable simulation to jointly optimise camera parameters and the perception task, applied to depth of field~ sitzmann2018end, sun2021end, yang2024curriculum , object detection~ tseng2019hyperparameter, tseng2021differentiable, robidoux2021end, cote2023differentiable , image classification~ chang2018hybrid, diamond2021dirty, zhang2022all, yang2023image , depth estimation~ he2018learning, chang2019deep, ikoma2021depth, baek2021polka , HDR imaging~ metzler2020deep, martel2020neural , and motion deblurring~ nguyen2022learning . These methods simulate cameras' effect on pre-captured 2D images, however, limiting generalisation to variable FoV, resolution, unconventional configurations, or multi-camera systems. Our approach instead constructs the full environment in 3D using 3DGS, supporting such scenarios while retaining differentiability. Coded Aperture Imaging Coded aperture imaging modifies the aperture to encode scene-dependent blur, improving depth and AiF recovery. Early work showed that appropriately designed aperture patterns improve the conditioning of depth-from-defocus and deblurring~ levin2007image, veeraraghavan2007dappled, zhou2009coded , and recent methods jointly optimise the aperture code and reconstruction network end-to-end using amplitude~ shedligeri2017data or phase masks~ haim2018depth, wu2019phasecam3d, ikoma2021depth . Ghanekar et al.~ ghanekar2024passive extended this to dual-pixel sensors, learning an amplitude mask that trades depth estimation against deblurring. These methods optimise the aperture mask alone, whereas we treat coded aperture imaging as a broader co-design problem, jointly optimising the mask with other camera parameters for task-driven objectives. This enables systematic exploration of trade-offs such as depth accuracy, noise, and defocus blur, and we further extend coded aperture imaging to stereo-camera systems. Methodology diff-sec:method We propose a differentiable framework that jointly optimises camera design and downstream perception tasks using a 3DGS scene representation, as illustrated in Figure~ diff-fig:method_overview . Scene Representation and Image Formation We represent the 3D scene using 3DGS~ kerbl20233d , a differentiable splatting-based representation reconstructed before optimisation from a set of input images, which renders RGB images and depth maps via alpha-compositing. We assume a pinhole projection model, though other camera models could be used; this yields analytical gradients with respect to camera parameters, enabling gradient-based joint optimisation of intrinsics (e.g., focal length, sensor dimensions) and extrinsics (e.g., placement, orientation). To simulate coded aperture defocus, we apply an occlusion-aware layered blur model adapted from Ikoma et al.~ ikoma2021depth : the rendered scene is quantised into discrete depth layers, each convolved with a depth-dependent point spread function (PSF) determined by the coded mask, focus distance, and f-number, then composited back-to-front using the depth maps to account for occlusion between layers. Following~ yan2025tacos , we augment the rendered image with an affine noise model~ foi2009clipped combining signal-dependent Poisson noise and thermal noise calibrated on a physical camera. The calibrated noise parameters generalise to arbitrary exposure, gain, pixel size, and aperture size by scaling the effective gain with the ratios of pixel and aperture areas relative to the calibrated configuration, including the coded mask's open-aperture fraction. Perception Task Our framework is compatible with any differentiable perception task, but here we focus on an RGB-D task that jointly estimates depth from defocus blur and reconstructs an AiF image, as it depends directly on the optical parameters we optimise. Our monocular network builds on the depth-from-defocus architecture of Ikoma et al.~ ikoma2021depth , which deconvolves the coded aperture image into a focal stack via a Tikhonov inverse filter and predicts the AiF image and depth map from the stack and coded image using a U-Net backbone. We augment this backbone with a frequency injection module that extracts local defocus cues from patch-wise Fourier spectra of the coded image and injects them at the U-Net bottleneck, improving depth separation. To demonstrate our method's ability to design beyond a single camera, we extend this network to a stereo setup: we deconvolve each view's coded aperture image into a focal stack as before, then fuse them into intermediate AiF images via a differentiable Laplacian sharpness measure for photometric consistency across views. Inspired by~ choi2025dual , a frozen pretrained optical flow network, RAPIDFlow~ morimitsu2024rapidflow , estimates disparity from these images and warps the right focal stack into the left view's coordinate frame. The left and warped right stacks, together with a disparity-derived depth cue, are then fed into the same task network to predict the left view's AiF image and depth map. Illustration diagrams of both setups are in the supplementary material. Optimisation diff-sec: optimisation We formulate our framework as a joint optimisation problem over the camera parameters and the perception task, as illustrated in Figure~ diff-fig:method_overview . At each step, the 3DGS scene is rendered into RGB and depth images, passed through the coded aperture and noise simulation, and fed to the perception network; the resulting task loss is backpropagated through the entire pipeline to jointly update all camera and network parameters using the Adam optimiser~ kingma2015adam . Camera Parameters We optimise the optics (focal length, f-number, coded aperture mask, focus distance) and image sensor (dimensions, pixel size) for the monocular setup, plus the baseline between cameras for the stereo setup. title: From Comparison to Selection: Enhancing Cross-Scale Generalization of Pointer Networks Trained with Reinforcement Learning for Capacitated Drone Delivery Routing
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) enable fast, flexible last-mile and emergency delivery, but their routing remains challenging as the number of clients varies. Classical approaches based on mixed-integer programming and heuristics can scale poorly or require problem-specific design, motivating learning-based alternatives. Reinforcement learning is particularly promising, provided a single policy can generalize across problem sizes without retraining. Although attention-based Pointer Networks are inherently size-agnostic, their solution quality degrades under both upscaling and downscaling. Using the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) as a controlled proxy, with fixed capacity reflecting drone payload constraints, we investigate this degradation and identify three contributing factors: shifts in node density, attention dispersion, and dilution of the mean-pooled graph context. We systematically compare architecture-wide, encoder-side, and decoder-side modifications to address these limitations and propose a learned, permutation-invariant graph-context aggregation mechanism, implemented as a weighted average and as Set2Set. Results reveal distinct requirements for transfer in each direction: entropy-based attention scaling reduces the CVRP20-to-CVRP100 performance gap by 1.41 percentage points, while the proposed aggregation methods achieve the largest improvement on the more challenging CVRP100-to-CVRP20 transfer, approximately 0.9 percentage points. Exploiting this complementarity, we introduce an approach selector that chooses the best model for each training-target size pair. The selector reduces cost relative to the reference model across all nine seen train-test pairs and eight of nine pairs involving unseen sizes (CVRP35, CVRP75, and CVRP200), achieving improvements of up to 3.2 percent.

Drone delivery Reinforcement learning Pointer network Graph-context aggregation Capacitated vehicle routing Size generalization Approach selection Introduction sec:intro The growth of e-commerce, on-demand services, and urban logistics pushes delivery operators to plan routes under tight constraints on capacity, distance, energy, and cost. Unmanned aerial vehicles complement ground vehicles because they bypass road congestion and fly directly between locations, which is valuable for medical, emergency, rural, and last-mile delivery, but they bring limited payload and battery range and sensitivity to weather, airspace regulation, and multi-drone coordination~ otto2018,macrina2020 . This work investigates AI-based route planning for drone networks under such constraints. From an optimization standpoint, the task is closely related to the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP): a fleet must serve customers with known demands within a capacity limit at minimal total route length~ dantzig1959,toth2014 . CVRP omits battery dynamics, charging infrastructure, and air corridors, but it isolates the capacity-constrained routing core and is a standard controlled benchmark for routing algorithms, including learning-based ones~ nazari2018,kool2019 . Exact methods scale poorly on this NP-hard problem~ fukasawa2006,pessoa2020 , and heuristics need problem-specific, hand-tuned design~ laporte2002,vidal2013 . Neural Combinatorial Optimization (NCO) instead trains a model to construct solutions directly, using reinforcement learning (RL) so that no optimal-solution labels, which are expensive for large CVRP instances, are needed~ bello2016,kool2019,bengio2021 . The central difficulty for a drone-routing policy is that the number of clients is not fixed: it varies from day to day and region to region. Training one policy per client count is not viable, so the policy must construct solutions for a variable, a priori unknown number of nodes, which is a known weakness of neural routing solvers~ manchanda2022 . A prominent size-agnostic approach is the Pointer Network with attention, which points to one of the input nodes at each decoding step instead of choosing from a fixed vocabulary, so the same trained policy can be applied to graphs of any size~ vinyals2015,kool2019 . Trained with RL, it has been benchmarked at scale in recent studies of neural routing solvers~ liu2023a,berto2023 , which show that it solves instances of the training size well but that generalization across problem sizes remains a clear bottleneck in both directions: performance degrades when the model is upscaled to larger graphs and when it is downscaled to smaller ones. This paper therefore investigates which modifications of the attention-based Pointer Network, applied architecture-wide, in the encoder or in the decoder, reduce the upscaling and the downscaling generalization gap for CVRP, and how their complementary strengths can be combined in one size-agnostic routing solver. The study focuses on the encoder--decoder architecture of the attention-based Pointer Network: the encoder embeds the nodes of an instance, and the decoder uses these embeddings to point to the next node at each step. This architecture is kept as the common frame, and every approach modifies it at one of three levels: architecture-wide, acting on the attention of both encoder and decoder; encoder-side, replacing how node embeddings are computed; or decoder-side, changing how the decoder summarises the instance and builds its query. To this end, we first identify the sources of the cross-size degradation of the reference policy, then assign to each source the levers that act on it, and finally compare all levers head-to-head under an identical training and evaluation protocol, scored by how much they reduce the cross-size optimality gap of the reference in each direction. Contributions The reference policy, the attention-scaling factors and the two alternative encoders are taken from the literature~ kool2019,xiao2025,hamilton2017,lee2019 and are re-implemented in one common framework. The contributions of this paper are: [label=( ),leftmargin=*,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt] A learned, permutation-invariant graph-context aggregation for the attention-model decoder, realised as a weighted average with a scoring network and as a Set2Set summary. It replaces the mean-pooled context and gives the largest gain of all evaluated approaches on the hardest downscaling transfer while keeping same-size quality. A diagnosis-driven, head-to-head comparison of seven levers at the architecture-wide, encoder and decoder levels of the Pointer Network, with fixed vehicle capacity so that only the number of clients changes. It shows that upscaling and downscaling respond to different levers. An approach selector that exploits this complementarity by choosing, for a given training size and target size, the approach with the lowest estimated cost. It lowers the cost of the reference on seen and unseen problem sizes. This paper is structured as follows: Section~ sec:related reviews related work, and Section~ sec:background introduces the necessary background on graph neural networks, attention and pointer decoding. Section~ sec:formulation formulates the CVRP as a sequential decision problem, gives the training objective and describes the reference policy. Section~ sec:method derives the sources of cross-size degradation and presents the evaluated approaches together with the proposed graph-context aggregation and approach selector. Section~ sec:setup details the experimental setup, Section~ sec:results reports and discusses the results, and Section~ sec:conclusion concludes the paper and outlines future work. Related Work sec:related Combinatorial optimization and routing Combinatorial optimization (CO) covers problems with a combinatorial explosion of feasible solutions~ korte2018 . Routing problems, notably the Traveling Salesman Problem and the Vehicle Routing Problem, are among the most studied because of their relevance to logistics~ toth2014,laporte2009 . The Capacitated VRP (CVRP) adds a capacity constraint that partitions customers across routes~ dantzig1959,clarke1964 . CVRP has been addressed with exact methods~ augerat1995,fukasawa2006 , heuristics such as the savings algorithm and 2-opt/3-opt~ clarke1964,lin1965 , and metaheuristics such as tabu search and hybrid genetic search~ gendreau1994,vidal2013 . Nevertheless, exact methods scale poorly and heuristics need problem-specific tuning~ toth2014,laporte2002 . Machine learning for combinatorial optimization Machine learning has assisted classical solvers by learning branching decisions~ khalil2016,gasse2019 , cutting-plane selection~ tang2020,huang2022 , solver configuration and algorithm selection~ hutter2011,kerschke2019 , and warm starts~ nair2020 , but the solver itself remains classical. NCO instead uses a neural network as the solver, learning to construct a solution end to end~ bengio2021,mazyavkina2021 . Early NCO approaches for routing used size-agnostic Pointer Networks~ vinyals2015 (Section~ sec:background ). Bello et al.\ trained a Pointer-Network policy with actor-critic RL for TSP~ bello2016 , and Nazari et al.\ extended it to CVRP with capacity-aware masking~ nazari2018 . Kool et al.\ replaced the recurrent encoder with a Transformer-style multi-head-attention (MHA) encoder and trained the resulting attention-model policy with REINFORCE and a rollout baseline, with strong results on TSP, CVRP, the Orienteering Problem, and the Prize-Collecting TSP~ kool2019,vaswani2017 . This architecture underlies RL4CO~ berto2023 and is the reference architecture used throughout this paper. The size-generalization bottleneck in attention-based NCO A systematic evaluation of neural routing solvers shows that the attention-based Pointer-Network policy performs well on instances matching its training size, but not when the graph size changes at test time~ liu2023a , as also reported by RL4CO~ berto2023 . The degradation is bidirectional: models trained on small graphs lose quality when upscaled, and models trained on large graphs do not transfer cleanly when downscaled. NCO models more broadly fail on unseen sizes~ manchanda2022 . Meta-learning~ manchanda2022 and test-time adaptation~ chen2025 address varying task distributions, including size variation. At the level of the attention computation, Wang et al.\ attribute part of the degradation to attention dispersion as the number of nodes grows~ wang2025 , and Xiao et al.\ counteract it with an entropy-based scaling factor applied to the attention scores at inference time~ xiao2025 . Architectural work asks whether the encoder or decoder composition can be changed: Berto et al.\ show that the encoder choice affects size generalization~ berto2023 , and Luo et al.\ propose a Light-Encoder-Heavy-Decoder (LEHD) composition, in contrast to the Heavy-Encoder-Light-Decoder design of Kool et al., with substantially improved generalization under supervised learning~ luo2023 . The Set Transformer~ lee2019 offers a further route to size-independent encoding through a fixed number of inducing points. Research gap Most studies target a single component in isolation and evaluate same-size performance or one transfer direction. title: OV-Foam: How 3D Representations Shape Semantic Feature Lifting
summary: Existing feature lifting approaches for open-vocabulary segmentation rely on simple backprojection to assign features to primitives. In the case of 3D Gaussian splatting reconstruction, the primitives overlap heavily, leading to suboptimal reconstructions, governed by many primitives per ray. Backprojection, however, reduces to a least-squares solvable problem, exactly when no two primitives share a ray. Motivated by this insight, we propose OV-Foam, which uses PowerFoam as the underlying representation. This representation uses a power-diagram to partition the scene, resulting in zero overlap between primitives and a substantial reduction in primitives per ray, which ultimately simplifies the lifting problem and allows for closer-to-optimal feature assignment. We show that the space partitioning primitives of OV-Foam reach near-optimal assignment, and our experiments demonstrate improved open-vocabulary segmentation over Gaussian baselines.
full_text: Existing feature lifting approaches for open-vocabulary segmentation rely on simple backprojection to assign features to primitives. In the case of 3D Gaussian splatting reconstruction, the primitives overlap heavily, leading to suboptimal reconstructions, governed by many primitives per ray. Backprojection, however, reduces to a least-squares solvable problem, exactly when no two primitives share a ray. Motivated by this insight, we propose OV-Foam, which uses PowerFoam as the underlying representation. This representation uses a power-diagram to partition the scene, resulting in zero overlap between primitives and a substantial reduction in primitives per ray, which ultimately simplifies the lifting problem and allows for closer-to-optimal feature assignment. We show that the space partitioning primitives of OV-Foam reach near-optimal assignment, and our experiments demonstrate improved open-vocabulary segmentation over Gaussian baselines. Introduction sec:intro Open-vocabulary 3D segmentation assigns vision-language aligned semantic features, such as those produced by CLIP~ radford2021learning , to reconstructed scenes, allowing objects and spatial regions to be identified using free-form language queries. This capability supports applications such as robotic manipulation~ gu2024conceptgraphs , complex scene understanding~ kerr2023lerf and medical-imaging~ wang2025sam . Existing approaches include grouping-based methods, training-based methods, and heuristic-based methods. We focus on the latter family, which directly lifts features from 2D images onto a 3D representation. The process of assigning these features to scene geometry is known as feature lifting. It associates features observed in rendered images with the primitives contributing to each pixel, using their rendering weights to aggregate information across views. This provides an efficient way to obtain semantic representations without training a 3D foundation model from scratch, but introduces a fundamental ambiguity: a 2D observation may be distributed across multiple primitives, while a primitive may collect observations from different objects. As a result, feature lifting can entangle semantic evidence before a classifier makes a prediction. This ambiguity is particularly important near object boundaries. Repeating the lifting process across views can produce feature entanglement and degraded semantic boundaries, even when the underlying image features are accurate. Recent work has begun to formalize this problem by treating feature lifting as a linear inverse problem and quantifying the ambiguity introduced by multiple primitive contributions~ xiong2026sfs . Existing feature-lifting methods largely operate on Gaussian-based reconstructions, where overlap leads to multiple primitives contributing to the same ray. This raises a more fundamental question: to what extent is feature-lifting ambiguity a property of the lifting procedure itself, and to what extent is it induced by the underlying 3D representation? In this work, we investigate feature lifting as a representation-dependent problem. We ask whether changing the geometric primitives used to represent the scene can reduce the mixing of semantic evidence, while keeping the image features and lifting procedure fixed. We consider PowerFoam~ govindarajan2026power , which represents a scene using bounded power diagrams whose cells partition 3D space. This non-overlapping spatial support reduces the number of primitives that can contribute simultaneously to a ray, reducing semantic feature mixing. We isolate this effect, by evaluating feature lifting independently of errors introduced by the upstream 2D semantic model. We replace predicted image semantics with ground-truth segmentation and text features, allowing us to measure the extent of semantic feature mixing caused by a feature lifting onto a chosen underlying 3D representation. Under this controlled setting, we compare Gaussian-based and PowerFoam reconstructions using the same lifting procedure and find that the reduced dispersion in PowerFoam leads to substantially more class-consistency in lifted features. This demonstrates that the choice of 3D primitive can itself impose a significant limitation on semantic feature lifting. Applied to real datasets, we observe that all our tested lifting methods achieve improved 3D open-vocabulary segmentation results using PowerFoam instead of 3DGS as underlying representation. Our contributions are: A controlled study of representation-dependent feature lifting. We isolate the feature-lifting stage from upstream semantic errors and systematically compare 3D primitives under the same image features and lifting procedure. An analysis of representation-induced feature dispersion. We show that space-partitioning primitives can substantially reduce semantic feature mixing compared with overlapping Gaussian primitives. An open-vocabulary 3D segmentation system based on PowerFoam. We incorporate these insights into a PowerFoam-based semantic representation and demonstrate improved performance on open-vocabulary 3D segmentation benchmarks. Related work sec:related Existing approaches for lifting 2D features to 3D primitives differ primarily in how the correspondence between image observations and 3D primitives is established: through training-based, grouping-based, and heuristic-forward methods. Early approaches fit continuous 3D semantic fields via scene-specific optimization. LERF, for example, distills CLIP features into a radiance field~ kerr2023lerf, radford2021learning , while LangSplat trains a scene-specific autoencoder to represent lifted features in a latent space~ qin2024langsplat . OpenGaussian similarly learns instance-level features together with a codebook for point-level understanding~ wu2024opengaussian . These methods can produce expressive semantic representations, but require computationally expensive per-scene optimization and may inherit inconsistencies from the underlying multi-view 2D predictions. An alternative is replacing continuous optimization with discrete associations derived from 2D masks (e.g., SAM~ kirillov2023sam ). LAGA decomposes scenes into object entities by clustering SAM mask descriptors across views~ cen2025laga , while THGS constructs Gaussian adjacency graphs with contrastive edge reweighting for hierarchical superpoint partitioning~ dai2025training . LUDVIG avoids training altogether by combining multi-view weighted feature averaging with graph diffusion across adjacent primitives~ marrie2025ludvig . Although these approaches eliminate dense feature optimization, they introduce multi-stage grouping heuristics and remain sensitive to primitive spatial overlap. More recent methods avoid additional optimization by directly inverting the image-to-primitive aggregation used during rendering. Occam's LGS~ cheng2024occam , CosegGaussians~ dou2024learning , and DrSplat~ jun2025dr independently use row-normalized splatting equations as zero-shot feature lifter. r 0.44 ! fig:overview Splat Feature Solver (SFS)~ xiong2026sfs formulates feature lifting as a sparse linear inverse problem and provides a closed-form row-sum estimator with a provable approximation bound. Specifically, SFS defines as a measure of the dispersion of the optimal lifted feature along a viewing ray. In the case where each ray intersects only a single primitive, each row of the system matrix contains a single non-zero entry of value one, yielding this zero-dispersion regime. Standard 3D Gaussians, however, have substantial spatial overlap, causing multiple primitives to contribute to the same ray and increasing feature dispersion (Figure~ fig:overview ). SFS therefore introduces Tikhonov Guidance, which modifies the opacity weights during lifting to increase diagonal dominance and reduce this coupling. Thus, while SFS provides a principled formulation and efficient solver, its lifting accuracy remains tied to the overlap structure of the underlying Gaussian primitives. An alternative to mitigating primitive overlap through the lifting procedure is to eliminate overlap at the representation level. Space-partitioning representations divide the scene into disjoint spatial cells, so each 3D location is associated with a single primitive by construction. Radiant Foam~ govindarajan2025radiant represents a scene using non-overlapping volumetric cells based on an unbounded Voronoi construction. However, its ray-tracing procedure relies on explicit cell stepping rather than tile-based rasterization, making it difficult to evaluate under the same rendering pipeline as standard 3D Gaussian Splatting. PowerFoam~ govindarajan2026power instead generalizes foam representations to bounded power diagrams, defining finite spatial cells through seed sites and per-cell radii. These bounded cells support tile-based rasterization while preserving disjoint spatial boundaries, making PowerFoam a suitable representation for studying feature lifting under otherwise comparable rendering conditions. Semantic Foam~ sharafeldin2026semantic jointly learns reconstruction and object-identity features supervised by segmentation masks. These features encode scene-specific identities rather than text-aligned semantics, so they cannot be directly compared with text embeddings for open-vocabulary queries. In contrast, we study feature transfer from fixed 2D observations onto an already trained reconstruction, allowing the effect of the underlying representation on lifting to be isolated from semantic optimization. Building on this setting, we introduce OV-Foam, an open-vocabulary 3D segmentation framework that lifts 2D vision-language features onto PowerFoam reconstructions. Method sec:method OV-Foam lifts image features onto a PowerFoam reconstruction. We first describe how the cells define rendering contributions, then use those contributions in the SFS feature estimator. We then examine how image observations are distributed across primitives and whether each primitive receives consistent features from one class or conflicting features from several classes. PowerFoam PowerFoam represents a scene with a power diagram~ govindarajan2026power . Each primitive is associated with a center and radius . For a 3D point x, its power cell is the region where primitive has the smallest power distance among all primitives . The rendering support further restricts this cell to the primitive's bounding sphere: The power cells partition space, so their interiors do not overlap, although a ray can traverse several cells. Each primitive is bounded to , so only the portion of its cell inside the bounding sphere can contribute to rendering. Within each support , a dipole defines an oriented boundary separating occupied space from empty space. The dipole provides a planar reference boundary, where occupied space satisfies , with denoting the outward unit normal and the primitive center. A displacement field can deform this boundary away from the reference plane. For a given ray , PowerFoam determines the resulting intersections with both the support and the occupied region. These intersections define the occupied ray segment and its length . Density is constant within the occupied region and zero elsewhere. During reconstruction, primitive centers, radii, densities, dipoles, and enabled displacement parameters are optimized. title: CrossFit-GS: Out-of-Fold Pose Estimation for COLMAP-Free 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Pose-free 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) aims to bypass cumbersome Structure-from-Motion (SfM) by directly reconstructing scenes from unposed image sequences. In this work, we present CrossFit-GS, a deferred-commitment progressive framework that mitigates cumulative trajectory drift and breaks the self-reinforcing loop of distorted-map error propagation. Specifically, we partition the input sequence into interleaved subsets and maintain two complementary submaps. Each candidate pose is cross-refined against a frozen opposite submap that has never been optimized using the target frame, thereby providing an independent geometric reference for pose estimation. Checkerboard validation and spatial coverage safeguards further reject unreliable updates, and only verified poses are committed to their corresponding owner submap. Once the trajectory has been refined, the intermediate submaps are discarded and the final global representation is trained from scratch using the fixed refined poses. Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that CrossFit-GS substantially reduces cumulative trajectory drift and consistently improves both camera pose estimation and novel-view synthesis over existing methods.

Extensive evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that CrossFit-GS substantially reduces cumulative trajectory drift and consistently improves both camera pose estimation and novel-view synthesis over existing methods. Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) kerbl20233d,10870258 has demonstrated remarkable success across a wide range of applications qian20243dgs, liu2024citygaussian,c3dgs,11093421 . However, standard 3DGS heavily relies on pre-computed camera extrinsics from classical Structure-from-Motion (SfM) pipelines like COLMAP colmap . However, SfM preprocessing is computationally expensive, sensitive to rapid camera motion, and prone to failure in texture-less or low-overlap regions, hindering the practical deployment of 3DGS in real-time or streaming scenarios huang20253r, guo2025robust, ICLR2025_bf11e0bb . Recent efforts explore pose-free reconstruction paradigms that estimate camera trajectories and scene geometry directly from unposed image sequences NEURIPS2025_7cdc4122, 10204053, Lin_2025_ICCV, dong2025betterrobustnessposefree3d . Initial implicit methods SCNeRF2021, nerfmm, 10.1609/aaai.v38i6.28464 , such as BARF barf and Nope-NeRF nope-nerf , pioneered this direction by fitting coordinate-based Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) mildenhall2021nerf alongside camera frame parameters. Leveraging the explicit representation and fast rasterization of Gaussians, frameworks like CF-3DGS cf-3dgs adapted this concept into a sequential regime by estimating relative poses with local Gaussian models while dynamically expanding a global scene representation. Follow-up studies improve complementary components of this pipeline by enhancing Gaussian coverage through hierarchical merging ji2025sfm , refining local pose estimation via feature and frequency regularization wei2025pcr , and introducing global trajectory constraints using long-range feature tracks shi2026trackgs . Despite these empirical advances, existing progressive paradigms fundamentally struggle to reconcile local tracking tractability with global geometric consistency. Standard sequential frameworks estimate pairwise relative transformations from local Gaussian representations and compose them into a global trajectory cf-3dgs,wei2025pcr,ji2025sfm . Although this localized formulation makes pose tracking tractable, residual pairwise errors can accumulate along the sequence and are absorbed by the global scene representation Huang_2025_ICCV,Mao_2025_ICCV . Spatially flexible Gaussians can deform to accommodate these registration offsets, yielding deceptively low training-view reconstruction errors despite inaccurate camera trajectories huang20253r,Kong_2026_CVPR . As additional frames are incorporated, the evolving representation is repeatedly optimized to explain new observations under accumulated pose errors, causing geometric distortion to propagate throughout the reconstruction. While scene-level pose refinement offers a theoretical remedy for such cumulative drift, optimizing a camera pose against a scene representation trained on that very same observation creates a self-explanation shortcut schmidt2024lookgaussposenovel, Peng_2025_ICCV, Truong_2023_CVPR . Unresolved, this underlying dilemma often leads existing methodologies to focus heavily on refining initial pose estimates, rather than addressing systemic trajectory drift at its root. We highlight this self-explanation loop as a critical bottleneck in progressive camera-free reconstruction. To overcome this fundamental limitation, we propose CrossFit-GS, a progressive pose-free reconstruction framework built on a deferred-commitment protocol. Centered on dual-map information-flow isolation, CrossFit-GS strictly decouples camera pose refinement from scene map updates for unposed image streams. Specifically, the input sequence is partitioned into two interleaved temporal subsets ( folds), each maintaining an independent Gaussian submap. For an incoming frame, a candidate pose proposal is generated from the preceding motion estimate and cross-refined exclusively against the frozen opposite submap. To improve optimization stability, this cross-map pose refinement is strictly regulated by checkerboard validation masks and spatial coverage gates. Following our deferred-commitment principle, candidate pose updates are committed to the global trajectory and integrated into owner submap updates only after passing these validation checks. Once all camera extrinsics across the sequence are verified and frozen, the intermediate submaps are discarded, and a single global Gaussian representation is initialized and trained from scratch under the fixed trajectory. Through these coordinated strategies, CrossFit-GS effectively breaks the self-reinforcing pose--map error propagation loop, substantially mitigating cumulative trajectory drift while yielding highly accurate camera estimates and superior novel-view rendering quality. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We diagnose a fundamental bottleneck in COLMAP-free 3DGS, highlighting how accumulated pairwise errors distort the evolving scene representation and how reusing this pose-contaminated map for scene-level refinement creates a self-explanation shortcut that closes a self-reinforcing pose--map fitting loop. We design a deferred-commitment progressive framework, CrossFit-GS, that prevents error propagation and suppresses trajectory drift by explicitly decoupling pose refinement from scene reconstruction through dual-map information isolation and cross-validation safeguards. Extensive experiments validate that CrossFit-GS significantly suppresses trajectory drift, achieving state-of-the-art camera tracking and view synthesis. Related Work Generalizable Feed-Forward Methods One line of research addresses unposed sparse-view reconstruction using generalizable models fang2026dens3r, wang2025vggt learned from large-scale multi-view data yu2021pixelnerf,Charatan_2024_CVPR,feng2025flashgs, venkatraman2026vggt, szymanowicz2024splatter, Huang_2025_ICCV . FreeSplatter Xu_2025_ICCV predicts pixel-aligned Gaussian primitives in a shared reference frame and recovers camera parameters from the predicted geometry. SPFSplat Huang_2025_ICCV jointly predicts camera poses and 3D Gaussians from unposed sparse views in a single feed-forward pass without pose supervision. Related approaches combine learned multi-view geometric priors with per-scene optimization. InstantSplat fan2024instantsplat , for example, initializes camera poses and dense geometry using a pretrained multi-view model and subsequently refines the scene through Gaussian bundle adjustment. These methods are primarily designed for rapid reconstruction from a small set of sparse, potentially unordered views. Their learned priors provide strong geometric initialization but introduce dependence on the training distribution and are not specifically formulated for incrementally processing long, temporally ordered sequences. Our work instead considers per-scene progressive reconstruction, where camera poses must remain globally consistent as observations are incorporated throughout an extended sequence. Sequential Pose-Free Reconstruction Sequential COLMAP-free methods exploit temporal continuity to estimate camera motion and scene geometry through per-scene optimization Lin_2025_ICCV, Gao_2026_CVPR . Early implicit methods achieve pose-free reconstruction by jointly optimizing camera parameters alongside radiance fields yang2023nerfvs, 10.1145/3664647.3681507, wang2023f2nerf , employing frequency annealing in BARF barf and monocular depth consistency in Nope-NeRF nope-nerf to prevent optimization collapse. Transitioning to explicit representations sun2024correspondence, chen2024zerogs , CF-3DGS cf-3dgs estimates relative transformations between adjacent frames using local Gaussian models, composes them into a camera trajectory, and progressively grows a global Gaussian representation. Subsequent work improves different components of this pipeline. PCR-GS wei2025pcr introduces feature-reprojection and frequency-domain oquab2023dinov2 regularization to improve local pose estimation. HT-3DGS ji2025sfm uses video frame interpolation to reduce the motion between adjacent observations and hierarchically trains and merges segment-specific Gaussian models to improve scene coverage. TrackGS shi2026trackgs incorporates long-range feature tracks, track-constrained Gaussians, and multi-view geometric losses to jointly optimize camera parameters and the Gaussian representation under global trajectory constraints. Despite these advances, sequential methods remain vulnerable to cumulative drift from locally composed pose estimates, whose errors can be absorbed by the flexible Gaussian representation. When long-range refinement is introduced, poses are typically optimized against a map trained on the same observations, leaving a self-explanation pathway between pose estimation and map fitting. Method sec:method Problem Formulation and System Overview sec:overview Given an unposed sequence of RGB images with known intrinsic matrix , our goal is to recover the camera trajectory and subsequently reconstruct a global 3D Gaussian scene representation ~ kerbl20233d . Differentiable rasterization renders a synthesized RGB image along with an accumulated opacity map . To reconcile local tracking with global geometric consistency and suppress cumulative drift, CrossFit-GS introduces an observation-isolated pipeline under a deferred-commitment protocol (Fig.~ fig:pipeline ). Rather than continuously updating a shared global map during pose estimation, our framework decouples trajectory solving from global scene synthesis through three functional components: (i) Alternating Split and Local Tracking, which streamwise partitions incoming frames into interleaved temporal folds and derives initial pose proposals; (ii) Cross-fit Refinement and Validation, which optimizes target camera poses against the frozen opposite submap while updating the activated owner submap only upon passing validation controls; and (iii) Final Reconstruction under Deferred Commitment, which discards intermediate submaps once all camera extrinsics are verified and frozen, utilizing the fixed poses to train a unified global 3DGS representation from scratch. title: Exploring Temporal Context-Aware Physical Grounding in Latent World Models
summary: Learning latent dynamics is fundamental to building action-conditioned world models for planning. Among existing families, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) offer a natural framework by modeling transitions directly in latent space rather than at the pixel level. However, two issues remain in JEPA-based world models: (i) physical grounding lacks explicit aggregation of temporal context and (ii) action planning always overly relies on generic sampling distributions. To this end, we propose $\mathcal{G}$-JEPA, which incorporates temporal context into physical grounding for latent world models and couples the learned models with prior-guided action planning. Specifically, during learning, we incorporate a shared causal temporal module that aggregates temporal context within observation and prediction sequences under physical state supervision, grounding both in task-relevant physical states. When planning, we further introduce action inference through stepwise conditioning of a generative action distribution on the current and goal latent representations together with their evolving discrepancy, yielding anchored proposals that guide model-based online refinement. Together, physical state supervision guides temporal representation learning, while the action prior guides search through the learned world model. Experiments demonstrate improved planning performance on manipulation tasks, including tasks with increasing temporal separation between initial and goal observations. Code is publicly available at https://github.com/myl11045/G-JEPA.

Introduction World models learn action-conditioned environment dynamics, enabling agents to anticipate and evaluate the consequences of candidate actions. For learning from visual observations, an important design choice is whether to generate future observations or predict their representations. Generative approaches synthesize future observations directly in pixel space lee2025edeline or through latent representations learned for visual reconstruction huang2026vid2world , requiring the preservation of appearance information beyond what may be necessary for control. Representation-predictive approaches instead learn action-conditioned dynamics by predicting the embeddings of future observations zhou2025dinowm,assran2025vjepa2 . Removing the reconstruction requirement offers the potential to learn representations that emphasize task-relevant dynamics over incidental visual detail. Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide a natural framework for this approach by predicting target embeddings from context representations without reconstructing the observations assran2023ijepa,bardes2024vjepa . World models such as DINO-WM and V-JEPA 2-AC train action-conditioned predictors on frozen DINOv2 and video-pretrained JEPA features, respectively oquab2023dinov2,zhou2025dinowm,assran2025vjepa2 . Although visual pretraining provides strong perceptual priors, freezing the encoders prevents interaction data from shaping representations around the task-specific physical structure needed for control and policy learning. LeWorldModel (LeWM) trains its visual encoder and action-conditioned predictor end to end from raw pixels using only future-embedding prediction and a distributional regularizer maes2026lewm . Its predictive objective aligns predicted embeddings with those of future observations, but does not explicitly identify or prioritize control-relevant physical information. Recent approaches introduce physical supervision to make this information explicit. PhyLatent zeng2025phylatent grounds individual latents in physical states, while PSG-JEPA yan2026psgjepa also supervises state changes between latent pairs (Figure~ fig:temporal_grounding_teaser A). Physical state estimation can also draw on information distributed across time, but these grounding heads do not explicitly accumulate this temporal context. For action selection, many JEPA-based world models zhou2025dinowm,assran2025vjepa2,maes2026lewm adopt model predictive control with the cross-entropy method (CEM). Conventional CEM refines a generic proposal distribution through online elite updates, without directly incorporating behavioral priors learned from offline trajectories (Figure~ fig:temporal_grounding_teaser B). Under a limited candidate budget, this can leave task-relevant action sequences insufficiently represented in the candidate set. To this end, we propose -JEPA , which incorporates temporal context into physical grounding for latent world models and combines the learned models with prior-guided action planning. The shared temporal physical grounding module is built on S4D gu2022s4d , a diagonal structured state-space model. Its observation and prediction branches separately aggregate temporal context from encoded observations and action-conditioned predicted latents through causal updates to estimate the corresponding physical states (Figure~ fig:temporal_grounding_teaser C). Physical state supervision on both branches complements latent matching, guiding the encoder and predictor to retain task-relevant physical information. Nuisance-invariant representation learning further reduces sensitivity to appearance variations that preserve physical states. We then freeze the world model and learn a conditional generative action prior from offline trajectories to propose action sequences based on the current and goal latent representations. These proposals are mixed with Gaussian CEM candidates and evaluated using the same latent objective (Figure~ fig:temporal_grounding_teaser D). A shared elite set updates the Gaussian search distribution, connecting the learned action prior with online refinement. After action execution, the updated observation conditions the next round of proposal generation and planning. Our contributions are: We introduce temporal physical grounding for JEPA world models. A shared causal S4D module aggregates context within observation and prediction sequences, using physical state supervision to jointly guide representation learning and latent prediction. We develop prior-guided action planning that integrates a learned latent-conditioned action prior with Gaussian CEM. Unified world-model scoring and shared elite updates connect offline behavioral priors with model-based online refinement. We evaluate -JEPA on PushT and OGBench Cube through planning comparisons and ablations of physical grounding and action selection, with additional PushT evaluations at increasing goal distances. The results support the effectiveness of combining temporal physical grounding with prior-guided action proposals for JEPA planning. Related Work and Background sec:related_work Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures sec:related_world_models JEPA has been applied to image representation learning with I-JEPA assran2023ijepa , video understanding with V-JEPA bardes2024vjepa , vision-language tasks with VL-JEPA chen2025vljepa , and robotic control with VLA-JEPA sun2026vlajepa . Building on V-JEPA 2 assran2025vjepa2 , pretrained on over one million hours of internet video, V-JEPA 2.1 murlabadia2026vjepa21 improves fine-grained visual understanding for tasks such as depth estimation, object tracking, and robotic planning. LeWM maes2026lewm introduces a lightweight JEPA world model trained end to end from pixels for action-conditioned prediction and planning. Subsequent work incorporates physical supervision, temporal progress, and online adaptation to strengthen these predictive models. PhyLatent zeng2025phylatent combines physical state grounding of encoded and predicted latents with appearance invariance and counterfactual dynamics constraints. PSG-JEPA yan2026psgjepa grounds individual latents in robot proprioceptive states and latent pairs in multi-horizon joint-angle changes. Beyond physical state supervision, TD-JEPA bai2026temporaldistancejepa learns directed temporal progress from offline trajectories to shape representations and planning costs, while AdaJEPA wang2026adajepa adapts the world model using newly observed transitions during planning. Our work introduces temporal aggregation into physical grounding and integrates learned action proposals with model-based online refinement. Structured State-Space Models sec:ssm_background Structured state-space models provide a framework for modeling temporal dependencies with compact recurrent memory. HiPPO gu2020hippo formulates online history compression through projections onto polynomial bases. S4 gu2022s4 develops structured state-space layers for long-range sequence modeling, while S4D gu2022s4d simplifies their parameterization through diagonal state transitions. More recent architectures, including Mamba-2 dao2024mamba2 , Gated DeltaNet yang2025gateddeltanet , and Gated DeltaNet-2 hatamizadeh2026gateddeltanet2 , further explore efficient sequence modeling with recurrent memory. We use a shared S4D module to aggregate temporal context separately within observation and prediction sequences for physical state estimation. Diffusion Policies and Model-Based Planning sec:related_diffusion_planning Diffusion models have been used for both action generation and trajectory planning. Diffusion Policy chi2024diffusionpolicy learns observation-conditioned action sequences for robotic manipulation, while Diffuser janner2022diffuser generates trajectories guided by goals or rewards. Further work combines diffusion-generated candidates with online planning. D-MPC zhou2025diffusionmpc learns separate diffusion models for action proposals and future dynamics, using predicted outcomes to select actions within an MPC loop. Diffusion-ES yang2024diffusiones combines trajectory generation with evolutionary search for autonomous driving. More closely related to hybrid planning, MODIP elasri2026modip mixes diffusion proposals with Gaussian candidates for latent model predictive control and uses the resulting trajectories to improve the policy. Our approach combines proposals from a learned latent-conditioned action prior with Gaussian CEM candidates, evaluated by a physically grounded JEPA world model using a latent goal-matching objective. The action prior remains fixed, while a shared elite set updates the Gaussian sampling distribution for online refinement. title: Learning from Automatic 3D Gaussian Splatting Edits for Online Bayesian Scene Change Detection
summary: Online scene change detection requires integrating incoming observations to determine which regions have changed relative to a reference scene. We update change beliefs as new images arrive using generalised Bayesian evidence fusion. However, the prior probability of change and evidence models are unknown beforehand, and numerical Bayesian inference can be costly. We address these challenges by learning offline from automatic edits to a reference 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model. These edits generate labelled training views without manual annotations. Together with unchanged reference observations, they provide supervision for learning scene-specific evidence models and estimating the effective pixel prior and response statistics. Online prediction combines current evidence with historical support, while closed-form local Bayes factors, parameterized by the learned response statistics, update an accumulated 3D Gaussian field. Object-guided refinement produces the final change masks. Our method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on PASLCD and CCS3D, with $67.64\%$ and $75.82\%$ mIoU, respectively. On PASLCD, the complete pipeline runs at $17.2$\,FPS over complete query sequences, the fastest among the evaluated online methods.
