Introduction sec:introduction Scene change detection identifies physical changes in an environment from images captured at different times. When captures follow different camera trajectories, viewpoint and visibility differences complicate direct image comparison lu2025gs3dcd,wu2026scenediff . A reference 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model kerbl2023gaussians enables rendering the earlier scene at query viewpoints, providing a common view for comparison. Recent methods, such as MV3DCD galappaththige2025mv3dcd and O-SCD galappaththige2026oscd , integrate multi-view change cues by optimizing per-Gaussian change parameters, using batch and online processing, respectively. In O-SCD, processing each new image requires iterative optimization using current and replayed observations, adding computational overhead during online inference. However, updating predictions as new evidence arrives does not inherently require repeated parameter optimization. This motivates updating change beliefs as new images arrive. Generalised Bayesian inference bissiri2016general provides a framework to combine a prior probability of change with incoming evidence. Putting this idea into practice requires a prior and models that translate image differences into change evidence, which are unknown beforehand. We estimate these quantities offline using automatic reference 3DGS edits and unchanged observations. The edits turn the reference representation into a source of labelled training views, supporting scene-specific learning without manual change annotations. This reduces dependence on large labelled datasets for training a single evidence model across diverse scene appearances and changes. The learned evidence models also support efficient Bayesian evidence accumulation. Evaluating Bayesian evidence can require numerical integration or sampling kass1995bayesfactors , adding substantial cost when repeated for incoming frames. We apply the learned evidence models to unchanged reference observations to estimate response statistics, which parameterize a local Bayesian model that admits closed-form Bayes factors. We combine current evidence with historical support for prediction and use these Bayes factors to update the accumulated field for subsequent queries. These updates require neither online backpropagation nor past-image replay. Finally, object-guided refinement sharpens boundaries and completes missed object regions. Our method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on PASLCD and CCS3D, with and mIoU, respectively. On PASLCD, it outperforms O-SCD Online by mIoU points while running at \,FPS, compared with \,FPS for O-SCD Online. Without refinement, the pixel output achieves mIoU at \,FPS. Our complete method also exceeds GS-Diff's reported mIoU galappaththige2026gsdiff without requiring a post-change reconstruction. Given an existing reference reconstruction, automatic editing and model fitting take approximately 3.6 minutes per PASLCD instance on average. Related Work sec:related Scene change detection. Image-pair methods identify changes through correspondence and appearance comparison. GeSCF uses SAM features and mask matching without task-specific training kim2025gescd , while SceneDiff compares objects across before--after captures using semantic and geometric information wu2026scenediff . A reference 3D representation additionally enables comparisons at matched viewpoints and integration across observations. 3DGS-CD associates image-level detections across views lu2025gs3dcd , and SCaR-3D combines change cues through multi-view voting and pruning zhou2026scar3d . MV3DCD optimizes Gaussian change channels from a collection of post-change images galappaththige2025mv3dcd ; O-SCD extends this approach to streaming queries, updating change parameters using current and replayed observations galappaththige2026oscd . CL-Splats uses detected changes to guide local updates of a Gaussian scene representation ackermann2025clsplats . GS-Diff instead compares geometry and colour between independently reconstructed scene states galappaththige2026gsdiff . Our method accumulates evidence on the reference Gaussians without online optimization or past-image replay. Learning from synthetic changes and 3D editing. CYWS constructs training pairs from object segmentation data sachdeva2023cyws , while CYWS-3D generates paired observations from synthetic 3D scenes sachdeva2023cyws3d . Both use synthetic supervision to train change detectors that generalize to unseen scenes, requiring training data to cover diverse scene appearances and changes. Advances in 3DGS segmentation ye2024gaussiangrouping,zhu2025unifiedlift , editing chen2024gaussianeditor,lee2025editsplat , and relighting liang2024gsir,gao2024relightable enable controlled scene modifications. RoboSplat edits Gaussian scenes and varies their appearance to train robot policies yang2025robosplat , while zanjani2025gaussiandata insert Gaussian objects into driving scenes to train 3D detectors. Given a prebuilt reference 3DGS and its associated unchanged observations, we generate labelled changes through automatic edits and fit scene-specific evidence models and a prior offline. This allows learning to focus on the appearance and response statistics of each reference scene, rather than requiring a single evidence model to cover many different environments. Bayesian evidence accumulation. Bayesian updates provide a way to combine successive observations with existing beliefs. In scene mapping, POCD updates probabilistic object states using geometric and semantic information to track changes and maintain volumetric maps qian2022pocd . bissiri2016general provide a generalised Bayesian framework that connects observations to belief updates through a loss function. For online time-series changepoint detection, altamirano2023robust construct generalised Bayesian updates with closed-form posterior parameters using diffusion score matching. We apply generalised Bayesian prediction to scene change detection, using offline-learned response statistics to evaluate local Bayes factors in closed form for accumulation on reference Gaussians. title: KoalaGS: Complexity-Aware Continuous Level of Detail for Gaussian Splatting
summary: Deploying a trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scene under shrinking compute budgets requires one primitive set to remain effective when rendered at smaller prefixes. In this continuous level of detail (LoD) setting, the challenge is to decide which Gaussians should retain capacity as the budget decreases. A pilot study on 3DGS-MCMC reconstructions shows that image complexity, computed from the input views before optimization, predicts where reconstruction error concentrates in image and 3D space. It also reveals that simple regions contain too many Gaussians and degrade as much as complex ones at lower budgets, despite being inherently cheaper to represent. Subsequently, in KoalaGS, during training we use this complexity prior to bias relocation toward poorly reconstructed areas while ensuring smooth degradation across LoDs. A primitive importance score then enables inference at low-capacity, while preserving the scene structure. Tested across three datasets, KoalaGS maintains competitive full-capacity quality while significantly improving quality across the budget spectrum, yielding smoother transitions across LoDs, and enabling faster progressive streaming.

A pilot study on 3DGS-MCMC reconstructions shows that image complexity, computed from the input views before optimization, predicts where reconstruction error concentrates in image and 3D space. It also reveals that simple regions contain too many Gaussians and degrade as much as complex ones at lower budgets, despite being inherently cheaper to represent. Subsequently, in KoalaGS, during training we use this complexity prior to bias relocation toward poorly reconstructed areas while ensuring smooth degradation across LoDs. A primitive importance score then enables inference at low-capacity, while preserving the scene structure. Tested across three datasets, KoalaGS maintains competitive full-capacity quality while significantly improving quality across the budget spectrum, yielding smoother transitions across LoDs, and enabling faster progressive streaming. Introduction sec:intro 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl20233dgs (3DGS) has made neural scene representations practical for novel view synthesis in real time. As the representation has matured, deployment under heterogeneous bandwidth and compute budgets has motivated a growing line of work on continuous level of detail (LoD) for 3DGS, where a single Gaussian set must remain useful when only a leading prefix of its primitives is retained~ guo2026matryoshka, cheng2026clodgs, milef2025clod3dgs . The central problem in this setting is determining which primitives should retain capacity as the budget shrinks. Existing methods answer it implicitly, ranking primitives by opacity~ guo2026matryoshka or by learned importance scores~ liu2025flexgs . A structural property of the representation suggests a complementary signal. A Gaussian does not contribute equally throughout a scene, as a single primitive may account for a broad region of nearly uniform appearance yet resolve only a fraction of a visually intricate one. We contend that this spatial variation in the value of capacity is what a continuous LoD policy should exploit, and we show that it can be anticipated from the input views alone. We investigate this claim through a pilot study. Prior work already showed that global image complexity predicts reconstruction error in neural scene representations~ beche2025claravid ; however, continuous LoD requires a localized signal that identifies not only which views are difficult, but where that difficulty lies within the scene. We therefore measure the correlation between local image complexity and reconstruction quality in the 2D image plane and, after multiview projection, on the Gaussian primitives. The correlation persists across DL3DV~ ling2024dl3dv and multiple complexity functionals in both domains, supporting complexity as a spatial prior for reconstruction difficulty that is available before optimization. We then examine how 3DGS-MCMC allocates capacity with respect to this structure. Gaussian density increases with complexity, approximately exponentially in regions of high complexity, yet even visually simple regions are represented by many low-opacity Gaussians. Under truncation according to opacity, quality degrades at comparable rates in simple and complex regions, showing that opacity alone does not expose the spatial redundancy required for robust continuous LoD. Together, these observations expose a mismatch between how 3DGS-MCMC allocates capacity at full budget and how effectively that allocation is preserved under truncation. Our continuous LoD method for Gaussian Splatting addresses this mismatch. The key insight is that image complexity, which is predictive of reconstruction error, provides an inexpensive spatial prior for allocating capacity and selecting primitives as the budget shrinks. During optimization, a relocation rule biased by complexity steers primitives toward difficult regions, while at inference an importance score modulated by complexity preserves broad primitives in simple regions and relies primarily on opacity in complex ones. A residual variance objective further discourages an abrupt degradation as the budget shrinks. We evaluate the resulting representation along three complementary axes. Our method matches the best baselines at full capacity, while outperforming all continuous LoD baselines across the budget spectrum, even in extremely low budget ( ). We show that this has great practical implication in streaming context, where our method improves drastically the time-to-quality performance. We summarize our contributions as follows: [leftmargin=1.7em] A pilot study on 140 DL3DV scenes showing image complexity predicts where reconstruction error concentrates, while capacity is allocated in a form that truncation cannot preserve. A continuous LoD method combining relocation biased by complexity during training, importance scoring modulated by complexity at inference, and a residual variance objective that discourages localized degradation across budgets. An evaluation of fixed budget quality, integrated spectrum quality, and transition variance, together with a streaming study showing a better time-to-quality tradeoff. Related Work sec:rel_work Gaussian Splatting. 3D Gaussian Splatting transformed neural rendering by using an explicit set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives optimized for visibility-aware rasterization, enabling high-fidelity novel view synthesis at real-time frame rates kerbl20233dgs . A large body of literature focuses on making this representation more stable, efficient, and deployable. On the optimization side, kheradmand20243dgsmcmc reformulates densification as probabilistic sampling over primitives, lu2024scaffoldgs introduces structured view-adaptive anchors, niemeyer2025radsplat incorporates radiance-field-informed optimization for robust high-speed rendering, while mallick2024taming,fang2024minisplat,kotovenko2025edgs reduce training cost or remove expensive densification mechanisms under constrained budgets. A complementary papantonakis2024reduce3dgs,fan2024lightgaussian line compresses the trained representation itself, reducing memory footprint and rendering cost to make Gaussian scenes practical on resource-constrained devices. In parallel, other works huang20242dgs, held2025trianglegs, held2025trianglegsp revisit the primitive parameterization, replacing or constraining 3DGS with 2D variants to improve geometric fidelity and compatibility with classical graphics pipelines. The flexibility of this representation also enables applications beyond static novel view synthesis, including dynamic scene modeling luiten2023dynamic,wu20244dgs , progressive and adaptive streaming shi2025lapisgs,sun2025dynamiclapisgs , mesh reconstruction guedon2024sugar , or higher-level scene understanding through language grounding, segmentation, and editing qin2024langsplat,ye2024gaussiangroupping . Altogether, these works establish 3DGS as a general explicit scene representation. Our work employs 3DGS for deployment under heterogeneous primitive budgets, exposing image complexity as a spatial prior over both densification and ranking. Level of Detail in Gaussian Splatting. A growing body of work ports classical Level of Detail hoppe1996progressivemeshes into the splatting pipeline. A first category imposes explicit hierarchies over the primitive set and exposes a small number of discrete operating points~ ren2025octreegs, kerbl2024hierarchical, seo2025flod , with spatial divide and conquer variants scaling to kilometer sized captures~ liu2024citygaussian, lin2024vastgaussian, kulhanek2025lodge . A second category approximates multi budget behavior through compression and importance pruning at varying targets~ fang2024minisplat,fan2024lightgaussian , where each operating point is optimized independently and a new model must be retrained for every budget. A third category pursues continuous LoD over a single primitive set: cheng2026clodgs, milef2025clod3dgs learn per Gaussian distance dependent opacity decay, while FlexGS~ liu2025flexgs learns a differentiable budget conditioned selector that achieves strong quality at targeted budgets but requires a fresh forward pass at every LoD change, precluding progressive streaming. Closer to our setting, Matryoshka-GS~ guo2026matryoshka introduces a nested prefix renderable ordering trained via stochastic budget sampling, so that any leading slice yields a coherent reconstruction. Our work belongs to this last category but departs from prior approaches in how the ordering is determined: we introduce image complexity as a scene side spatial prior over both densification and ranking, and train for spatial uniformity of the residual between full capacity and prefix renders. Pilot Study sec:pilot This section studies image complexity as a predictor of 3DGS reconstruction quality, computed from the input views before any optimization. The outcomes will shape our method, which must decide where to spend capacity at the moment when reconstruction error, the signal that would otherwise guide it, is not yet available. The intuition is that deploying under a primitive budget is a spatial decision. As primitives are withdrawn, some regions tolerate the loss while others do not, so the capacity that remains should sit where reconstruction error concentrates. Image complexity addresses this, since prior work~ beche2025claravid shows that it predicts reconstruction error and is read from the input images before optimization rather than recovered after training. What that work leaves open is whether the signal is spatial, since an image level score ranks views by difficulty but not where the error lies within them. We therefore investigate two questions: (i) Does complexity localize reconstruction error in space, across the image plane and the 3D world? (ii) Are trained models already allocating capacity where complexity predicts it should? For experimental details we refer to Sec.~ sec:supp_implementation:pilot_study . Does complexity spatially correlate with reconstruction error? title: MindView: Benchmarking Generative Multi-View Spatial Intelligence
summary: Spatial intelligence has recently been assessed through generative tasks such as spatially grounded image editing, yet language-guided generation of spatially consistent views from partial multi-view observations remains underexplored. We introduce MindView, a benchmark for generative multi-view spatial intelligence with 1,500 samples from 513 scenes across three indoor datasets. Its seven tasks form two families: geometry-dominant tasks specify changes in camera position and orientation, while semantics-dominant tasks require inferring target viewpoints by grounding referred objects and interpreting spatial relations and reference-frame cues. Evaluation of eleven generators reveals substantial room for improvement on MindView. A paired context analysis further shows that all eleven generators obtain lower overall scores under the expanded context setting. These findings motivate us to investigate whether task-specific supervision can improve target-view generation and whether models can use additional multi-view evidence effectively. We therefore fine-tune BAGEL on the MindView training dataset, improving its overall score by 24.3 points and yielding gains across all seven MindView tasks. Beyond these generation gains, the fine-tuned model also yields higher scores on three spatial-understanding benchmarks without training on their annotations, suggesting that learning to generate spatially grounded views may benefit spatial understanding. To improve evidence utilization under expanded context, we propose MindCue, a training-free spatial evidence selector guided by a target-view hypothesis. MindCue reverses the drop in overall score under expanded context and outperforms the standard-context baseline. Overall, MindView provides a concrete testbed for generative multi-view spatial intelligence.

strategies for improving performance in this setting.\ Introduction Benchmarks such as MindCube , MMSI-Bench , and SAT-v2 evaluate the spatial intelligence of multimodal understanding models through question answering.\ On the generation side, GenSpace and GSI-Bench have begun this exploration by asking whether spatial instructions are realized in a generated or edited image.\ We focus on across views, infer the requested viewpoint, and predict what would be visible from it while remaining consistent with the observed scene.\ Related work differs in how reference images are used and how target viewpoints are specified.\ Multi-reference benchmarks such as MICE-Bench and MultiBanana emphasize preserving and combining reference content, which alone does not establish that a Related Work Spatial Intelligence Benchmarks and Generative Reasoning. Spatial intelligence is evaluated through both question answering and image generation.\ MindCube , MMSI-Bench , and SAT-v2 assess spatial understanding through question answering, whereas GenSpace and GSI-Bench evaluate whether generated images satisfy spatial instructions.\ The latter also reports understanding gains from generation-focused training.\ Thinking with Novel Views uses generated views for spatial question answering, while UniG2U-Bench examines unified models' understanding and the effects of intermediate image generation.\ MindView evaluates generated views of observed scenes and tests whether target-view supervision aids spatial understanding.\ Novel-View Synthesis and Viewpoint Control. View generation methods differ in target-view specification, from explicit camera parameters to language instructions.\ NeRF , ZeroNVS , EscherNet , and LVSM use supplied camera controls.\ CapFrame grounds language-specified viewpoints within a reconstructed 3D Gaussian scene, while Object-Uni uses explicit object poses for controllable generation.\ Astra generates language-guided imagined views for spatial question answering and also evaluates them against real targets.\ Existing methods either rely on explicit geometry or consider constrained language-specified viewpoints, leaving viewpoint inference and scene-consistent rendering from partial multi-view evidence underexplored.\ Multi-Reference Image Generation and Editing. title: AEON: Unifying Video and 3D World Models
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026. Project Page: https://weiqi-zhang.github.io/AEON
summary: Current world models for explicit world simulation typically follow two distinct pathways: (1) video generative models (e.g., Sora), which simulate realistic appearances but fail to preserve 3D consistency; and (2) 3D generative models (e.g., Marble), which generate geometrically consistent scenes but often yield static, less realistic observations. We present AEON, a unified framework that bridges video-based and 3D-based world models and combines the benefits of both. The key insight of AEON lies in a generative model that operates within the text- or image-conditioned video latent space while producing renderable 4D graphics primitives---specifically, 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS)---as the explicit world representation. We train a 4D reconstruction model to predict both 4DGS and camera poses from monocular videos, serving as our initialized 4D decoder. Furthermore, we design a domain adapter that translates generative video latents into reconstructive 4D latents through a distillation process on the video VAE. AEON naturally supports video-based world modeling by rendering 4DGS at predicted camera trajectories, and constructs a persistent 4D environment with scene dynamics for realistic world simulation. Consequently, AEON empowers a diverse range of world modeling applications and achieves state-of-the-art performance on standard benchmarks. Project Page: https://weiqi-zhang.github.io/AEON

Introduction sec:introduction World modeling has rapidly advanced to the forefront of AI research, driven by its immense potential in embodied AI, autonomous driving, and game design. Despite this progress, there remains a lack of consensus on the optimal representation for explicit world simulation, leaving the field divided between two dominant paradigms: video-based~ openaisora2024,wan2025wan and 3D-based world models~ worldlabsmarble,hy2026hy . As highlighted in Table~ tab:comparison , these approaches possess orthogonal strengths and suffer from fundamental, paradigm-specific bottlenecks. Consequently, a more powerful and unified representation is imperative to achieve comprehensive world modeling. We begin by asking a fundamental question: What constitutes a good world model? To train robots to understand physical laws and perceive scenes, a world model should exhibit the following properties: (1) generating realistic appearances that align with real-world domains; (2) modeling dynamic scene evolution (e.g., fire, waves) and moving objects; (3) maintaining 3D consistent environments free from geometric ambiguity; (4) ensuring scene persistence for continuous and repeatable simulation; and (5) supporting real-time exploration to facilitate efficient interaction. We argue that a representation unifying video- and 3D-based world models, thereby benefiting from their complementary strengths, is the key to achieving such an ideal world model. We present AEON, a generative world model that introduces 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS)~ wang2025freetimegs,yangreal as its foundational representation, unifying video and 3D models to benefit from both paradigms. 4DGS represents scenes as a set of explicit graphics primitives localized in spatial geometry, and models scene dynamics through the velocity-driven movement and time-varying visibility of these primitives. Consequently, a learned 4DGS representation provides two independent yet crucial capabilities: it models world appearances through direct rendering along user-defined camera trajectories, and it establishes a persistent 4D environment that supports highly controllable 3D simulations. Additionally, it enables explicit modeling of world geometry and physical states, including depth, normals, motion, and optical flow. Despite the comprehensive capabilities inherent to the 4DGS representation, most existing approaches restrict its application to reconstruction tasks, and generating a persistent 4DGS world directly from text or image conditions remains largely unexplored. In AEON, we propose a novel framework that integrates the generative latent space of a pretrained video Diffusion Transformer (DiT)~ wan2025wan,peebles2023scalable with the reconstructive latent space of a 4D reconstruction model. Specifically, we train a 4D Gaussian Reconstruction Model (4DRM) to jointly predict 4DGS attributes and camera poses from monocular videos. By utilizing a large-scale annotated 4D video dataset and pretrained geometric priors from MapAnything~ keetha2025mapanything , a scalable geometry model, the 4DRM develops robust reconstructive capabilities to recover world geometry and dynamics. A primary challenge, however, is the significant domain gap between the video and 4DRM latent spaces. We address this by introducing a domain adapter that seamlessly bridges the two. Finally, we employ a multi-stage training pipeline that optimizes the adapter and fine-tunes the reconstruction model through end-to-end distillation from the video model, supervised by video VAE-decoded outputs. Consequently, AEON unlocks an extensive array of world modeling applications, including text/image/video-to-4DGS generation, 3D world generation, robotics simulation, physical state estimation (e.g., depth, normals, and optical flow), scene editing, and novel view and timestep synthesis. Our main contributions can be summarized as follows: We introduce AEON, a unified world modeling framework that represents worlds as explicit 4D Gaussians, effectively bridging video-based and 3D-based models to benefit from their complementary strengths. We propose a novel methodology that integrates the generative latent space of a pretrained video DiT with the reconstructive latent space of a 4D Gaussian reconstruction model. To achieve this, we train a specialized domain adapter through an end-to-end distillation of the video model. AEON demonstrates comprehensive versatility, natively supporting a diverse spectrum of world modeling tasks, and establishes new state-of-the-art results on standard benchmarks. Related Work Video and 3D World Models World modeling aims to generate explorable and realistic environments from conditional inputs (e.g., text or images), serving as a foundation for embodied AI and autonomous systems. Current paradigms primarily rely on video-based~ openaisora2024,veo22025,ren2025gen3c,kuaishou2024kling,cogvideox,wan2025wan or 3D-based~ worldlabsmarble,team2025hunyuanworld,yang2025matrix,hy2026hy,shen2026lyra,bahmani2026lyra,go2025vist3a approaches. Within the video-centric domain, JEPA-style methods~ assran2023self,assran2025v excel at forecasting future latent states but lack explicit visual synthesis. Conversely, video world models~ openaisora2024,wan2025wan,kuaishou2024kling and their action-conditioned variants~ bruce2024genie,wang2026matrix,team2026inspatio,team2026advancing can synthesize photorealistic frames, yet they struggle with 3D consistency and incur heavy computational costs due to massive per-frame token generation. Alternatively, 3D world models~ worldlabsmarble,hy2026hy construct explicit environments for simulation. Recent works have explored panoramic generation~ team2025hunyuanworld,yang2025matrix , progressive expansion~ hy2026hy , or leveraging video priors~ bahmani2026lyra . However, these methods typically employ static representations such as 3DGS~ kerbl20233dgs or meshes, precluding the modeling of world dynamics and limiting their ability to scale on dynamic internet video datasets. The same holds for 3D generation and reconstruction more broadly, which mostly build on static Gaussians~ zhou2024diffgs,zhang2025gap,zhang2026gaussiangrow,zhang2025materialrefgs,xiang2026vggs or distance fields~ zhou2024udiff,zhou2026udfstudio,noda2025bijective,noda2024multipull . To bridge this gap, we propose AEON, a framework that generates renderable 4D Gaussian Splatting~ yangreal,wang2025freetimegs (4DGS) primitives as an explicit world representation. AEON effectively unifies the strengths of both paradigms, achieving dynamic modeling with 3D consistency while overcoming their respective limitations. 4D Gaussian Splatting from Videos 4D Gaussian Splatting~ yangreal,wang2025freetimegs advances the success of 3D Gaussian Splatting~ kerbl20233dgs for modeling scene dynamics. 4DGS learns from multi-view videos to predict Gaussian primitives with explicit temporal attributes such as lifespan, velocity, and time-varying opacity, allowing Gaussians to appear, move, and vanish independently. However, predicting 4DGS from monocular videos remains significantly more challenging due to limited observational data. While optimization-based methods~ wang2025shape,lei2025mosca,sun2024splatter can achieve faithful visual appearances, they require lengthy fitting processes and struggle to generalize or scale. More recently, feed-forward frameworks~ ren2024l4gm,xu20254dgt,yang2026neoverse,lin2026movies,zhang2026gamma have been proposed for fast and scalable video-to-4DGS reconstruction, including bullet-time reconstruction at arbitrary timestamps~ liang2025btimer and online reconstruction from uncalibrated video streams~ wu2026streamsplat . Some of these works predict deformable 3DGS~ lin2026movies,pan2025diff4splat as their foundational representation, which often falls short when modeling complex and diverse dynamics. Related feed-forward models also recover dynamic geometry and camera poses from monocular videos~ fang2026more . All of these methods reconstruct scenes from observed videos. Native 4DGS generation has also been explored for animated objects~ zhang2026tesla . Closer to our setting, Diff4Splat~ pan2025diff4splat and Lyra~ bahmani2026lyra build Gaussian scenes on top of video diffusion priors, but both require a camera trajectory as input and represent dynamics with deformable 3DGS and per-frame 3DGS, respectively. AEON differs in both respects: it generates a world from a text prompt or a single image without camera input, and it represents the world as one persistent set of 4D primitives, each with its own reference time, duration, and velocity, so that content can appear, move, and vanish independently and can be rendered at any continuous timestep. sec:relat Method sec:method We present AEON, a generative world model that operates within the latent space of a pretrained video diffusion model while producing explicit 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) as the world representation. Given a text prompt or conditioning image, our goal is to generate a set of 4D Gaussians encoding both appearance and dynamics, enabling photorealistic rendering and persistent 3D simulation. The overview of AEON is shown in Fig.~ fig:pipeline . We begin by introducing the 4DGS representation in Sec.~ sec:3.1 , which models dynamic scenes through velocity-driven motion and time-varying visibility. In Sec.~ sec:3.2 , we present the 4D Gaussian Reconstruction Model, whose four task-specific heads jointly predict depth, Gaussian appearance, dynamic evolution, and camera poses from monocular videos. We then describe our domain adapter in Sec.~ sec:3.3 , which bridges the generative video latent space and the reconstructive 4D latent space through distillation. Finally, Sec.~ sec:3.4 details our multi-stage training strategy that optimizes the full pipeline end-to-end. 4D Gaussian Splatting as the World Representation sec:3.1 An ideal world model should jointly capture realistic appearances, scene dynamics, and 3D-consistent geometry within a persistent and efficiently renderable representation. To this end, AEON adopts 4D Gaussian primitives~ wang2025freetimegs,yangreal,zhang2026gamma as its foundational scene representation, where each primitive simultaneously encodes geometry, appearance, and temporal evolution.
